SEC1-01.title: A Read role gets the full running configuration, secrets included, from MCP `kcc_rci_read` and the Web explorer
SEC1-01.rule: project rule (d) "Secrets … never reach … tool results"
SEC1-01.impact: Take an API key created exactly as the README shows (`kcc apikey create claude --role viewer`), or a prompt-injected agent using it. It calls `kcc_rci_read {"catalog_path":"show running-config","path":["show","running-config"]}` and receives every `ns3` blob and any plain-text secret the configuration holds (e.g. `community`, `obfs-key`). The data then goes to the model provider. A Web viewer gets the same through the explorer. Both bypass `RevealSecrets`.
SEC1-01.fix: Treat `show running-config` (and any other raw read that returns configuration text) as secret-bearing. Either require `RevealSecrets`, or parse the reply with `kcc_config` and run `secrets::redact` before shaping, on both surfaces.
SEC1-01.reasoning: `show running-config` is in the catalog with `kind: Show`. It is not on the destructive or management lists, so `risk()` gives `Risk::Read`. MCP `rci_read` checks only `authorize_host(Permission::Read, …)`, and the Web explorer route and handler need only `command_permissions(Risk::Read) = [Read]`. `RciResponse::from_value` keeps the whole JSON value. MCP `redact_secrets` and Web `mask` both match on key names only, and text bodies are shown verbatim, so configuration lines under any non-secret key such as `message` pass through unchanged. Web `reveal` (RevealSecrets) only controls name-based masking, so it gives no protection here. Every other path to the same text redacts it or needs RevealSecrets: firewall read redacts the AST, explorer preview uses `redact`/`ns3_redacted`, and the full backup download needs RevealSecrets. The configuration does hold plain-text secrets as well as ns3 blobs (the `secrets.rs` test fixture has `web-api password delta`).

SEC1-02.title: Anyone can grow the audit log by 1 MiB per failed login, filling the disk and stopping `kcc serve`
SEC1-02.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §10 "Validate and sanitize all external input at system boundaries", "Length limits" (line 2738)
SEC1-02.impact: An unauthenticated LAN client first does a GET on `/ui/login` for a cookie and CSRF token, then POSTs logins whose username is about 1 MiB. Each one appends a hash-chained entry of about 1 MiB. Within hours the disk fills; the audit writer then dies and `server_shutdown.rs:45-57` stops the server. Before that, `/ui/admin/audit` loads the whole log into memory on every view (`admin_audit.rs:340-364`).
SEC1-02.fix: Reject or truncate the username at the login boundary (the account name rules are short, e.g. ≤64 bytes) before authentication and audit, and bound `Actor.id` in `AuditEvent`.
SEC1-02.reasoning: `LoginForm.username` is an unbounded `String`. An unknown user goes through dummy Argon2 to `Authentication::Invalid`, then `login_failure`, then `audit(…, &username, …)`, and finally `Actor::new(ActorKind::Web, username.to_owned())`, which is `const` and copies the name unchanged. Nothing between the 1 MiB body limit and the audit writer bounds the size. The lockout counter applies only to existing accounts, so it never stops this. Rotation does not delete live data, retention is age-based (365 days), and when the writer closes, `serve_until_shutdown` stops the server. The admin audit view and export load and verify the whole log.

SEC1-03.title: Behind the documented HTTPS reverse proxy, the session cookie has no `Secure` flag and no `__Host-` prefix
SEC1-03.rule: project rule (e) "Web UI hardening"; overlay http-services "DO: Set OWASP-recommended HTTP response headers"
SEC1-03.impact: Take the supported setup: `public_url = "https://kcc.lan"` with `trusted_proxies`, and kcc listening on plain HTTP behind the proxy. A LAN attacker who can make the browser load any `http://kcc.lan/...` URL (injected ``, ARP-spoofed HTTP) receives the admin's `kcc_session` in cleartext. Cookies are not bound to a port, so any HTTP service on that host also receives it. Without `__Host-`, a network attacker can also plant a session cookie.
SEC1-03.fix: Choose `CookieSecurity::Tls`, and the TLS CSP, when the listener has TLS *or* `web.public_url` is `https`. Pass that decision from `Config` instead of recomputing `tls` in `server.rs`.
SEC1-03.correction: Exploiting this needs an active or observing network attacker and a browser making a plain-HTTP request to that host. It also applies only to the HTTPS-proxy mode, not to the shipped Podman example, which uses listener TLS. The control is weakened, not fully defeated, so medium rather than high. The fix stands: derive `CookieSecurity` and the CSP from `tls || public_url.scheme == "https"`, computed once in `Config`.
SEC1-03.reasoning: The code matches the finding. `tls` is derived only from `tls_cert_path`/`tls_key_path`, and `CookieSecurity::LoopbackHttp` is used whenever it is false. `web_allowed_origins` explicitly allows a non-loopback Web UI with `public_url` https plus `trusted_proxies` and no listener TLS, and that mode is documented. In that mode the cookie is `kcc_session=…; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict`, with no `Secure` and no `__Host-` prefix. No other code path chooses `CookieSecurity::Tls`.

SEC1-04.title: MCP secret redaction misses hyphenated and short secret keys that the Web masks
SEC1-04.rule: project rule (d); BRIEF anti-pattern "copy-paste duplication that drifts"
SEC1-04.impact: `"private-key"` does not contain `"private_key"` (hyphen versus underscore). A `kcc_rci_read` of a WireGuard or SNMP node that returns `{"private-key": …}` or `{"community": …}` reaches the MCP client unmasked, although `docs/PRIVACY.md` says "MCP tools never reveal secrets".
SEC1-04.fix: Move one classifier (the Web's `is_secret`, with `-`/`_` normalised) into a shared crate, e.g. `kcc-config` or `kcc-catalog`, and use it in both `mask` and `redact_secrets`.
SEC1-04.reasoning: The MCP list matches by substring on `private_key` with an underscore, while the catalog arguments are `private-key`, `obfs-key`, `preshare-key` (which contains neither `preshared` nor `psk`) and `community`. None of these is redacted by MCP. The Web catches all four through `-key` and the exact `community`, so the two classifiers have drifted, and PRIVACY.md promises "private key … always replaced". `shape()` is the only redaction applied to `kcc_rci_read` results, including GETs of setting nodes.

SEC1-05.title: Disabling an account or resetting its password from the CLI does not end its Web sessions
SEC1-05.impact: In incident response, an operator runs `kcc user disable mallory` or resets the password on the host. Mallory's open browser session keeps full access for up to 12 h (`session_absolute`), with the 30 min idle timer refreshed by every request.
SEC1-05.fix: In `authentication_middleware`, re-check the account's `disabled` flag and a password/role generation counter from `AccountStore` (it can be cached briefly), and drop the session on mismatch.
SEC1-05.reasoning: The middleware checks only that the session exists and that its role name still resolves. It never checks whether the account still exists, is enabled, or has changed its password. `invalidate_user` is called only from `admin_users.rs`. The SIGHUP `reload` reloads roles and keys but not sessions or accounts, and the CLI runs as a separate process with no channel to `kcc serve`. SECURITY.md:106-107 says "a password or role change ends the account's other sessions", and that does not hold for CLI changes.

SEC1-06.title: Open event streams keep sending data after logout, account disable or role reduction
SEC1-06.impact: A user whose role is reduced, who is disabled in the Web UI (`invalidate_user`), or who logs out in another tab keeps receiving router logs, traffic and fleet status on streams already open (up to 4 per session) until the TCP connection closes.
SEC1-06.fix: Have `guarded` end the stream when the session is gone, e.g. a `sessions().peek(id)` check per event or every N seconds, or a cancellation token fired by `invalidate*`. Also cap the stream's total lifetime.
SEC1-06.reasoning: Authorization runs once, when the stream opens. `guarded` only forwards events while it holds the permit. The `invalidate*` functions only remove HashMap entries and signal nothing to open streams, and the stream limiter is not tied to session validity. Streams have no lifetime cap.

SEC1-07.title: Every login-page GET without a valid cookie creates a new anonymous session, with no cap
SEC1-07.impact: An unauthenticated client gets 600 sessions per minute per IP, about 18,000 per IP for each 30-minute idle window. With many source addresses (an IPv6 /64), memory and the time `retain` holds the global `RwLock` grow without bound, slowing every authenticated request.
SEC1-07.fix: Cap anonymous sessions (global and per client IP), give them a short idle timeout (e.g. 5 min), or use a stateless signed pre-auth CSRF token for the login form.
SEC1-07.reasoning: A GET with no cookie, and every failed POST without a live session, calls `create_anonymous()`, which is an unconditional insert. Sessions are evicted only by the idle sweeper, which runs every `min(idle, absolute)/2`, i.e. 15 minutes by default. The only bound is the kit's per-IP limit of 600/min. One IPv4 client stays around 18k sessions (a few MB), but a LAN client using many IPv6 addresses is effectively unbounded.

SEC1-08.title: The audit log page and export ignore the viewer's router scope
SEC1-08.impact: A custom auditor role scoped to `lab-*` sees and exports audit entries for every router: actions, targets, router URLs and logins from `router.profile_*` params, and client names. This contradicts the per-router scope model used everywhere else.
SEC1-08.fix: Drop entries whose `router` is set and outside `user.role().router_scope` (`scope_matches`), in both `page` and `export`. If global audit visibility is intended, document it as an owner decision.
SEC1-08.correction: Treat this as a decision. Either filter entries by `scope_matches(role.router_scope, entry.router)` in `page` and `export`, or document ViewAudit as fleet-wide.
SEC1-08.reasoning: The code does what the finding says: `/ui/admin/audit*` maps to ViewAudit with no router, and `Filter::matches` never consults `router_scope`. But SECURITY.md defines scope as a check "before any router request". Reading the audit log is not a router request, and like ManageUsers it lives in the global admin area. Neither code nor docs say ViewAudit is router-scoped, so this is an undocumented design gap rather than a broken control. Secret values are already excluded from audit params.

SEC1-09.title: A failed router edit leaves the new credential sealed for the old profile
SEC1-09.impact: An admin moves router `a` to a new URL and types the new router's password. If `registry().update` fails (a state write error, or a scope change in between), the sealed `a` password is already overwritten while the profile still points at the old URL. The next poll sends the new router's password to the old router, which also fails sign-in and can trip the router's own lockout.
SEC1-09.fix: Seal to a temporary path and rename after `update` succeeds, or restore the previous sealed record when `update` fails.
SEC1-09.correction: The ndw2/ndw4 sign-in is challenge-response (SECURITY.md:89-90), so in password mode the new password is not disclosed to the old router. The consequence is failed sign-ins and possible lockout on the old router. Only the token mode might send the secret, and I did not verify that.
SEC1-09.reasoning: The bug is real. `seal` writes to `store.sealed_path(id, kind)`, a fixed path per router and credential kind, before `registry().update`, and nothing rolls it back on failure (`create` does roll back). `update` can still fail after the handler's checks: a state I/O error, `NotFound` after a concurrent delete, `ConfigDefined` after a concurrent SIGHUP, or `profile.validate()`. Because the client cache is cleared only on success, a later sign-in uses the new secret against the old URL.

SEC1-10.title: HTML is passed around as plain `String` and rendered with `|safe`, against "askama auto-escaping only, no bypass"
SEC1-10.rule: project rule (e) "askama auto-escaping only, no bypass"
SEC1-10.impact: Every producer I checked passes pre-rendered askama output (`request::rendered`), so this is not exploitable today. But the type `String` cannot tell markup from router text: one future `changed(outcome, None, Some(router_text), …)` is stored XSS from a hostile router reply, and the compiler will not catch it.
SEC1-10.fix: Add a `Markup(String)` newtype whose only constructor is `rendered(&impl Template)`. Make these fields `Option<Markup>` so `|safe` applies only to that type.
SEC1-10.correction: The fix stands: a `Markup` newtype that only `rendered()` can construct. Severity is low because no producer of unescaped text exists today.
SEC1-10.reasoning: Rule (e) says "askama auto-escaping only, no bypass", and there are 29 `|safe` uses carried in plain `Option<String>` fields. No deviation entry covers this. Every producer I traced (`Changed::new`, `with_report`) passes `request::rendered(&impl Template)` output, which askama has already escaped. No XSS is shown; the cost is latent and only type-level.

SEC1-11.title: Login timing reveals disabled or locked accounts; all logins are serialised on the users file
SEC1-11.impact: An attacker sends `max_failures`+1 bad logins for a guessed name. A fast final reply shows the account exists (and the attempts lock it). Because each attempt does Argon2 inside the `users.json` update (INFERRED: `update` takes the file lock), a login flood also delays every legitimate login and account change.
SEC1-11.fix: Run the dummy verification on the disabled and locked paths too, and do Argon2 outside `state.update`: read, verify, then update the counters.
SEC1-11.reasoning: An unknown user runs dummy Argon2, but `disabled` and an active `Locked` return before any Argon2. That timing gap lets an attacker tell disabled or locked accounts apart from unknown ones. `StateStore::update` holds the file lock across the closure, so Argon2 runs under the lock, and it rewrites `users.json` on every login attempt, including attempts for unknown users. That serializes all logins and account changes.

SEC1-12.title: A self-service password change keeps the current session id
SEC1-12.impact: A user who changes their password because they suspect their session cookie was stolen does not evict the attacker who holds that same cookie.
SEC1-12.fix: Call `rotate_privilege` (new id and CSRF token) on every successful password change and set the new cookie.
SEC1-12.reasoning: A normal password change calls `invalidate_other_user_sessions(&username, current.id())` and keeps the same id. Only the forced-change path calls `rotate_privilege`.

SEC1-13.title: `app.js` carries review-process labels and three copies of the same swap override
SEC1-13.impact: The labels mean nothing to a maintainer. The three status overrides (422, 413 with `HX-Retarget`, 403 with `HX-Retarget`) live in three places, so a change to swap policy must be made three times.
SEC1-13.fix: Remove the labels. Merge into one `beforeSwap` handler with a status table.
SEC1-13.reasoning: The comments `todo 44/36/37/39/70/121` are review-process labels. Three separate `htmx:beforeSwap` listeners each set `shouldSwap=true; isError=false` for 422, for 413 with `HX-Retarget`, and for 403 with `HX-Retarget`.

SEC1-14.title: Route-table scope checks use the raw path, handlers use the decoded one
SEC1-14.impact: Today this can only refuse (`/ui/r/%68ome/...` is denied for a `home`-only scope). It would bypass scope for a glob whose literals contain `%`/hex digits, and only if a handler stopped re-checking.
SEC1-14.fix: Percent-decode the segment before `registry::authorize`, or rely only on the handler check.
SEC1-14.reasoning: `router_scope` takes the raw segment, while handlers use the decoded `Path`. `context::target` rejects anything failing `is_profile_id` and re-checks scope through `lookup`, so a percent-encoded id can only be refused. There is no bypass today.

SEC2-01.title: Router and log-sink HTTP clients honour HTTP(S)_PROXY / ALL_PROXY, bypassing the resolved-IP policy
SEC2-01.rule: overlay project rule (a) "the resolved address must fall inside allowed_networks"; http-services SSRF rule
SEC2-01.impact:
When kcc runs with `HTTP_PROXY` set (common on corporate hosts and in containers), every router request goes to the proxy instead of the pinned address.
  - That includes the ndw2 login hash, session cookie, `/ci/startup-config.txt` with ns3 secrets, and writes.
  - The `allowed_networks` and metadata checks are run against an address that is never connected to.
  - The proxy resolves the name itself, so the DNS pin is lost.
  - For `http://` routers the proxy sees everything in clear text.
SEC2-01.fix: Add `.no_proxy()` in `OutboundPolicy::pinned_builder` and in both sink builders. If proxies must be supported, make that an explicit per-sink setting.
SEC2-01.reasoning:
`auto_sys_proxy` defaults to true. `build()` adds `ProxyMatcher::system()`, which reads `ALL_PROXY`, `HTTP(S)_PROXY` and `NO_PROXY`. There is no localhost exclusion, and the CGI check only suppresses `HTTP_PROXY`. The repo calls `.no_proxy()` exactly once, in `tls.rs:102`. Nothing scrubs proxy variables: the only `remove_var`/`env_clear` hits are unrelated. `resolve_to_addrs` only overrides DNS for the router host, so with a proxy the TCP connection goes to the proxy, and the `allows()` check is made against an address that is never dialled.
- Nuance: for `https` routers the CONNECT tunnel keeps TLS verify or pin end-to-end, so the proxy sees only host:port. The clear-text exposure (ndw2 hash, cookie, `startup-config` with ns3) is for `http://` routers, which is the usual LAN case. With an IP-literal router such as `192.168.1.1`, the proxy connects to that address on its own network, which can be a different router. A loopback `http` log sink would also go through the proxy.

SEC2-02.title: Free-text catalog values go unquoted into router CLI lines (MCP and CLI reachable)
SEC2-02.rule: project rule (b) "validated against the catalog and the identifier validators before it reaches a router"
SEC2-02.impact:
- A name with a space (common, for example "Anna phone") produces extra router arguments, so the command fails or is misparsed.
  - A prompt-injected MCP agent can choose the tokens after a fixed prefix. For example `name="Home range 10.0.0.2 10.0.0.3"` becomes a different `ip dhcp pool Home …` subcommand, while the audit log and risk classification record the validated `ip dhcp pool` name.
  - The MCP `access` op on an unregistered client with no `value` sends `known host  <mac>` (empty name).
SEC2-02.fix: Pass these values through `cli_token::quoted` (names and free text) or `cli_token::validate` (keys, ids), as `interfaces.rs`, `mesh.rs` and `wan/render.rs` already do. Consider making `CliCommand::new` re-run `validate_cli` on the rendered line.
SEC2-02.reasoning:
- **Catalog types.** `known host` name, `ip dhcp pool` name, `ip dhcp host` host, `interface wireguard peer` key and every `wireguard asc` field are typed `String`, and `valid_argument` only checks `is_string()`.
  - **MCP input.** `text()` checks only length (1-256 characters) and control characters.
  - **Sending.** A non-template `CliCommand::expose_for_send` sends the line verbatim after the same control-character check, and `apply_cli` passes it to `client.parse(line)`. Spaces therefore become extra router CLI tokens, which the router splits on whitespace and protects only inside double quotes. This is why `cli_token::quoted` exists.
  - **Rule (b).** The rule requires "the identifier validators" for tool and CLI arguments, and they are not applied on these paths.
  - **Mitigation.** Injection is limited to tokens after a fixed prefix at the same permission. For VPN lines, `classify_generated` still checks the first interface token for management risk.

SEC2-03.title: A profile with a read-only login opens a new router session (and ndw4 Argon2) on every poll and never logs out
SEC2-03.impact:
- Each poll performs a full login: 1-2 fresh router sessions every 15 s per router, never closed.
  - On ndw4 firmware each login runs an Argon2 derivation with router-chosen cost under the single global permit (`ndw4_keys.rs:18`), which delays every other router's login.
  - This floods the router's login log. INFERRED: it may exhaust the router's session table and block the admin's own UI logins.
SEC2-03.fix: Cache the read-only client per id like `client()` does (invalidate on reload/update), and use it in both `poll_client` and `poll_info`.
SEC2-03.reasoning: When `read_login` is set, `poll_client` builds a new `RciClient` on every call. `fetch` calls it every light round, and `fetch_heavy` calls `poll_info` → `poll_client` again. The ndw4 key cache is per manager, so each new client runs Argon2 under the global semaphore. `logout()` exists but no drop path calls it. The router-side session-table effect is still unverified, as the reviewer says.

SEC2-04.title: One torn or partial audit line permanently stops the audit writer and stops `kcc serve` from starting
SEC2-04.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES error handling (recoverability of persisted state)
SEC2-04.impact:
1. A disk full or crash during `write_all` (`audit.rs:621-624`) leaves a partial JSON line.
  2. The writer stops at once, and every later change is refused because `require_alive` fails.
  3. After a restart, `AuditLog::spawn` fails on the same line, so the server does not start until someone edits `audit.jsonl` by hand.
SEC2-04.fix: Treat an unterminated last line of the active file as torn. Truncate it, or move it to a quarantine file and log that, before verifying. Do this both in `spawn_with_policy` and before each append.
SEC2-04.reasoning: `verify_files` rejects any line that does not parse, and it runs in both `spawn_with_policy` and every `append_locked`. A failed `write_all` (ENOSPC or a crash) can leave a partial line. The writer then stops, `require_alive` refuses router work, and the next start fails at `AuditLog::spawn`. `SECURITY.md:325-327` says `kcc serve` exits non-zero "so its supervisor can restart it". The torn line turns that recovery into a crash loop that needs a manual edit. Neither BACKLOG nor the owner decisions cover it.

SEC2-05.title: Every audit append re-reads and re-hashes the entire retained chain (O(N) per entry)
SEC2-05.impact: Cost grows with a year of audit data, multiplied by the number of appends. Logins, forbidden attempts and each change append. Once hundreds of MB are retained, each append takes seconds while holding the cross-process lock, and change receipts time out into "pending".
SEC2-05.fix: Verify the full chain only at startup or `kcc audit verify`. Before each append, read only the tail of the active file (or the last rotated file when the active one is empty) to get `seq` and `prev_hash`.
SEC2-05.reasoning: Each `append_locked` lists all rotated files plus the active one, parses every line, recomputes each canonical hash, and holds all entries in a `Vec`. This happens under the cross-process lock. With a 365-day retention and 50 MiB rotation, the cost per append grows with the whole retained log. Failed Web logins are audited too (`kcc-web/src/auth.rs:363`), so even rate-limited traffic grows it. The docs say the writer "re-read[s] its tail", but the code re-reads everything.

SEC2-06.title: `OutboundPolicy::default()` is permissive, and public migration entry points connect with it plus loopback
SEC2-06.rule: project rule (a); AI anti-pattern "dead code shipped in production"
SEC2-06.impact: These are `pub` APIs. Any future caller ignores the operator's `allowed_networks` and adds loopback. A secure-looking default (`RciClient::connect`) quietly admits all private space.
SEC2-06.fix: Make `OutboundPolicy::default()` deny everything (empty lists, matching settings). Delete the unused `from_live`/`load_source`/`InventoryClient::connect`, or make them take a `&OutboundPolicy`. Keep the permissive set behind a `#[cfg(test)]` helper.
SEC2-06.correction: This is latent dead code and a footgun, not a weakened control today. The fix is still sound: a deny-all `Default`, plus deleting the unused entry points or making them take `&OutboundPolicy`.
SEC2-06.reasoning: The code is as the finding describes: the default is permissive and `from_live`, `load_source` and `InventoryClient::connect` add loopback. However, there are no production callers. Grep finds only tests and `planner/buildability_tests.rs`. Every production `RciClientOptions::default()` (`registry.rs:304,754,772`) overwrites `outbound` with the operator policy, and `registry.rs:392-395` replaces the networks, suffixes and loopback. The README and CONFIG "empty by default" statement describes `[outbound]` in `kcc.toml`, which is accurate. Rule (h) says the crates are not a published library, so "a future caller" is a latent risk with no demonstrated consequence.

SEC2-07.title: Redaction registry blanks the IKE key name instead of the PSK, and misses ipsec-profile secrets
SEC2-07.rule: project rule (d) "secrets never reach … tool results"
SEC2-07.impact:
- When the router stores these values as plaintext words rather than `ns3`, they are shown to Read users. The affected surfaces are the explorer "stored lines" (`kcc-web/src/advanced/preview.rs:165`), presets and migration lines (`presets_page/lines.rs:30`, `migrate_wizard/analysis.rs:147`), downloads and MCP backups.
  - Those surfaces also mask `ns3` tokens, which protects only the ns3 form.
SEC2-07.fix: Map `crypto ike key` to `rest[1]` (the `psk`, accounting for `ns3`). Add `crypto ipsec profile _ preshared-key|xauth-password`. Fix the fixture to the real syntax.
SEC2-07.correction: This is a defect in the redaction registry, backstopped by ns3 masking. Raise it to medium only if live firmware is shown to store IKE or profile PSKs as plaintext words.
SEC2-07.reasoning: The registry bug is real. `["crypto","ike","key", rest @ ..]` → `argument_index` points at `rest[0]`, which is the key name. Nothing matches `crypto ipsec profile <n> preshared-key|xauth-password`, and the fixture `crypto ike key theta` pins the wrong shape. However, every surface I opened also masks all `Token::Ns3` payloads: preview, config text and download, preset lines (through `shown_line`), migration leftovers, MCP backups and the CLI redact. So exposure happens only if the firmware stores these PSKs as plain words, which is unverified. Also, `presets_page::lines::secret()` still flags the line as secret, because redacting the name changes the line.

SEC2-08.title: KNOWN-BACKLOG: one hostile LAN router can stall ndw4 logins for the whole fleet
SEC2-08.rule: project rule "router responses are untrusted input" (BRIEF trust boundaries)
SEC2-08.impact:
- BACKLOG calls this "derives one after another". The worse case is a compromised router, or a MITM on an `http://` router, answering every challenge with 256 MiB, t=64 and a fresh salt.
  - That holds the single global permit almost continuously; a cancelled derivation keeps the permit (detached).
  - Every other router's ndw4 login waits, and polls, changes and brackets time out. SEC2-03 makes logins frequent.
SEC2-08.fix: Lower the default memory cap to what real firmware uses. Bound iterations and memory per router id, or fail the router's login when it exceeds a per-router time budget.
SEC2-08.reasoning: The mechanism (one global Argon2 permit, so derivations run one after another across the fleet) is already `docs/BACKLOG.md:62`, and the reviewer labels it KNOWN-BACKLOG itself. The hostile-parameters angle is the same root cause. The cap is operator-tunable through `max_argon2_memory_kib` (8..=262144), and the reviewer's own derivation times are inferred. Under CRITIC rule 3 this is not a new finding. The adversarial angle could be added as a note to the backlog item.

SEC2-09.title: `RouterRegistry::client` holds the fleet-wide client mutex across DNS resolution and blocking file I/O
SEC2-09.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES async "no blocking in async / locks across await"
SEC2-09.impact: One router whose hostname resolves slowly (seconds to tens of seconds) stops `client()` for every other router. Every connect also runs `mkdir`+`chmod` and file reads on a runtime worker.
SEC2-09.fix: Build the client outside the lock with a per-id `OnceCell`, and move the credential reads into `spawn_blocking`.
SEC2-09.correction: Cite rule `:1112` (blocking I/O) and the head-of-line blocking, not lock-across-await.
SEC2-09.reasoning:
The guideline allows "use tokio::sync::Mutex if you must hold across await" (`RUST_GUIDELINES.md:1165`), and `clients` is a tokio mutex. The "locks across await" rule is therefore not violated. What holds:
  1. `client()` for every router is serialized behind one router's DNS resolution, which is `spawn_blocking` but awaited under the fleet mutex.
  2. `std::fs` reads plus `create_private_dir` (mkdir and chmod) run on a runtime worker (`credentials()` → `stored::secret` → `CredentialStore::open/directory`). This does violate "DON'T: Call blocking I/O in async functions" (`:1112`).

SEC2-10.title: IPv6-literal router URLs always fail the outbound policy
SEC2-10.impact: `http://[fd00::1]` is refused as `Policy`, even though the default networks include fd00::/8. This fails closed, but the error is misleading and no test covers it.
SEC2-10.fix: Use `parsed.host()` and match `Host::Ipv6`/`Ipv4` directly instead of resolving the bracketed text.
SEC2-10.reasoning: `host_str` returns the slice `host_start..host_end`, which for IPv6 includes the brackets. `RouterUrl` accepts `http://[fd00::1]`. `("[fd00::1]", port).to_socket_addrs()` does not parse as an IP and goes to the resolver, which fails, so the result is `RciError::Policy`. No repo test covers an IPv6 router. It fails closed.

SEC2-11.title: The metadata deny list misses other link-local cloud credential endpoints
SEC2-11.rule: project rule (a) "cloud-metadata addresses (169.254.169.254 and equivalents) are always refused"
SEC2-11.impact: If an operator allows 169.254.0.0/16 (link-local routers), kcc can still reach the AWS ECS task-credential endpoint 169.254.170.2 and the AWS DNS address 169.254.169.253.
SEC2-11.fix: Add 169.254.170.2 and 169.254.169.253 (and the ECS IPv6 equivalent), or always refuse 169.254.169.0/24 and 169.254.170.0/24.
SEC2-11.correction: Treat this as defence-in-depth hardening (also deny `169.254.170.2`). It does not open a credential-exfiltration path.
SEC2-11.reasoning:
The deny list is as described, and allowing `169.254.0.0/16` would admit `169.254.170.2`. Two things limit the impact:
  - `RouterUrl` is origin-only: the path must be `/`, with no query or userinfo, and kcc requests only fixed RCI and auth paths. The ECS credential endpoint needs a secret per-task path (`/v2/credentials/<id>`), so kcc cannot fetch credentials from it.
  - `169.254.169.253` is a DNS resolver, not an HTTP credential service. Reaching either also needs an admin-configured link-local allowlist.

SEC2-12.title: Every login attempt, including unknown users, rewrites and fsyncs `users.json` under its exclusive lock; disabled and locked accounts answer fast
SEC2-12.impact:
- Unauthenticated requests cause a disk write plus fsync and a serialized Argon2 each, under the per-IP rate limit.
  - A legitimate admin's login waits behind the queue.
  - Disabled or locked accounts skip Argon2, so response timing reveals them.
SEC2-12.fix: Run the Argon2 verification before taking the lock, and write only when counters change. Run the dummy hash for the disabled and locked branches too.
SEC2-12.correction: Drop the "locked answers fast" part. Keep the unconditional write, the Argon2 under the lock, and the timing leak for disabled accounts.
SEC2-12.reasoning: `authenticate` runs inside `StateStore::update`, which always calls `write_locked` (rewrite plus fsync), including for unknown users. Argon2 runs under the exclusive `users.json` lock. Disabled accounts skip Argon2 and get the same "invalid" response, so timing does reveal them. However, `Locked` already gets a distinct `"locked"` outcome in the response (`auth.rs:232-233`), so its timing reveals nothing extra.

SEC2-13.title: Preset records bypass the state store's private atomic writer
SEC2-13.rule: project overlay owner-only state; RUST_GUIDELINES reuse existing abstractions
SEC2-13.impact: After a crash a preset file can be empty or torn, and then `list` fails for every preset. Permissions differ from the rest of state.
SEC2-13.fix: Use `kcc_app::persist::write_atomic` and `create_private_dir`, as the credential and backup stores do. Skip and log a malformed record in `list`.
SEC2-13.correction: The impact is crash durability and `list` failing on a torn record. The fix needs a public atomic-write API on `StateStore` (or exporting the helper) before kcc-migrate can use it.
SEC2-13.reasoning: Durability gap confirmed: plain `fs::write`, no fsync and no directory sync, and `list` fails on the first malformed record (`read_record(...)?`). The permission part is weak. `StateStore::open` makes the state directory 0700 (`persist.rs:167`), so umask-mode files below it cannot be reached by other users, and the records are AEAD-sealed. The suggested fix is also not directly available: `write_atomic` and `create_private_dir` are `pub(crate)` in kcc-app.

SEC2-14.title: Log-sink clients have no timeouts, and the Elasticsearch reply body is unbounded
SEC2-14.rule: http-services "timeouts on every outbound client"; DoS bounds
SEC2-14.impact: A sink that accepts the connection and never answers stalls its delivery worker indefinitely, so logs pile up and are dropped. A misbehaving sink can return a huge body that is read fully into memory.
SEC2-14.fix: Set `connect_timeout` and `timeout` on both builders, and read the Bulk reply through a capped reader like `loki_reply::read_body`.
SEC2-14.reasoning: Neither builder sets `timeout` or `connect_timeout`, reqwest has no default timeout, and nothing wraps `client.send` in a timeout. `response.json::<BulkResponse>()` buffers the whole body, while Loki has a cap. Sinks are operator-configured, which keeps this low.

SEC2-15.title: `CredentialStore` path methods build paths from an unvalidated router id, and their docs say otherwise
SEC2-15.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES "validated constructors / newtypes"; comments that lie
SEC2-15.impact: Today registry ids are validated upstream, and the AEAD binding to the id prevents opening a planted file. A future caller passing `../x` would read outside `router-credentials/`. The doc promise is false.
SEC2-15.fix: Call `lock_name(router)?` (or take a `RouterId` newtype) at the top of every public method.
SEC2-15.reasoning: `open`, `exists`, `manages`, `sealed_path` and `legacy_path` join `router` into a path without calling `lock_name`. Their docs promise `CredentialError::Record` for an invalid id, which never happens. Today registry ids are validated upstream and the AEAD binding resists planted files, so this is a docs and robustness issue.

SEC2-16.title: Gaps in zeroizing decrypted and downloaded secrets
SEC2-16.rule: project rule (d) "Secrets live in secrecy/zeroize types"
SEC2-16.impact: Copies of plaintext configs and passwords stay in freed heap memory longer than the type contract promises.
SEC2-16.fix: Wrap the buffers in `Zeroizing<Vec<u8>>`. Pre-size `read_capped` from `Content-Length` or zeroize on growth.
SEC2-16.reasoning: On the error path, the decrypted `Vec` is dropped inside `FromUtf8Error` without zeroizing. ns3 `padded` and `bytes` are plain buffers. `read_capped` grows a plain `Vec` (realloc copies), and the upload does `expose_secret().to_vec()`. Some copies cannot be avoided (hyper and reqwest `Bytes`), which keeps this low.

SEC2-17.title: Two write and delete helpers follow symlinks with predictable temp names
SEC2-17.impact: When the output is placed in a shared writable directory, another local user can pre-create `<out>.kcc-tmp` as a symlink to overwrite the victim's files. Linux's `protected_symlinks` blocks this in sticky world-writable directories; macOS has no such protection. `secure_remove` is reachable only by the same user.
SEC2-17.fix: Open the temp file with `create_new(true)` and a random suffix (as `persist::write_atomic` does). Use `symlink_metadata` and `O_NOFOLLOW` in `secure_remove`.
SEC2-17.reasoning: With `fresh=false`, the code opens the predictable `path.with_extension("kcc-tmp")` with `create(true).truncate(true)`. That follows a planted symlink or reuses a planted regular file, and mode 0600 applies only on creation, so a file pre-created by someone else stays readable to them. `secure_remove` uses `fs::metadata` and opens without `O_NOFOLLOW`, but only inside the kcc-owned 0700 credentials directory. Linux `protected_symlinks`/`protected_regular` mitigate the problem in sticky directories.

SEC2-18.title: info: AEAD associated data has no record-type prefix for router passwords and account hashes
SEC2-18.impact: A router `home` and a user `home` share the associated data, so a sealed record can be moved between the two stores. This needs state write access and gains nothing today. Backups, presets and wizards already use prefixes.
SEC2-18.fix: Prefix with `router:` and `account:` (plus a migration step).
SEC2-18.reasoning: A router password record uses AD = the bare router id, and an account hash uses AD = the bare username, under the same key. Swapping records needs state write access and gains nothing: a router password would fail PHC parsing, and a PHC hash sent as a router password fails the login.

SEC2-19.title: info: The privilege floor ignores GID 0
SEC2-19.impact: `--user 1000:0` (the OpenShift style) runs with root-group file access.
SEC2-19.fix: Refuse GID 0 too, or at least log it.
SEC2-19.reasoning: Only `uids.contains(&0)` is checked. Note that OpenShift deliberately runs with GID 0, so the "log it" variant of the fix is the safe one.

SEC2-20.title: info: `MasterKey::load_or_create` forces the key file's parent directory to mode 0700
SEC2-20.impact: `KCC_MASTER_KEY_FILE=$HOME/kcc.key` with no file yet silently changes `$HOME` to 0700. A root-owned parent returns EPERM and startup fails.
SEC2-20.fix: Change the mode only on directories kcc creates itself.
SEC2-20.reasoning: `load_or_create` calls `create_private_dir(parent)`, which runs `set_permissions(0o700)` on an existing parent. For a custom `KCC_MASTER_KEY_FILE` path, that silently re-modes the parent, or fails with EPERM when the parent is owned by someone else.

A-01.title: `secrets::redact` misses router-written ns3 secrets and blanks the wrong word for `crypto ike key`
A-01.rule: project rule (d); RUST_GUIDELINES.md §13 "Testing quality" (the unit test checks shapes the router never writes)
A-01.impact:
- In the second arm group the computed index lands on the literal `ns3` word. `replace_expanded_word` only matches the payload slot, so the ns3 blob stays readable.
  - `crypto ike key office ns3 B any` gets index 3, so the key name `office` is replaced and the PSK blob is left.
  - `crypto ipsec profile … preshared-key|xauth-password` is not in the registry at all.
  - ns3 can be reversed with the public algorithm in `ns3::decode`.
  - Today nothing leaks only because consumers each re-mask every ns3 token. Copies are at `kcc/src/cli/redact.rs:54-63`, `kcc-mcp/src/config_tools/backups.rs:157-168`, `kcc-web/src/config_page/text.rs:64-74`, `kcc-web/src/advanced/preview.rs:258-266`, `kcc-migrate/src/presets/model.rs:198-205` and `kcc-testkit/src/anonymize.rs:298`. A new caller that trusts the function's doc ("every registered command secret replaced") would leak.
  - A plaintext PSK under `crypto ipsec profile` in an uploaded or preset file is redacted by no one (INFERRED that such text reaches a viewer).
  - The unit test (`secrets.rs:146-165`) uses `crypto ike key theta` and `ipsec preshared-key epsilon` without `ns3`, so it cannot catch this.
A-01.fix: Run every arm through `secret_after_kind`. Index `crypto ike key` past the name. Add `crypto ipsec profile _ preshared-key|xauth-password`. Mask all `Token::Ns3` payloads inside `redact` itself and delete the six consumer copies. Rebuild the test fixture from the `ns3` lines the testkit actually stores.
A-01.reasoning:
- I traced each case by hand. For `interface X ipsec preshared-key ns3 B`, the index is 4, which is the expanded `ns3` word. `replace_expanded_word` only matches `expanded+1` on an `Ns3` token, so nothing is replaced.
  - For `crypto ike key office ns3 B any`, the index is 3, so `office` is replaced.
  - `crypto ipsec profile … preshared-key|xauth-password` matches no registry arm.
  - Every consumer I found re-masks `Token::Ns3`, so router-written text does not leak today.
  - Plaintext input is still exposed, because consumers mask only ns3 tokens. A hand-written preset or upload line `crypto ike key office PLAINPSK any` keeps `PLAINPSK`.
  - The unit test's `crypto ike key theta` has no name argument, so it cannot catch this.

A-02.title: Cookie refresh writes any `Set-Cookie` into the current session, including on 401 and from requests sent with an older cookie
A-02.impact:
1. If a 401 carries `Set-Cookie: <name>=<new pending id>`, as the router's `/auth` challenge does, that unauthenticated cookie is installed. `reauthenticate_after` then sees a "different" cookie and skips login. The replay gets 401 and the caller sees `Http{401}`. Every later request repeats this until the local `Max-Age` (300 s) expires.
  2. Request R1 is sent with cookie A. Meanwhile R2 re-authenticates to cookie B. R1's sliding-refresh `Set-Cookie: A` then overwrites B with the dead A, which forces another login.
  3. A malformed matching cookie on a successful POST returns `Err(Auth)` even though the router already applied the change.
A-02.fix: Refresh only on non-401 responses, and only while the current cookie `same_cookie(&snapshot)`. Never turn a refresh-parse failure into an error on a response that was already applied.
A-02.reasoning:
- `refresh_session` runs before the 401 check. It overwrites the cookie value for any same-name `Set-Cookie`.
  - `reauthenticate_after` then sees a different cookie and skips login. The replay is sent with the unauthenticated cookie.
  - The R1/R2 overwrite also holds. A local `Max-Age` expiry starts a new login while the request with the old cookie A is still in flight, and its refresh writes A back over B.
  - Point 3 is more reachable than the finding implies. `parse_set_cookie` returns `Err(Auth(Rejected))` for an empty matching value (`:780-782`), so a `name=; Max-Age=0` clear on an applied POST turns success into an error.
  - The precondition, a real router sending `Set-Cookie` on 401 or a cookie-clearing header, is still unverified.

A-03.title: `RciClient::show` drops the query on the POST fallback and caches the path as POST-only
A-03.impact: Callers pass queries: `kcc-app/src/poller.rs:444` uses `show(&show/interface/stat, &[("name", id)])`, and `kcc-mcp/src/generic/rci.rs:204` uses the agent's `input.value`. If GET answers 404 once, the POST is sent with `{}` and no `name`, so the unfiltered answer is returned as if it were the filtered one. The path is then cached POST-only for the client's lifetime, so every later query on it is ignored too. The poller would store the same unfiltered stats for every WAN id.
A-03.fix: POST the serialized query as the body: build the POST body from `query` (`serde_json::to_value(query)`) instead of `{}`, or refuse the fallback when the query is not empty.
A-03.reasoning:
- The fallback POSTs `{}` and drops `query`.
  - The cache key is `path.to_string()` only, so after one 404 every later query on that path goes unfiltered POST.
  - The poller, MCP, CLI and Web all pass non-empty queries to `show`.
  - Which resources answer 404 to GET is inferred; for example, an unknown `name` might.

A-04.title: `batch` never checks the reply length and drops completed chunks on a later error
A-04.impact:
- If the router returns fewer elements than the chunk had, the missing items count as neither succeeded nor failed, and the change is reported as fully applied.
  - Extra elements shift which item each result belongs to, across chunks.
  - A transport error on chunk 2 returns `Err` for the whole call, so the caller cannot tell that chunk 1 was already applied.
  - `stop_on_error` cuts off the results of items the router already ran in the same POST.
A-04.fix: Return `Decode` (or a typed partial error that carries the results so far) when `values.len() != chunk.len()`. On a mid-batch failure, return the completed results together with the error.
A-04.correction: Drop the `stop_on_error` impact. The concrete consequence is an applied but unaudited multi-chunk batch on a later-chunk failure, plus silent miscounting if the reply is short.
A-04.reasoning:
- There is no length check, and `completion` zips, so missing items count as neither succeeded nor failed.
  - A transport error on chunk 2 makes `apply_batch` return through `?` at `:1059-1064` before the audit record (`:1089-1098`). Chunk 1 is then applied and unaudited. This needs a batch over 900 KiB.
  - The `stop_on_error` bullet is unreachable: nothing in the workspace sets it, and it defaults to `false`.
  - A router replying with a short array is unverified.

A-05.title: Status items that do not fully deserialize are dropped, so error-level replies count as success
A-05.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §10 "Validate and sanitize all external input at system boundaries"
A-05.impact: An item like `{"status":"error","code":7405600,...}` (numeric code), or one missing `message`, or carrying an unknown level, fails to deserialize and is skipped. `RciResponse::from_value` then returns `Ok`. A rejected raw or batch write is reported as applied (`workflow_batch::completion` counts it as succeeded). Curated writes are read back; raw writes are not.
A-05.fix: Decide the level from the `status` member alone. Make `code`, `ident` and `message` lenient (string or number, optional). Treat any unrecognized level as an error.
A-05.correction: This is defense-in-depth. Decide the level from `status` alone and treat unknown levels as errors. The claim that rejected writes are reported as applied is inferred only.
A-05.reasoning:
- The code fails open as described. An item that does not deserialize is skipped, and `from_value` returns `Ok`.
  - Every fixture and the documented router format use a string `code` and the levels message, warning and error. Nothing shows a firmware sending a numeric code, a missing `message` or another level.
  - So this is a weakened boundary check with no demonstrated trigger.

A-06.title: Tab-indented config text quietly flattens nested commands to the top level
A-06.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §10 "Validate … external input at system boundaries"
A-06.impact: `interface Bridge0\n\tip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0` produces two top-level nodes. `flatten` then emits a bare `interface Bridge0` and a root-level `ip address …` instead of a `ParseError`. A tab-indented migration source or preset (uploaded or hand-edited) is restructured without any warning. Whether the result hits a valid root command depends on the catalog (INFERRED).
A-06.fix: Return `InvalidIndent` (or a new variant) when the leading whitespace contains anything other than `' '`.
A-06.correction: The issue is real; it is a minor bug on a rare input. Reject non-space leading whitespace.
A-06.reasoning:
- `trim_start_matches(' ')` leaves a leading tab, so `spaces == 0` and the line becomes top-level. `tokenize` then skips the tab as whitespace.
  - Router-generated text never contains tabs. Only hand-edited uploads or presets do.
  - Orphaned children usually fail catalog lookup and show up as unsupported in the plan or preview, so this is not silent. The only valid stray command is the bare context line, for example `interface Bridge0`.
  - No lockout or wrong-router command is demonstrated.

A-07.title: Every background operation logs in afresh and never logs out
A-07.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §5 "Audit Drop impls of async resources"
A-07.impact:
- Each `start()` (every diagnostic and every continued log read in `kcc-domain/src/diagnostics.rs:174,209`) does its own DNS lookup and builds a new HTTP client.
  - It also starts a new `Manager` with an empty ndw4 key cache. On ndw4 routers that means a full Argon2id derivation under the global single permit, stalling logins to every other router.
  - The router session is never released (INFERRED: router session-table pressure).
  - User cancellation is reported as `Timeout`.
  - The process id from the router is put into the URL without encoding.
A-07.fix: Reuse the parent's key cache (or `Arc<Cache>`). Call `logout` when the Handle finishes or is dropped (from a spawned task). Use `encode_query(&[("id", &process_id)])`. Add a distinct cancellation error.

A-08.title: DELETE risk is not enforced by the catalog; three frontends patch it themselves
A-08.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §3 "Use the newtype pattern / validated constructors" (the invariant should live in the type); BRIEF anti-pattern "copy-paste duplication that drifts"
A-08.impact: `validate("ip hotspot host", Delete, {"mac":…})` comes back as `Write`, while the same removal written as `{"no":true}` is `Destructive`. Every caller has to remember `.max(Destructive)`; one that forgets lets a Write-only role delete.
A-08.fix: In `ValidatedRequest::capture`, raise the risk to `Destructive` when `method == Delete`, then drop the three frontend patches.
A-08.reasoning:
- `capture` ignores `method`. Only `interface` DELETE is raised to destructive.
  - The repo's own test (`removals_have_the_delete_risk_floor`) asserts `deleted.risk.max(Risk::Destructive)`, so raising the floor at the call site is deliberate.
  - Every raw DELETE caller applies it. Curated DELETEs authorize through `request.permission`, not `validated.risk`.
  - No current bypass exists. The cost is duplication that may drift, and the cited newtype rule is a stretch.

A-09.title: Digest proxy state is not safe under concurrent requests
A-09.impact: Two requests that get 401 each build a fresh `Challenge` with `count = 0`, and the last one overwrites shared state that another task may have advanced. If the proxy reuses the nonce, `nc` values repeat. The replay then gets 401, which maps straight to `Err(Auth(Rejected))`: concurrent requests through KeenDNS fail spuriously with "authentication failed". It also uses `|_| RciError::Transport`, so timeouts are lost (see A-15).
A-09.fix: Under the lock, reuse the stored challenge when the nonce is the same; otherwise replace it. Do not reset the count for an identical nonce.
A-09.reasoning:
- The race exists: two 401s each build `count = 0` and the last writer wins.
  - A spurious `Err(Auth(Rejected))` needs two unverified things: the proxy reuses the nonce across 401s, and it enforces strictly increasing `nc` even though each request sends a fresh random `cnonce`.
  - The path is only used in DigestProxy (KeenDNS) mode, under the default concurrency of 2.

A-10.title: Secret bytes are copied into buffers that are never zeroized
A-10.impact: Plaintext router configs, PSKs and passwords stay in freed heap memory; anyone who can read process memory or a core dump recovers them.
A-10.fix: Read into `Zeroizing<Vec<u8>>` with a capacity reserved up front. Pass `Bytes` built from the secret without an extra copy. Zeroize ns3 buffers on every path. Move the value into `capture` instead of cloning it.
A-10.correction: Limit the finding to `read_capped` (and `SecretSlice::from(Vec)`, which can reallocate), the multipart `to_vec`, and the ns3 error path.
A-10.reasoning:
- These parts hold:
    - `read_capped` grows a plain `Vec`, so each reallocation frees an unwiped copy of config bytes.
    - `Part::bytes(…to_vec())` copies the startup config without zeroizing.
    - ns3 `decode` drops the plaintext `bytes` unwiped on the `InvalidUtf8` path.
  - Two sub-claims are wrong:
    - `runtime.rs` `value.clone()` moves straight into `SecretValue::new`, which takes the secret leaves into `SecretString`. The replaced `request.protected` is then dropped through that type.
    - `session.rs:622` sends the ndw2 response digest, which is bound to the challenge, not the reusable password.

A-11.title: Unbounded edit-distance work on attacker-controlled field names
A-11.impact: An MCP or Web request whose root object has a 1 MB unknown key computes a ~1M×(len+1) matrix for each of about 100 root siblings. That is seconds of synchronous CPU on a Tokio worker per request (bounded only by the frontend body limit, INFERRED).
A-11.fix: Skip the suggestion when `field.len()` exceeds the longest sibling plus 2, which already guarantees a distance above 2.
A-11.reasoning:
- The MCP value cap is 900 KiB, so a single key of about 900k characters passes. `nearest` then builds a full matrix per sibling: roughly 900k by 15 cells of 8 bytes, about 100 MB each, sequentially, in synchronous code.
  - Any role with `Read` can reach this through `rci_read`.
  - BACKLOG:63 covers only the hand-written helper, not this bound.

A-12.title: `connect_bootstrap_with` loses the observer, and request accounting differs per method
A-12.impact: Self-metrics under-count logins and requests (bootstrap logins, batches, config downloads are invisible), and bootstrap logins bypass the per-router concurrency budget.
A-12.fix: Chain `.with_observer(client.options.observer.clone())` in bootstrap and background sessions. Route all request paths through one helper that takes the permit and reports.
A-12.correction: Missing login metrics are limited to bootstrap and background sessions.
A-12.reasoning:
- The bootstrap and background managers have no observer. `is_bootstrap` logs in without a permit. Only `send` reports request outcomes.
  - One correction: `batch`, `download_config` and `upload` use `self.session`, which has the observer, so their logins are reported. Only their per-request outcomes are missing.

A-13.title: `OutboundPolicy::default()` is permissive, contrary to the documented "empty by default"
A-13.impact: Any caller that does not override all three fields (the registry does, at `kcc-app/src/registry.rs:392-395`) contacts LAN, CGNAT, loopback and cloud-suffix hosts that the operator never allowed.
A-13.fix: Make `Default` deny-all. Keep the current lists as an explicit named constructor for tests.
A-13.reasoning:
- `Default` is permissive, and README's "empty by default" refers to `kcc.toml`, which the registry respects by overriding all three fields.
  - `InventoryClient::connect`, `SourceConfig::from_live`/`load_source` and `RciClient::connect` have no production caller; only tests and the testkit capture tool use them.
  - So no production frontend reaches the permissive policy. It is a latent public-API trap against rule (a).

A-14.title: Router-controlled Argon2 iterations are not capped locally
A-14.impact: Before mutual authentication, any LAN host answering as a router can demand 64 passes over 256 MiB per login. With the single global permit, that stalls ndw4 logins to every router. A-07 multiplies the effect.
A-14.fix: Add a local `max_argon2_iterations` (or a combined memory×iterations budget) to `Options` and refuse with `CostTooHigh`.
A-14.reasoning:
- `iter` is accepted in `1..=64` and only memory is compared with `cap`, so a responding host can demand 64 passes over 256 MiB.
  - BACKLOG:62 covers the single permit but not the missing iteration cap, so this part is new.

A-15.title: Timeout errors are mapped differently on each auth path
A-15.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §2 "Propagate errors with `?`" (keep the error type intact)
A-15.impact: Under token, digest or ndw4 auth, a read timeout is reported and labelled (`RequestOutcome::Transport`) as a transport failure, so the user sees the wrong error.
A-15.reasoning:
- The mapping is inconsistent as described. However, `RequestOutcome::of` maps both `Transport` and `Timeout` to `Transport`, so the metric label does not change.
  - Only the error the user sees, Transport instead of Timeout, is wrong.

A-16.title: Duplicated magic numbers and helpers
A-16.impact: Changing any of these limits requires editing every copy, and a missed copy leaves the code paths enforcing different values (e.g. a raised response cap that `detect` keeps refusing).
A-16.fix: One shared constant or helper per item, exported from the owning crate.
A-16.reasoning:
- All the duplicates exist, and `detect` ignores the configured `response_bytes`.
  - The `secret_value.rs` lines are actually 30 and 285. The file has 296 lines, so the cited `:545` cannot exist.

A-17.title: Dead or speculative API shipped in production
A-17.rule: BRIEF §4 "dead or test-only code shipped", "defensive checks inside trusted code"
A-17.impact: Maintenance surface, plus traps: a future caller of `Manager::connect` loses its TLS pin.
A-17.fix: Delete them, or move them to `#[cfg(test)]` or testkit.
A-17.correction: Losing the TLS pin means a refused connection, not a weakened one.
A-17.reasoning:
- Every item is as described. `Manager::connect*` is used only by tests in several crates.
  - The trap is overstated: `TlsMode::Verify` against a pinned self-signed router fails closed. A future caller would get a connection error, not lose security.

A-18.title: Cancel-safety comments contradict each other
A-18.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §5 "Annotate every async fn with cancel safety"
A-18.impact: The annotations carry no reliable information; someone putting `is_bootstrap` or `detect` inside a `select!` cannot trust them.
A-18.fix: Use one rule: a cancelled login that leaves only a remote session is or is not cancel-safe, chosen once. Correct the callers to match the callees.
A-18.reasoning:
- `is_bootstrap` says "cancel-safe" but calls `ensure_session`, which is marked "NOT cancel-safe".
  - `get` says "cancel-safe" for the same reason that `ensure_session` gives for being NOT cancel-safe (an interrupted re-authentication is recovered by the next call).
  - The DNS-only builders are marked NOT cancel-safe while saying nothing partial happens.

A-19.title: `FirmwareVersion` mixes derived equality with hand-written ordering
A-19.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §3 "DON'T: Mix manual and derived comparison impls" (line 663)
A-19.impact: The two agree today, but the rule exists so that adding a field (e.g. a build suffix) cannot make them disagree without the compiler noticing. Here the manual impl is identical to `derive(Ord)` anyway.
A-19.fix: `#[derive(PartialOrd, Ord)]` and delete the manual impls.
A-19.reasoning:
- It is a mix of manual and derived impls, but the manual `Ord` compares every field in declaration order, so it equals `derive(Ord)` and agrees with the derived `Eq`.
  - The rule's hazard is an inconsistency, and none exists today.

A-20.title: Generated argument types fall back to an unconstrained `String`
A-20.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §3 "Use exhaustive match – avoid wildcard catch-all"
A-20.impact: A new or renamed generator type (e.g. `Password2`, `Ipv6Mask`) silently loses validation and secret protection instead of failing to load.
A-20.fix: Map `"String" | "Filename"` explicitly and return `InvalidGeneratedCatalog` for unknown types.
A-20.correction: The lines are `data.rs:198-207`. Return an error for unknown strings instead of citing the enum rule.
A-20.reasoning:
- The `_ => ArgumentKind::String` fallback exists and catches `String` and `Filename`.
  - The cited rule is about wildcard arms over enums; this is a string match, where a catch-all is unavoidable.
  - The generator emits a closed `ValueType` set, so drift needs a code change in xtask. It is still a real cross-workspace drift risk.

A-21.title: Tests that cannot fail, duplicated scenarios, and source-grep tests
A-21.impact: Green tests that pin nothing (two cannot fail at all), plus a source-grep check that `.pointer(&format!(..))` evades.
A-21.fix: Delete the tautology, the duplicate and the const pin. Replace the grep with a type-level guard (already present per its own header).
A-21.correction: Only one test cannot fail (the tautology). Keep the cookie-name pin.
A-21.reasoning:
- `print(parse(x)) == normalize(x)` is a tautology, and the ns3 length test duplicates `rejects_invalid_length`. The idempotence assertion next to it is not a tautology.
  - The i18n pin is at `:141-144`, `COOKIE_NAME == "kcc_lang"`. It does fail on a rename and guards a machine-consumed cookie contract, so it is not "cannot fail".
  - The catalog background test adds catalog validation of the start, poll and stop methods, so it only partly duplicates the RCI test.
  - The source-grep test describes itself as a backup guard behind a type-level one.

A-22.title: Review-process labels left in code and tests
A-22.impact: The comments describe a past review process rather than the code.
A-22.fix: Rewrite each as a statement of the behaviour it pins.
A-22.reasoning: The mutation-run wording and the `A1`-`A7` labels are present exactly as cited.

B-01.title: Every audit append re-reads, re-parses and re-hashes the whole retained log, under the cross-process lock
B-01.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §4 "DON'T: Clone gratuitously" (scale); the writer design itself
B-01.impact: Rotation is 50 MiB and retention is 365 days (`audit.rs:35,39`), so the retained log only grows. Each audited action (login, MCP call, change) costs CPU and a transient allocation proportional to the whole retained log, and blocks every other kcc process sharing the state directory for that time. As the log grows, receipts pass `AUDIT_WAIT` and changes are reported as `audit_pending`. Once 128 entries are queued, B-04 makes callers block. On a small host the per-append allocation can reach hundreds of MB.
B-01.fix: Under the lock, read only the tail of the newest file (seek back to the last newline) to get `seq` and `hash`. Keep full verification for `verify_chain` and startup. Detect rotation by another process with file identity and size checks.
B-01.correction: The O(retained log) append under the cross-process lock is real and contradicts `SECURITY.md:315`. The latency and memory figures are unproven. The fix stays as proposed: read the tail of the newest file under the lock and keep full verification for `verify_chain` and startup.
B-01.reasoning: The mechanism is accurate. `append_locked` calls `audit_files` and then `verify_files`, which parses, hashes and collects every retained entry into a `Vec`, only to use `.last()`. It runs inside `spawn_blocking` while `writer_task` holds the `StateLock` from `locked()`. Startup does the same full pass synchronously, both in `kcc serve` and in every CLI run (`context.rs:294`). `SECURITY.md:315` says appends "re-read its tail", but the code re-reads everything, so the docs promise the cheap design. Pruning only removes complete rotated files older than 365 days, so the cost per append grows with a year of log. "High" depends on inferred figures, though. Reads are not audited: only logins, changes and refusals/failures are (`kcc-mcp/src/support/audit.rs`). Hitting `AUDIT_WAIT` (30 s) per append would take a very large log. The demonstrated consequence is a slowdown that grows over time, plus a growing pause for other processes, not a broken main flow. One aggravating factor: per `SECURITY.md:303`, refusals are audited per call with no MCP rate limit, so a low-privilege key can grow the log on purpose.

B-02.title: The conflict check needs both checksum and agent to differ, so a change by any other RCI client goes unnoticed
B-02.rule: project change-workflow invariant ("refuses if someone else changed the router in between")
B-02.impact: Any other HTTP RCI client produces the same agent as kcc: another kcc install, a script, or (INFERRED) the router's own web UI, which also talks RCI. If such a client changes the router between kcc's read and its write, the checksum differs but the agent matches, so no `Conflict` is raised and kcc writes over a configuration it never read. The same gap applies between writes inside a change set.
B-02.fix: Compare `checksum` alone against kcc's own last observed state, which already tracks kcc's own writes. If kcc's own changes from other sets must be allowed, compare `(agent, user)` against kcc's login rather than agent alone.
B-02.correction: This is a plan-mandated rule that does not deliver the README/ARCHITECTURE promise ("refuses if someone else changed the router"). In `check_conflict`, the agent clause protects nothing from kcc's own writes, so use checksum only, as `ensure_unchanged` already does. Separately, the "since the actor's last read" check is unused (see NEW-1).
B-02.reasoning: The "both differ" rule is intended, not a typo. Plan step (3) at `.omo/plans/keenetic-control-center.md:433` says "if it changed since the actor's last read **by a different agent**, return `Conflict`". The save/commit wording there is "another agent changed". The code knows about the gap: `ensure_unchanged` (`workflow.rs:854`, "including the same agent") does a checksum-only check, but only the migration finish (`finish.rs:34,63`) uses it. No test or comment states a firmware reason for tolerating same-agent changes. The only test invents `"another-agent"`, and the fake reports `http/rci` for every writer. The impact needs correcting in two ways. First, every production `begin` passes `last_read = None` (`kcc-web/src/save.rs:64`, `page_kit/change.rs:405`, `system_pages/component_commit.rs:83`, `kcc-mcp/src/support/access.rs:113`, `kcc/src/cli/change.rs:220`, `cli/dom_jobs.rs:223`), so the begin-time check at `:692-700` never runs in production. Second, the live gap is `check_conflict` (`:1341`). Inside a set, `expected` is re-read after each of kcc's own writes (`:997,1076,1141`), and the cross-process lease keeps out other kcc writers. So the agent clause can only excuse a non-kcc client that reports the same agent. The window is short (baseline to write, or between writes), and kcc sends individual CLI commands rather than replacing the whole config, so "writes over a configuration it never read" overstates it.

B-03.title: A torn last audit line (crash or full disk mid-append) stops `kcc serve` from starting and kills the writer
B-03.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §2 error handling at a persistence boundary
B-03.impact: A power loss or a partial `write_all` on ENOSPC leaves half a JSON line. The writer stops (any non-lock error is fatal), and every later `kcc serve` start and every audited CLI command fails until someone edits `audit.jsonl` by hand. A partial write is crash damage, not tampering, yet it is treated the same way.
B-03.fix: On open, if the last line has no trailing `\n`, truncate the file back to the last newline and log it (an incomplete line has no hash to protect). Treat only complete lines that fail verification as tampering.
B-03.reasoning: `BufReader::lines()` returns a final unterminated fragment as a line. `serde_json::from_str` then fails, and `verify_files` returns `AuditError::Json`. That one path is used by `spawn_with_policy` (serve startup and every CLI services build) and by every `append_locked`, in every process sharing the state directory. A partial `write_all` (ENOSPC) or a crash before the data reaches disk can leave such a fragment. `SECURITY.md:325-327` says log I/O failures end the writer "so its supervisor can restart it". The restart then fails in the same check, so it loops until someone edits `audit.jsonl` by hand. I found no truncation or repair path (no `truncate`/repair in the audit code or CLI). Ending the writer on I/O failure is documented design. Never recovering from crash damage is not.

B-04.title: "Bounded" audit waits block without limit once the 128-slot queue is full, including inside a safety bracket
B-04.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §5 cancellation/timeouts; the receipt invariants in `audit/receipt.rs:1-13` and `workflow_receipts.rs:8-10`
B-04.impact:
The writer keeps retrying while another process holds the append lock (`writer.rs:85-104`), for example a stalled process or a slow append from B-01. Once 128 entries are queued, every `submit` waits indefinitely:
  - a bracket's `apply` never reaches its disarm, and shutdown waits on the open bracket;
  - Web sign-ins hang despite their 5 s bound.
  
  The module docs promise the opposite.
B-04.fix: Put the reserve under the caller's limit, e.g. `timeout(limit, sender.reserve())`. For deferred receipts, use an unbounded queue or `try_reserve` and return a `Pending` that reports "not queued".
B-04.reasoning: `submit` awaits `self.sender.reserve()` with no bound. Capacity is 128, and `locked()` retries forever while another process holds the append lock. Once the channel is full, every `submit` waits without limit. That includes `Receipts::record` in deferred mode, inside the bracket's arm, work and disarm, so the disarm can be delayed until the router's own timer fires. It also includes `audit_login`, whose `LOGIN_AUDIT_WAIT` only starts after `submit` returns, and failed-login `append`. `SECURITY.md:332` ("Callers wait for their entry a bounded time") and ARCHITECTURE ("another process holding the audit append lock cannot delay the disarm") both promise the opposite. Reaching the state needs a long-held lock in another process, such as a stopped or stalled CLI, or slow appends (B-01). That is uncommon but realistic.

B-05.title: Login runs Argon2 and rewrites `users.json` with fsync under the exclusive cross-process lock, on every attempt
B-05.impact: An unauthenticated client sending login attempts with random usernames forces, per attempt, one Argon2id run (19 MiB, t=2) plus one durable rewrite, all serialized behind one cross-process lock. Real logins, password changes, account administration and `has_admin` writers queue behind them, and the Web `spawn_blocking` pool fills with threads parked on `flock`.
B-05.fix: Read the document without the lock, run Argon2 outside it, then take `update` only when the failure counters or lockout actually change. Give `update` a "no change, skip write" result.
B-05.correction: Remove `has_admin` from the impact. Fix: skip the write when nothing changed, and move Argon2 out of the file lock but behind a small semaphore.
B-05.reasoning: `authenticate` runs inside `StateStore::update`. That takes the blocking `users.json` flock, runs Argon2 (the dummy verify for unknown users, the real verify otherwise), and always calls `write_locked`: temp file, fsync, rename, directory sync. It does this even when nothing changed, and even when the closure returns `Err` (for example `DuplicateAccount` in `create`). I found no rate limit on `POST /ui/login`. The result is that unauthenticated attempts serialize every account operation behind one lock and one fsync each. One correction: `has_admin` uses `state.read` and takes no lock (`accounts.rs:429-437`), so it does not queue. The proposed fix also needs a caveat. Running Argon2 outside the lock with no other bound would allow parallel 19 MiB derivations, which is a worse memory DoS. Keep a concurrency bound.

B-06.title: With a read-only login, the poller opens a new router session every round
B-06.impact: Every 15 s light round, plus a second time on each heavy round, a new `RciClient` and session is created and signs in again. On ndw4 routers that means an Argon2 derivation each time, which BACKLOG says is serialized one at a time. Router sessions also churn (INFERRED: sessions accumulate until they time out). The shared-client design is bypassed exactly for the profiles that set up a dedicated polling login.
B-06.fix: Cache the read-only client per router beside `clients`, and invalidate it on the same profile changes.
B-06.reasoning: When `read_login` is set, `poll_client` builds a new `RciClient` on every call. `connect_with` creates a new session with no cookie, and sessions are "reactive" (`kcc-rci/src/session.rs:1`), so the first request signs in again. That happens on every light round (`fetch`) and again on each heavy round (`fetch_heavy`, via `poll_info`). `begin_with_client` (`workflow.rs:704`) also calls `poll_info`, so each change set opens one more read-only session. On ndw4 every sign-in costs a serialized Argon2 derivation (`BACKLOG.md:62`).

B-07.title: Blocking file I/O and blocking `flock` waits run directly on Tokio workers
B-07.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §5 "DON'T: Call blocking I/O in async functions" (line 1112)
B-07.impact: When the CLI or another process holds a backup, routers or job lock, a Tokio worker is parked inside `flock()`. With only a few workers, a handful of waiting writes freezes all of the async server's Web, MCP and poller work. Slow DNS for one router stalls `client()` for every router.
B-07.fix: Wrap these synchronous store calls in `spawn_blocking`, as `kcc-web` already does for accounts. Release `clients` before connecting, then insert with a re-check.
B-07.correction: This is a guideline violation with small, bounded stalls. Keep the fix (`spawn_blocking` for the store calls, and connect outside the `clients` lock).
B-07.reasoning: The calls are real. Blocking `flock`, fsync and rename run directly in async functions, which breaks §5 "DON'T: Call blocking I/O in async functions". `client()` holds the Tokio `clients` mutex across `connect_client(...).await`, and per the engine's own comment that includes synchronous DNS resolution. However, every cited flock guards a short critical section: a backup seal and write, a `routers.json` update, a job record write. The claim that a handful of waiting writes freezes all async work assumes long holds that nothing shown here produces. The DNS stall only affects hostname URLs.

B-08.title: `CliCommand` does not tie the line it sends to the request it validated
B-08.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §3 "DO: Force construction through validated constructors" (line 424); project rule (b)
B-08.impact: The type called `validated` guarantees nothing about the bytes sent to the router. About 35 production call sites (`kcc-domain/**`, `kcc-migrate/**`, `kcc-web`, `kcc-mcp`) build lines with `format!` next to a separately validated value. Any drift between the two, such as a wrong interface name or a different argument, reaches the router unvalidated, and the audit target still shows the validated path.
B-08.fix: Render the line from the `ValidatedRequest` (or check it against the request's synopsis, as `from_template` already does with `validate_grammar`), and make `new` crate-private or fallible.
B-08.reasoning: The type weakness is real. `CliCommand::new` and `::secret` accept any line next to an unrelated `ValidatedRequest`, and replay validates only the request (the test pairs `Bridge9` with a validation that never saw it). But project rule (b) covers raw input, and every raw path builds the request from the line itself: MCP `validate_cli(&input.line)`, Web `validate_cli`, and the migrate `build` either tokenizes the line or runs `validate_cli` on it. That leaves about 40 domain sites that build the line with `format!` from values validated separately. No drift is shown. So this is a missing type-level guarantee with a hypothetical cost, not a demonstrated rule (b) bypass. The count is about 44 `::new`/`::secret` sites including the raw ones, not 35.

B-09.title: Every job leaves two lock files in the state root forever
B-09.impact: Two files per job (diagnostics, migrations, presets and so on) build up in the state root without limit. Every `read_dir` of that root walks them, including `backup_before_migration` (`persist.rs:348`), audit `rotated_files` and job paths.
B-09.fix: Drop the per-record lock (ownership already serializes writers) and remove the `job-owner-*.lock` file when pruning the finished record.
B-09.reasoning: Confirmed. `persist` creates `<state>/job-<id>.lock` and ownership creates `job-owner-<id>.lock`. `prune_finished` deletes only `jobs/<id>.json`, and no code removes the lock files. The consequence is zero-byte files that accumulate at the rate operators start jobs. The `read_dir` cost they add to the state root is real but marginal, so this is minor quality, not medium.

B-10.title: A failed final write of a job record is dropped silently, and the next start reports a false interruption
B-10.impact: If the final status write fails (disk full, I/O error), nothing is logged and the record stays `Running`. On the next start, `recover` marks it `Interrupted`, probes the router and writes a `job.recovered` audit entry for a job that actually completed or failed.
B-10.fix: Log the error with `job_error_kind` at minimum.
B-10.reasoning: `drop(owner.persist(&record))` discards the final-write error with no log. The record stays `Running`. The next start's `recover` sees no live owner, marks it `Interrupted`, probes the router and appends `job.recovered`, all for a job that actually finished.

B-11.title: Module-wide `#![expect]` blankets with "the plan mandates" reasons hide wildcard arms
B-11.rule: AGENTS.md "No `#[allow]` … `#[expect]` on the narrowest item"; BRIEF item 4 (review-process labels)
B-11.impact: New wildcard arms, bare arithmetic or string slicing anywhere in these modules pass lint silently. The reason text refers to a planning document, not to the code.
B-11.fix: Move each `expect` onto the item that needs it, with a code-level reason, and drop `wildcard_enum_match_arm` from the module level.
B-11.reasoning: The guideline asks for `#[expect]` "on the narrowest item" (`RUST_GUIDELINES.md:1650`; overlay `:101`). The profile's own list of module-level exceptions covers only `pub_use` facades and `float_arithmetic` (`:2087-2100`). `workflow.rs` expects `wildcard_enum_match_arm` and `arithmetic_side_effects` for the whole module, which hides `_ =>` at `:1301` and `other =>` at `:1477`. Note that this is repo-wide: 156 files carry a module-level `#![expect]`. Other lanes probably report the same class.

B-12.title: `WorkflowError::InvalidResponse` reports "invalid last-change response" for unrelated failures
B-12.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §2; error text must be accurate
B-12.impact: An unsupported firmware (no catalog) or an undecodable backup tells the operator that `show last-change` was invalid, which sends troubleshooting in the wrong direction.
B-12.reasoning: One variant whose text reads "invalid last-change response" covers a missing catalog, a non-UTF-8 config, an unexpected body kind, a running-config parse failure and an `RciPath` build failure. The Web shows a generic localized "failed" and logs the misleading `Display` (`failure.rs:53`). The CLI maps all of these to `Exit::Router`. So the wrong text reaches logs and the exit class, not the page text.

B-13.title: Router-profile and router-id validation is duplicated and has drifted
B-13.impact: `Config::validate` accepts `url = "http://r/x"`, and the failure appears later from `RouterRegistry::new` with a different message. The field doc misstates the accepted ids.
B-13.fix: Have `RouterProfile::validate` call one shared profile validator, use `is_valid_router_id` everywhere, and fix the doc.
B-13.correction: Drop the auth/token_file claim. Keep the URL-shape gap, the doc mismatch and the duplicated id rule.
B-13.reasoning: Confirmed: there are duplicate validators. Only the registry checks host, path, query and fragment, so `Config::validate` accepts `http://r/x`, and the failure only shows later from `RouterRegistry::new` with a different message. The doc at `:645` (`[A-Za-z0-9._-]`, 1..=64) contradicts the enforced `is_valid_router_id` (1-32, `[a-z0-9-]`).
