F-01.title: Revoking a key or disabling a user from the CLI does not reach a running `kcc serve`
F-01.rule: project rule (d) intent / overlay mcp-servers.md (revocation of credentials); none of the vendored rules names it directly
F-01.impact: An operator runs `kcc apikey revoke leaked-agent` or `kcc user disable mallory` and gets "deleted"/"disabled" with exit 0. The running server keeps accepting the key until a SIGHUP or restart. Mallory's live Web sessions stay valid until their idle or absolute timeout, and a SIGHUP does not end them either. The README limitation mentions only `apikey create`.
F-01.fix: Make the SIGHUP reload also drop sessions of disabled or reset accounts. Have the CLI print a localized "takes effect after SIGHUP or restart" note after revoke, disable and reset. Longer term, have the server re-check the key and the account against state on each request.
F-01.reasoning: The kit keeps the keys in an in-memory `ArcSwap`. They are installed once at `server.rs:136` and swapped only by `TransportReload::install_keys`, which runs on a Web key create or revoke (it re-reads `api_keys.json`) or on a SIGHUP (`reload()` at `server.rs:583-598`). Nothing checks a key against state on each request. `record_key_use` even gets `persist() == false` for a deleted key and ignores it (`Ok(Ok(_known))`). A Web session is an in-memory record. `authentication_middleware` re-reads only the role's live definition, never `disabled`. `reload()` does not touch sessions, so after a CLI `user disable` or an admin `passwd` reset the sessions last until their idle or absolute timeout, even across a SIGHUP. That contradicts SECURITY.md:106-107 ("a password or role change ends the account's other sessions"). The README limitation mentions only `apikey create`. The Web paths do the extra steps the CLI skips; the reviewer's `:495` is the delete path, while disable is the `signs_out` branch at `:560`.

F-02.title: `router edit` seals the new credential before the profile is validated
F-02.impact: `kcc router edit home --url http://192.168.1.10/ui --new-password --password-file new.pw` exits 4 ("url must be an http(s) origin"). The unchanged `home` profile now signs in with `new.pw`'s password, and the old sealed password is gone; the README invites users to delete their input files. The doc comment "a refused change writes nothing" (`router_secrets.rs:102`) is false. Unlike `add` (`:49`), `edit` also skips `outbound::check` for a new URL.
F-02.fix: Call `profile.validate()` (plus `outbound::check` when the endpoint moves) before `seal`. Alternatively, seal to a temporary record and rename it only after `update` succeeds.
F-02.reasoning: `parse_url` is plain `Url::parse`, so `http://h/ui` passes `plan()`. `seal()` overwrites the deterministic sealed path, and then `registry.update` → `profile.validate()` refuses "url must be an http(s) origin". The stored profile keeps its old URL but now resolves the new sealed password, and the old one is gone. The doc comment "a refused change writes nothing" is false. `edit` also skips `outbound::check`. The connection-time check still enforces the policy, but SECURITY.md says it is "checked before a router profile is stored", which `update` does not do.

F-03.title: Session cookie loses `Secure` and `__Host-` in the HTTPS-proxy deployment
F-03.rule: project rule (e) "Web UI hardening"; overlay http-services.md
F-03.impact: In the documented setup (https `public_url` behind a trusted TLS proxy), browsers see HTTPS but get a `kcc_session` cookie without `Secure`. Any plain-HTTP request to that host, such as a proxy's http→https redirect or a forced request from a LAN attacker, sends the session cookie in cleartext.
F-03.fix: Pick `CookieSecurity::Tls` when `tls || public_url.scheme() == "https"`, and pass the same flag to `security_headers`.
F-03.reasoning: The cookie mode depends only on listener TLS. Validation accepts a non-loopback plain listener when `public_url` is https and `trusted_proxies` is set, and then the cookie is `kcc_session` without `Secure`. SECURITY.md says "on TLS listeners `Secure`", so it is literally consistent, but the `LoopbackHttp` doc ("the listener is loopback-only") is false in this mode. Browsers will send the cookie to `http://<same host>`, so an active LAN attacker can provoke a cleartext request and take the session. HSTS at the proxy would mitigate it; kcc does not ensure that.

F-04.title: `kcc show running-config` hands out secrets with only `Read`
F-04.rule: project rule (d) "Secrets … never reach … tool results"; README "revealing a secret needs the RevealSecrets permission"
F-04.impact: A CLI principal limited to `Read` (for example a scoped `[cli] role`) gets the full running configuration, with whatever registered secrets it carries. The same principal is refused `backup get --output`.
F-04.fix: Pass `show running-config` and `show startup-config` text through `redact::redacted_copy`, and mask JSON answers the way the Web viewer does, unless the role grants `RevealSecrets`.
F-04.correction: This is a contract inconsistency on the CLI, not a privilege escalation. The real exposure is in MCP (see the first NEW item in the Summary).
F-04.reasoning: The code does print `show running-config` unmasked with only `Read`, and NS3 is key-less reversible scrambling (`ns3::decode`), so the output holds real secrets. That contradicts the README rule that revealing a secret needs `RevealSecrets`, which the CLI itself enforces for `backup get --output`. But the CLI is not a security boundary for whoever runs it. `Ctx::services` loads the master key, so the caller can open every sealed router credential, and `--config` lets the caller pick a `kcc.toml` with any `[cli] role`. Also, `rci get` requires `RawRci` plus `Read`, not just `Read`.

F-05.title: `kcc mcp stdio` has no signal handling, so a signal skips the bracket wait, job drain and audit flush
F-05.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §5 "Audit Drop impls of async resources"; BACKLOG "Known gaps" (CLI SIGINT) claims stdio waits
F-05.impact: An MCP client that stops its child with SIGTERM (or a Ctrl-C) during a management change kills the process at once. The disarm is never sent, so the router's timer rolls back an applied change later. Queued audit entries are lost and jobs are not drained. BACKLOG line 43 ("kcc mcp stdio do[es] wait for open brackets") holds only when stdin reaches EOF.
F-05.fix: Wrap `serve_stdio` in a `select!` with `tokio::signal::ctrl_c()` and a SIGTERM stream, then fall through to the existing wait, drain and flush.
F-05.reasoning: `serve_stdio` awaits only `service.waiting()`. The kit's ctrl_c/SIGTERM handling exists only on the HTTP path (`:4551`), and kcc installs no handler anywhere except SIGHUP inside the HTTP reload callback. With the default disposition, SIGTERM or SIGINT kills `kcc mcp stdio` at once. That skips `wait_for_brackets`, the job drain and `flush_audit`. The MCP stdio shutdown sequence (close stdin, then SIGTERM after a client-chosen timeout) can hit this during the 10 s bracket grace, and Ctrl-C hits it directly. BACKLOG:32/43's "stdio waits for brackets" holds only on stdin EOF. The router timer still rolls back, which is the safe direction, so the loss is the change plus its queued audit entries. The cited §5 "Audit Drop impls" rule is a loose fit.

F-06.title: CLI `apikey create` and `user add` skip the role-dominance check the Web enforces
F-06.rule: project rule "same permission checks on every surface" (README "Permissions"); duplication
F-06.impact: With a custom `[cli] role` holding `ManageUsers` but not `Destructive` or `RevealSecrets`, or one scoped to some routers, `kcc apikey create x --role admin` mints an unscoped admin key and `kcc user add` an admin account. Revoke also lacks the Web's `manages` check. The default CLI role is `admin`, so only custom configurations are exposed.
F-06.fix: Move `dominates` into `kcc_app::api_keys::create_api_key` and `AccountStore::create` (taking the actor's role), or call it from the CLI before both.
F-06.correction: This is a consistency issue, not a security escalation.
F-06.reasoning: The CLI really does skip `dominates` and `manages`. Escalation is not real, though: the CLI user can read the master key, write `api_keys.json` and `roles.json`, and choose its own `--config` with `[cli] role = "admin"`. What remains is a cross-surface consistency gap against README "Permissions".

F-07.title: `backup diff` compares sets of redacted lines, so it misses real changes, and its help text says "Count"
F-07.impact: A changed password, PSK or WireGuard key becomes `<redacted>` on both sides and is invisible. A repeated line (`up`, `exit`, `shutdown`) added to one block while it exists elsewhere is also invisible. `kcc backup diff` prints nothing (exit 0) for backups that differ. The help promises a count; the command prints lines.
F-07.fix: Diff the full-text digests in order (as the Web does), print `shown[i]`, and fix the help text.
F-07.correction: Drop the claim about `up`/`exit`/`shutdown` in other blocks. The defect is invisible secret changes, plus set semantics for reordering and exact duplicates.
F-07.reasoning: Comparing redacted lines does hide a changed PSK, password or key: both sides read `... <redacted>`, so the diff prints nothing. The Web compares full-text digests instead. The help text "Count the lines" is wrong; the command prints lines. The repeated-line claim is wrong, though: `flatten` prefixes every leaf with its ancestor tokens (`interface X up` and `interface Y up` differ), so only exact duplicates within one block, or reordering, are missed.

F-08.title: The redaction pipeline exists three times
F-08.impact: A security-relevant transform maintained in three places. The copies have already drifted in how diffs use them (F-07).
F-08.fix: Move `redacted`, `mask` and `redacted_copy` (with the mark constant) into `kcc_config::secrets` and call that from all three.
F-08.reasoning: The three `redacted` + `mask` copies, and the CLI copy of `redacted_copy` with a literal `"kcc-redacted"`, are real and currently identical in behaviour. The "already drifted" claim is wrong: F-07 is a drift in the diff algorithms, not in redaction.

F-09.title: Two composition roots, and some CLI commands build them twice
F-09.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §7 / AI anti-pattern; focus item "one ChangeWorkflow per process"
F-09.impact: `kcc backup create`, `kcc backup get` and `kcc user passwd` spawn two `AuditLog` writers and two `ChangeWorkflow`s, run credential migration twice, and print the external-password-file note twice on stderr. The two roots can drift; the CLI already reports differently than the server (stderr notes versus tracing).
F-09.fix: Pass `&Services` into `backup_create`, `backup_get` and `passwd`. Extract one `kcc_app` builder used by both `Services::open` and `Ctx::services`, and load the key once with `duplicate()`.
F-09.reasoning: Every cited double `ctx.services()` and every master-key load is there. Each `services()` call spawns an `AuditLog` writer, runs `migrate_all` (a no-op the second time) and prints the external-password notes again. The outer `Services` in `backup create`/`get` is used only for `router_id`; its workflow never begins a change set, so there is no lease conflict. The concrete cost is duplicate stderr notes and wasted work, plus two near-copies of the composition root.

F-10.title: User-visible English strings outside `kcc-i18n`
F-10.rule: project rule (f) "Every user-visible string comes from kcc-i18n"
F-10.impact: `--lang ru`, `de`, `kk` and the other locales get English detail lines. `Detail::Text` is documented as typed-error text, but these are hand-written sentences.
F-10.reasoning: Every cited literal is a hand-written English sentence passed through `Failure::text` or `ServerError`, and it reaches the user. Rule (f) says "Every user-visible string comes from `kcc-i18n`".

F-11.title: `dhcp pool` defaults the default router to the first leased address and wipes options on replace
F-11.impact: `kcc dhcp pool _WEBADMIN --begin 192.168.1.33 --end 192.168.1.120` advertises 192.168.1.33 (a client) as the gateway and clears the DNS servers. The LAN loses internet on lease renewal. Read-back passes because the router applied exactly that.
F-11.fix: Make `--gateway` required (as the Web does), or default it to the pool interface's own address. Refuse to replace an existing pool without the options the user omitted.
F-11.correction: Drop "clears the DNS servers". The harmful default is the gateway, and the replace resets only lease and state.
F-11.reasoning: `--gateway` defaults to `begin`, so with the Keenetic default pool (begin .33, router .1) a client address is advertised as the gateway. The LAN loses its route on renewal, and the read-back passes. `plan_pool` emits `dns-server` only when `--dns` is given and `bind` only when `--interface` is given, so DNS servers and the binding are not cleared. Lease (86400) and enable state are reset to defaults.

F-12.title: Inconsistent confirmation gates for the same action
F-12.rule: focus item "confirmation gates on every write"
F-12.impact: The same rollback, which reboots the router into its saved configuration, needs only `--yes` on `apply`/`copy` but `--confirm-destructive <id>` on `finish`. A scripted `--yes` therefore also authorizes a rollback.
F-12.fix: When `finish == Rollback`, also run `confirm(Risk::Destructive, ...)`. Give `preset delete` a confirmation.
F-12.reasoning: The inconsistency is real: `apply --finish rollback` needs only `--yes` (Management confirm), while `finish rollback` needs `--confirm-destructive <id>`. `Destructive` permission is still required up front (`authorize_apply` with `finishing_with_rollback`). The rollback also only has to be requested explicitly with `--finish rollback`, so "a scripted `--yes` also authorizes a rollback" overstates it. `preset delete` takes the id as an argument, which is itself typed.

F-13.title: Permission refusals on local-state commands are not audited
F-13.impact: A refused attempt to export a full backup with secrets, delete a backup, or add, edit or remove a router leaves no audit entry. Router commands and the Web do audit refusals. `preset show --reveal` audits, but with a different shape (`ctx.audit(..., "forbidden")`).
F-13.fix: Route every refusal through one `Ctx::authorize_audited(services, perms, routers)` helper.
F-13.reasoning: These refusals return through `principal().authorize()?` or `require()?` with no `attempt()`. That contradicts SECURITY.md:292 ("Every change, handler-level refusal, login and secret reveal appends an entry"). Since the CLI role is not a boundary against its own OS user (see F-04 and F-06), the forensic cost is small.

F-14.title: Two parsers for `--from`, and preset sources copy the startup configuration into a plain `Vec<u8>`
F-14.rule: project rule (d) secrets in secrecy/zeroize types; duplication
F-14.impact: Full startup configurations (password hashes, PSKs, private keys) sit in non-zeroizing heap memory for every `preset capture`, `preset apply` and `copy`. Users must learn two grammars for the same option.
F-14.fix: One `--from` parser and reader returning `SecretBytes`, shared by migrate and preset.
F-14.reasoning: The preset path does copy the configuration into a plain `Vec<u8>`, and there are two `--from` grammars (bare id accepted versus `router:` required). But both paths parse into `SourceConfig { ast: Ast, .. }`, which holds the whole configuration, secrets included, as plain `String`s for the life of the plan. The extra short-lived `Vec` adds almost nothing. The `split_once`/`rsplit_once` mismatch only matters for names containing `/`.

F-15.title: Rollback results report `"unsaved": true`
F-15.impact: `kcc --json config failsafe rollback` and `migrate finish rollback` claim unsaved changes exist after the router restored its saved configuration. Scripts that save on `unsaved` will act wrongly.
F-15.fix: Use `applied(false)` for rollback, or take the flag from the closing result.
F-15.reasoning: `applied(step == Close::Rollback)` sets `"unsaved": true` exactly on rollback, `labelled` keeps it, and `run_completed` passes the document through, so the JSON reports unsaved changes after the router restored its saved configuration.

F-16.title: VPN secret writes use a fixed gate and a hard-coded `unsaved`
F-16.rule: consistency with the domain planner (compare the BACKLOG item for Web `dns_checks.rs:82`)
F-16.impact: No management detection, so there is no fail-safe timer when the tunnel carries kcc's own traffic, and `unsaved` is always true. `vpn secret ppp X` and `wan password X` reach the same router setting through two domain paths.
F-16.fix: Have `client_secrets` and `server_secrets` return a `ChangeOp` (risk from the planner) and use `Gate::of` plus `result.unsaved`.
F-16.reasoning: The domain planners themselves return a fixed `Risk::Write` and `Permission::Write`, with no management detection (`vpn_clients::secrets::plan` and `wan::plan_password`). So `Gate::of(&plan)` would give the identical gate, and the "no fail-safe timer" consequence is not caused by the CLI. A credential CLI line leaves the configuration unsaved, so `applied(true)` matches what `result.unsaved` would report. Only the code shape differs.

F-17.title: Credential misbinding through the single `KCC_PASSWORD` fallback
F-17.impact: `KCC_PASSWORD=adminpw kcc router add home --url … --read-login ro` silently seals the admin password as the read-only password, with no prompt. Polling then fails to authenticate.
F-17.fix: Use `KCC_PASSWORD` for only one secret per invocation, or refuse when two secrets need it.
F-17.reasoning: With `--read-login` and no `--read-password-file`, the read-only secret falls back to `KCC_PASSWORD`, the same value as the primary secret, with no prompt. Line 46 guards only the opposite combination.

F-18.title: `ServerError` is a stringly-typed error, and one constructor is dead with a false doc
F-18.impact: `source()` chains are lost and `kcc serve` failures cannot be classified (always exit 1). The doc comment states something untrue.
F-18.fix: Delete `unsupported_command`. Make `ServerError` an enum wrapping `#[source]` errors.
F-18.correction: Same facts, but cite error-type guidance instead of §7's String-parameter rule.
F-18.reasoning: `unsupported_command` has no caller, and its doc ("used by the binary dispatcher") is false. `ServerError(String)` drops `source()` and always maps to exit 1. The cited §7 rule ("Overreliance on `String` in APIs") is about `&str`/`impl Into<String>` parameters, not error types.

F-19.title: The privilege `Report` is discarded, so a kept bounding set is never reported
F-19.impact: On a host without `CAP_SETPCAP`, the bounding set stays full and nothing says so. The README states "drops every capability".
F-19.fix: Keep the report and log it after tracing starts, or delete `Report`.
F-19.reasoning: `Ok(Report)` is dropped, and the "returned for logging" doc is false. An unprivileged user cannot clear the bounding set, so `bounding_cleared = false` and verification skips it, silently. Permitted, effective, inheritable and ambient are verified at zero and `no_new_privs` is set, so the full bounding set cannot be used to gain anything.

F-20.title: Dispatchers have arms that return success for "unreachable" variants
F-20.impact: Moving a variant without updating the second match makes the command exit 0 having done nothing.
F-20.fix: Destructure into disjoint sub-enums, or make those arms `unreachable` through a typed split.
F-20.reasoning: The arms exist, but both matches are exhaustive with no wildcard, so a new variant forces a compile error. The hazard needs someone to deliberately reroute a variant.

F-21.title: `Family<B, W>` encodes development history
F-21.rule: AI anti-pattern (speculative abstraction; comments that describe history)
F-21.impact: Every domain is split across two or three modules and dispatch functions for no behavioral reason.
F-21.fix: Flatten each domain into one subcommand enum.
F-21.reasoning: The history-shaped names and comments are real. The split itself is partly motivated by CONTRIBUTING's ~250-line file ceiling, so "no behavioral reason" understates why it exists. This is a naming and style issue.

F-22.title: `write_private` reuses a predictable temporary file and follows symlinks
F-22.impact: `migrate plan --out /tmp/p.json` and `migrate report --out` open `/tmp/p.kcc-tmp` without `O_EXCL`, so a pre-planted file or symlink is truncated or written through (Linux `protected_symlinks` mitigates this). `a.json` and `a.html` share one temporary file.
F-22.fix: Create the temporary file with `create_new(true)` and a random suffix in the same directory.
F-22.reasoning: The temporary file is a fixed `<path>.kcc-tmp`, opened with `create(true).truncate(true)` and no `O_EXCL`/`O_NOFOLLOW`, and mode 0600 applies only on creation. A pre-planted file keeps its permissions and is renamed into place. Linux `protected_symlinks` and `protected_regular` mitigate this in `/tmp`.

F-23.title: Startup and shutdown edges in `run_serve`
F-23.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §5 "Audit Drop impls of async resources"
F-23.impact: A `systemctl reload` during startup kills `kcc serve`, because SIGHUP's default action is termination. When the transport fails, the log sinks are not flushed.
F-23.fix: Install the SIGHUP stream at the top of `run_serve`, shut the logs down before `serve_result?`, and abort `_updates` once shutdown starts.
F-23.reasoning: SIGHUP is installed only inside the reload callback, which runs after `Services::open`, `JobRunner::open` and the log start that contacts routers. Until then SIGHUP's default action kills the process. `serve_result?` returns before `logs.shutdown()`, and `_updates` lives until the function returns, so it runs through the drain.

F-24.title: `authorize_apply` restates code in comments and repeats a permission-label table
F-24.impact: Noise, plus a mapping that will drift when a permission is added (a missing one is silently dropped by `filter_map`).
F-24.fix: Delete the comments and use one shared permission-label function from `kcc-i18n` or `kcc-web`.
F-24.reasoning: The comments do restate the code. `apply_permissions` can only return Read, Migrate, Write, Save or Destructive, and all five are in the table, so nothing is dropped today; drift is hypothetical.

F-25.title: Unix-time helper copied five times; audit request ids are not unique
F-25.impact: Duplicated code, and audit entries from the same second share a request id.
F-25.fix: Use `SystemClock::unix_seconds()` and a random or sequenced request id.
F-25.reasoning: The time code is copied five times despite `SystemClock`. `cli-{timestamp}` request ids collide across invocations within the same second.

F-26.title: Duplicated CLI commands
F-26.impact: Two help entries and two code paths for one operation.
F-26.reasoning: `logging::read_log` just calls `diagnostics::read_log`, so it is one code path with two CLI spellings. `wan password` and `vpn secret ppp` are separate planners, but both are `Risk::Write`. Removing a spelling breaks CLI compatibility.

F-27.title: `--json` contract is broken for argument errors
F-27.fix: When `--json` is present in argv, wrap clap errors in the JSON envelope.
F-27.reasoning: Clap parse errors print as clap text before `--json` is known. That breaks the documented `{"error":{...}}` contract on stderr.

F-28.title: Root cause of the `-` router in confirmation messages (KNOWN-BACKLOG)
F-28.impact: Every non-interactive confirmation refusal prints `-`, not just `migrate apply`.
F-28.reasoning: The root cause is correct: `ask()` hard-codes `("router","-")` without a terminal, and `require()` uses `denied("-")`. The symptom is already the backlog item `cli-confirm-missing` (BACKLOG:51), so it is not a new finding. It only adds the root cause and wider scope.

F-29.title: Test quality: a vacuous assertion, prose pins and a review label
F-29.impact: These tests pass whatever the code does, or break on wording-only changes.
F-29.fix: Parse the JSON and compare fields, assert localized `tr(...)` strings, and drop the label.
F-29.correction: Drop `outbound.rs:62` and `serve.rs:440` from the prose-pin list.
F-29.reasoning: `emit` pretty-prints (`"applied": true`), so `!contains("\"applied\":true")` cannot fail; that assertion is vacuous. The "R-MCP2 incident" label is real. `"[outbound] allowed_networks"` and serve.rs's `allowed_networks` pin a configuration key name, a machine identifier, so they are not prose pins. `"verification"` (a negative check) and `"SHA-256"` are weak text pins.

F-30.title: Test quality: port race, copied helpers, time windows, source greps
F-30.impact: Parallel runs can collide on ports, and the 3 s window passes trivially on a slow machine.
F-30.fix: Pass `listen_port = 0` and read the bound port from the log, put shared helpers in a `tests/support` module, and wait on the drain log line instead of the window.
F-30.reasoning: A port is bound, dropped and reused, which races. `write_master_key` is copied. `exit_within(3s) == None` is a fixed-window negative check. The source guard greps `main.rs`, which is why `#[expect(clippy::absolute_paths)]` is there. None of these are in BACKLOG's "Tests" list.

F-31.title: `live_smoke` checks only the serial allowlist, not `test_device`
F-31.impact: The read-only smoke test can run against any allowlisted router. Writes are correctly gated.
F-31.fix: Require the `KCC_LIVE_TARGET_CONFIG` profile check here too, or document the exemption in the overlay.
F-31.reasoning: It checks the serial allowlist only, with no `test_device`/`KCC_LIVE_TARGET_CONFIG` check, even though its `#[ignore]` reason says "needs ... a test_device router". It is read-only.

G-01.title: Lines carrying an `ns3` secret or a WireGuard key ignore interface, port and radio mappings
G-01.rule: project rule (b), spirit (the line sent is not the reviewed mapped line) | none
G-01.impact: the operator maps `PPPoE0 → PPPoE1` or `Wireguard0 → Wireguard2`. Every line is remapped except `interface PPPoE0 authentication password ns3 …` and `interface Wireguard0 wireguard private-key …`. Those go to the source-named interface on the target, which is a wrong router command: the credential or key lands on an interface the operator did not choose, and the mapped one has none. Remapped Wi-Fi access-point PSK lines have the same problem. These lines also skip the `scalar-conflict` check, so they silently overwrite a different target secret.
G-01.fix: apply mappings inside `explicit_item` for `Copy` too. A simpler alternative is to move `remap-mapped-reference` (and `scalar-conflict`) above the two copy rules. Add a rules test for an `ns3` line plus a mapping.
G-01.reasoning: The first matching rule wins (`classify_line` loop at 412-433). `copy-wireguard-private-key` and `copy-ns3-secret` come before `remap-mapped-reference`, and `explicit_item` only calls `apply_mappings` for `Disposition::Remap` (522-536). Nothing later re-applies mappings: `retain_supported_item` only checks catalog syntax, and `execution_phases` copies `item.output` as it is. The path needs no unusual operator action. `InterfaceMap::propose` sets `target: None` when the source name collides with a target default of a different type (103-109), so a mapping is required in that case. The secret or key line then goes to the source-named interface, and the mapped interface gets none. Verification passes because `expected_lines` holds that same unmapped output. The preset planner maps the interface word on these lines (classify.rs:30-46), so the two planners do diverge. No guard elsewhere prevents this.

G-02.title: Preset capture silently overwrites any existing preset, including one outside the caller's router scope
G-02.rule: overlay mcp-servers.md "authorization per tool / least privilege" | project rule (none specific)
G-02.impact: an MCP client (possibly prompt-injected) or a Web or CLI user who has `Migrate` only on `lab-*` captures a preset named like an existing `prod` preset. The `prod` preset is destroyed (data loss) and replaced with lab-derived lines. A `prod`-scoped admin who later applies "their" preset pushes foreign configuration. Same-scope overwrites are also silent.
G-02.fix: in `capture`/`save`, refuse when `self.path(id)` exists (`create_new`), or read the existing record and require `authorize_source` on its `source_router`, the same check `delete` does.
G-02.correction: Vector: an MCP identity with `Migrate` on any router can overwrite and destroy a preset of another scope by naming its capture so the slug matches. Fix as proposed: `create_new`, or `authorize_source` on the existing record.
G-02.reasoning: `capture` checks only the new source's scope, then `save` renames over any existing `<id>.json` with no existence check and no check of the old record's `source_router`. `delete` does check that scope, and `source_scope_hides_and_refuses_saved_presets` shows the store is meant to refuse out-of-scope deletes. Overwriting is therefore an out-of-scope delete-and-replace. The finding overstates the reach. The Web path uses `fresh_id(now)` (random), so it cannot collide. The CLI uses the name as the id, but a CLI user already has the state directory. The real vector is MCP, where `slug(&input.name)` is deterministic. The attacker has to guess the victim id, because `list` hides out-of-scope presets. The replaced record then carries the attacker's `source_router`, so a prod-only admin no longer sees it rather than applying it unaware.

G-03.title: The management phase reconnects with the *new* password before that password has been sent
G-03.impact:
two cases break.
  - The kcc login `kcc` and the user `admin` both need new passwords (different realm). `user admin …` sorts first and runs first. The reconnect then authenticates as `kcc` with the new password, which is not set yet. That fails for 120 s, then `recover` waits out the timer and the result is `RolledBackByRouter`.
  - The same happens when the management IP line runs before the login's password line. The plan fails every time; the router timer protects the router.
G-03.fix: track the credential per line. Use the old credential until the login's own `user <login> password plain` line has been applied, then switch `applier.credential`.
G-03.reasoning:
Front ends set `management_password` whenever a password for the profile's login is supplied. `prepare` turns it into a single `Credentials(login, new)` for the whole run. The management phase runs in source order and is never re-sorted. After every management line, `complete_line` calls `changes.reconnect(url, applier.credential.clone())`. `retarget` then uses the new credential, and `read_last_change` authenticates with it. Nothing switches to the new credential only after the login's own password line has been applied.
  - Scenario A (verified from code): a cross-model migration (realm differs, so `user <login> password plain` is required and becomes management) that also changes the management bridge IP. The `interface Bridge0 ip address …` line runs first and reconnects to `reconnect_url` with a password the router does not have yet. That fails for 120 s, then `recover` returns `RolledBackByRouter`.
  - Scenario B: another user's `password plain` line comes before the login's line. The fake router clears every session on any password change, so a reconnect is forced, and it fails the same way.
  - Interface blocks preceding user blocks in real configs is INFERRED. Scenario B does not depend on order beyond "another user comes first".

G-04.title: Changes to kcc's own login password bypass the management safeguards (preset path, same-realm path, Mirror mode)
G-04.impact: a preset with `router-users` (or a migration with overwrite) changes the password of the account kcc uses. There is no `PasswordRequired` check, no reconnect and no credential update, and the result can be reported verified and committed. After the save, kcc can no longer log in to that router until someone runs `router edit`. In Mirror mode, the target's `user <login> …` lines that are absent from the preset are pruned the same way. INFERRED: if the firmware drops sessions on a password change, the rest of the run fails mid-way.
G-04.fix: run `is_management_line` (extended to `md5|nt` for the login user) in `convert::migration_plan` and in the planner's prune and copy paths, and require `management_password` there as `validate_credentials` does.
G-04.correction: The demonstrated consequence is that a `router-users` preset (or a migration that overwrites a same-realm hash) touching kcc's own login always fails and is rolled back by the timer. There is no password check and no clear refusal. Lockout after save is only possible if the firmware keeps sessions (unverified). The fix stands: classify the login's password lines (`plain|md5|nt`, including `no` forms) as management in `convert::migration_plan` and in the planner, or refuse them.
G-04.reasoning:
The mechanism is real. Preset items, including a rewritten `user <login> password plain X` or a same-realm `user <login> password md5 H`, all go to `additive` (or to `prune` in Mirror mode), and `reconnect_url` is `None`. `validate_credentials` only scans `phases.management`, which is empty here. `is_management_line` matches only `password plain`. So the README promise ("refuses to change the password of the router account it logs in with") does not hold for presets, or for migrations that overwrite a same-realm hash.
- The impact as written is wrong. The repo models firmware ending every session on a password change (fake router `sessions.clear()`, and the comment in `kcc-domain/tests/users.rs:78`). The next read-back or keep-alive then re-authenticates with the old stored credential and fails. A non-management line takes `complete_line`'s `ReadBack => finish::recover` path, and the router timer restores the old password. The run therefore cannot reach "verified" and cannot be committed. A lockout happens only if the firmware keeps sessions, which the repo itself says real routers do not.

G-05.title: Finish failures report "timer not armed" while the timer is still armed
G-05.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES §2 error handling (typed error must carry the right fact)
G-05.impact: the operator clicks Keep. A transient `detect()` failure or a concurrent change makes the UI, CLI or MCP report a plain failure with the timer off, while the router timer is still armed. The router then rolls back the changes the operator believed were kept.
G-05.fix: map every pre-close failure in `commit`, `keep_unsaved` and `rollback` (including `ensure_unchanged`) to an armed variant: `FinishFailed`, or a new `Drift`-with-armed fate.
G-05.correction: `Drift` comes from `commit` and `keep_unsaved`, not from `rollback`. The harmful cases are commit and keep; rollback's misreport is cosmetic.
G-05.reasoning: `ensure_unchanged` maps to `Drift` in both `commit` and `keep_unsaved`, and `keep_unsaved`/`rollback` use `context(applier).await?`, which gives `Unreachable` or `Validation`. All of these have `fate() == None` while the timer is still armed, so the Web and CLI audit `fail_safe_armed: false`. The CLI one-shot `commit` that fails with `Drift` prints "plan again" and exits, while the router later rolls the run back. In the Web path the applier stays in its slot, so the operator can retry, which softens the impact. In `rollback`, a wrong "not armed" report is harmless because the timer does what the user asked.

G-06.title: Verification always fails without WAN Internet or without `Bridge0`; the management interface is guessed as "first bridge"
G-06.impact: pre-staging a replacement router on the bench (no uplink), the typical migration flow, can never reach `verified`. Commit and Keep are refused, and only rollback remains. A router managed through `Bridge1` gets its management-IP change classified as additive (no reconnect), and verification still checks `Bridge0`.
G-06.fix: make the Internet check informational or an explicit option. Derive the management interface from the interface carrying the management URL's address, and check that interface's link.
G-06.reasoning: `health` hard-requires `internet == true` and `/Bridge0/link == "up"`, and there is no option to skip it. A bench target with no uplink can never set `verified`, so commit and keep are refused (`Verification`). The management interface is the first `Bridge` in the inventory list. This is not documented as a requirement anywhere.

G-07.title: Prunes run before the management phase and are never classified as management
G-07.impact: the source changes the LAN IP. The operator (or the Web residual list) prunes the old `interface Bridge0 ip address 192.168.1.1 …`, which is a residual target line. It runs before the new IP is set, so kcc cuts itself off. The next submit fails with `Workflow` (fate `None`, see G-05) instead of recovering, and the router rolls back later.
G-07.fix: classify prune lines with `is_management_line` (including `no` forms) and refuse them, or move them into the management phase after the replacement line.
G-07.reasoning: The operator-prune path is unreachable. `Choices.prune_lines` is written nowhere outside the planner. `Choices` is not `Deserialize`, and no Web, CLI or MCP code sets the field, so "the operator (or the Web residual list) prunes the old Bridge0 IP" cannot happen. The only reachable prunes are preset Mirror removals, and no settings group includes `interface * ip address`, `ip http port|ssl` or the management security level. The one dangerous Mirror prune, `user **` lines, is already covered by G-04. The plumbing is latent public API with no live consequence.

G-08.title: Log-sink transport errors are not retried; the batch is dropped as "permanent"
G-08.impact: any Loki or Elasticsearch restart, connection reset or DNS blip permanently loses up to 1,000 records per batch. The retry and backoff machinery covers only HTTP 429 and 5xx.
G-08.reasoning: `Transport` and `BulkError::Delivery(_)` are not retriable, so the batch goes to `dropped(...,"permanent")`. This contradicts the doc claim "Delivery is at-least-once while kcc runs" (MONITORING.md:112). Up to 1,000 records are lost per connection reset or sink restart.

G-09.title: No HTTP timeout and unbounded retries: a stuck sink stalls the worker, and shutdown aborts records without counting them
G-09.rule: overlay http-services.md "timeouts on every outbound call"
G-09.impact: a sink that accepts the TCP connection but never answers, or keeps answering 503, blocks that worker forever while the queue overflows. On shutdown the in-flight batch and the queue are aborted, and none of them reach `kcc_log_records_dropped_total`, so loss counting is incomplete.
G-09.fix: set request and connect timeouts on both clients. Select `worker.cancellation.cancelled()` against `clock.wait` and `send`. On abort, count the pending and in-flight records as `dropped{reason="shutdown"}`.
G-09.reasoning: Neither client sets a timeout. The retry loops have no attempt cap and never check cancellation. On shutdown, `abort()` drops the in-flight batch and the queue without any `log_records_dropped`. The docs claim that "records still queued at exit … are counted in `kcc_log_records_dropped_total`", which the code does not do.

G-10.title: One malformed router log record silently blocks all forwarding for that router
G-10.impact: none of the records in a failing response pass dedupe, so every poll or stream read returns the same bad record and drops the whole batch again. Forwarding for that router stops until the record leaves the router's 200-line window. Nothing is logged and no metric counts it.
G-10.fix: parse per record, skip and count the bad ones (`log_records_dropped("collector","parse")`), and keep the rest.
G-10.reasoning: `collect::<Result<…>>()?` fails the whole response on one bad id, message or prefix, and `emit` returns silently with no log line and no metric. In poll mode every snapshot returns the same 200-line window, so forwarding stops until the bad record ages out. In stream mode, if each chunk carries only new lines (INFERRED), the loss is per chunk rather than perpetual, but it is still silent.

G-11.title: Router-local log timestamps are stamped as UTC
G-11.impact: for a router at UTC+3, every record is sent 3 h in the future (INFERRED: Loki then rejects these as "too far in the future", and Elasticsearch stores the wrong `@timestamp`). Year inference near midnight on New Year's is also off by the offset.
G-11.fix: obtain the router's UTC offset (for example from `show clock date`) per collector and pass it to `parse_records`. Otherwise label the field "naive local time" and do not claim UTC.
G-11.reasoning: Production always passes a `+00:00` "now", so bracket times (router-local wall clock) are stamped as UTC. For a router at UTC+3, records are 3 h in the future. Loki's future-timestamp rejection (INFERRED) would then answer 400, and per G-08 that is a permanent drop. The test uses a +03:00 "now" that production never supplies.

G-12.title: Log-collector shutdown waits out uncancellable sleeps, one router after another
G-12.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES §5 "Use `tokio::select!` for cancellation" (1136); KNOWN-BACKLOG (likely the cause of BACKLOG "Known gaps": exit about 4.4 s after "jobs drained")
G-12.impact: `kcc serve` (`crates/kcc/src/server.rs:213`) takes up to about 5 s × routers to shut down in stream mode, and up to 30 s × routers in poll mode or after the stream falls back to polling.
G-12.fix: wrap each sleep in `select!` with `cancellation.cancelled()`, and cancel all collectors before awaiting them (`join_all`).
G-12.correction: Treat as the root cause of BACKLOG "Known gaps" `server.rs:203-206`, plus the per-router multiplication.
G-12.reasoning: The sleeps at service.rs:201, 226, 236 and 255 are outside `select!`, and collectors are shut down one after another after "jobs drained". The default stream mode (5 s interval) explains the BACKLOG "exit about 4.4 s after jobs drained" symptom. So this is the root cause of a known BACKLOG gap, not a new defect. The finding does add the multiplication by router count (poll mode 30 s × N, which can exceed the shipped 80 s StopTimeout and get the process SIGKILLed, losing only queued log records).

G-13.title: Batch selection re-encodes the whole batch for every record while holding the queue's std `Mutex`
G-13.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES §5 "Use `yield_now()` in CPU-bound async loops" (1183) / "DON'T hold locks …" (1147)
G-13.impact: up to about 500,000 record serializations (O(n²)) per 1,000-record batch run on a runtime worker thread. Meanwhile every relay's `push` blocks on the same std mutex and stalls its executor thread during log bursts.
G-13.fix: add each record's encoded size incrementally (plus a fixed envelope), and pop the batch under the lock but measure it outside.
G-13.reasoning: `encoded_len(&batch)` re-encodes the growing batch on every pop, under the queue's std mutex. That is about 500k record encodings per 1,000-record batch, and every relay `push` blocks on the same lock meanwhile.

G-14.title: Shipped but unused public APIs bypass the configured outbound policy and allow loopback
G-14.rule: project rule (a) "Outbound requests go only to registered router profiles that pass the router outbound policy"
G-14.impact: the first front end that wires these up contacts any private or loopback address regardless of `[outbound]`.
G-14.fix: delete `MigrationSource`, `LiveRouterProfile`, `load_source` and `from_live`. Move `InventoryClient::connect` into test support, or make it take the registry's policy-checked client.
G-14.correction: This is dead public API that would bypass the outbound policy if wired up, not a reachable bypass. The fix stands.
G-14.reasoning: The code is as described: the default policy allows RFC 1918, CGNAT and fd00::/8 plus loopback, and ignores `[outbound]`. But no production path reaches it today, so the consequence is hypothetical.

G-15.title: Migration reports contain no command text at all, and the HTML/Markdown skeleton is English-only
G-15.rule: project rule (f) "Every user-visible string comes from kcc-i18n"
G-15.impact: the Web download, CLI `migrate --report` and MCP report list every line as `<redacted> → <redacted>`, even though `ClassifiedItem.before`/`after` already hold properly secret-redacted text. Non-English users get English headings.
G-15.fix: copy `item.before`/`item.after` (already redacted by `redact` and `redact_ns3`) into `PlanItem`, and localize the template strings.
G-15.reasoning: Every item renders as `<redacted> → <redacted>`, so `report_safe_line` is dead. Preset reports have no items, and the headings and `lang="en"` are hardcoded. The docs promise "lines in replay order, with redacted reports".

G-16.title: `kcc_metrics_series_dropped_total` grows per scrape, not per event
G-16.impact: with 10 clients over the cap, two Prometheus servers scraping every 15 s add 80 per minute. `rate()` measures scrape frequency, not dropped series. Entries are never removed on `unwatch`.
G-16.fix: export the current drop count as a gauge (`kcc_metrics_series_dropped`).
G-16.reasoning: The counter adds the current overflow on every scrape, so its rate tracks scrape frequency, and entries are never removed. The "summed over scrapes" semantics are documented, but the counter is still misleading.

G-17.title: The per-client pseudonym map grows without bound and is shared across routers
G-17.rule: project rule (i) "No stored client telemetry history"
G-17.impact: every MAC ever seen, including randomized phone MACs and those of guest networks, stays in memory for the life of the process. That is an unbounded, process-lifetime client history driven by LAN input.
G-17.fix: keep pseudonyms only for MACs present in the current snapshot (rebuild each scrape), or hash the MAC with a per-process key.
G-17.correction: This is an unbounded-memory and identifier-retention issue, not a rule (i) violation. Prefer a keyed hash (HMAC with a per-process key).
G-17.reasoning: The map only grows and is shared across routers, so its memory is unbounded under randomized MACs. Rule (i) ("no **stored** client telemetry history") is misapplied: this is an in-memory MAC-to-pseudonym set with no telemetry values. Rebuilding it on every scrape, as proposed, would also break pseudonym stability.

G-18.title: `keenetic_interface_up` carries the free-text interface description as a label
G-18.impact: renaming an interface's description creates a new series and resets alert `for:` timers. Arbitrary text (which may contain personal data) becomes a label.
G-18.reasoning: The free-text `description` is a label on `keenetic_interface_up`, which causes series churn and puts arbitrary text into labels.

G-19.title: The `kcc_jobs` gauge drifts on broadcast lag
G-19.impact: if a job's terminal event is lagged, the `running` gauge stays +1 forever and the `known` entry leaks.
G-19.fix: on `Lagged`, re-read every `known` id from `jobs.get` and settle its state.
G-19.reasoning: `Lagged` is skipped without resyncing. A missed terminal event leaves the `running` gauge incremented and the `known` entry leaked.

G-20.title: Wrong or missing cancel-safety annotations
G-20.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES §5 "Annotate every async fn with cancel safety" (1188); KNOWN-BACKLOG pattern (these locations are not in the BACKLOG list)
G-20.impact: wrapping `recover` in a timeout on the strength of its comment would leave the connection half-restored.
G-20.fix: correct the `recover` comment to NOT cancel-safe and add the missing annotations.
G-20.correction: The new part is the wrong `recover` comment. The missing annotations are instances of BACKLOG:77.
G-20.reasoning: The `recover` annotation is wrong: it calls `wait_restored`, which is marked NOT cancel-safe, and it mutates `report.finished`. The missing annotations are all on non-`pub` functions. That is exactly the BACKLOG cleanup item, whose fix ("extend the check to `pub(crate)` and private functions") would catch them, even though these specific locations are not listed there.

G-21.title: Copy-paste duplication that has already drifted
G-21.impact: fixes land in one copy only. G-01 and G-04 are already examples of the two classifiers diverging.
G-21.fix: extract one helper for each and reuse it.
G-21.reasoning: All the cited duplicates exist, and the reconnect loops have different bounds. This is not the BACKLOG "two glob matchers" decision.

G-22.title: `PresetStore` duplicates a method and does blocking file and crypto I/O on async handlers
G-22.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES §5 "DON'T: Call blocking I/O in async functions" (1112)
G-22.impact: this stalls executor threads on slow disks, and one corrupt file breaks the preset list.
G-22.fix: drop one of the two methods, call the store through `spawn_blocking` (or `tokio::fs`), and skip and log bad records in `list`.
G-22.reasoning: `load_for_apply` and `get_for_apply` have identical bodies. Synchronous `std::fs` and decryption run in async handlers. One malformed in-scope record makes `list` fail with `?`.

G-23.title: The `ContinueOnNonCritical` retry path is test-only, and its Indeterminate case is not recovered
G-23.impact: this is a shipped option no front end can select, and its unknown-outcome handling differs from the main path.
G-23.fix: remove it, or wire it up and match the outcome the same way as the main loop.
G-23.reasoning: No front end can select the option. On retry, `Indeterminate` falls through to `Stopped`, while the main loop calls `recover`.

G-24.title: The Loki `level` stream label comes straight from untrusted router input
G-24.impact: a router or LAN device writing arbitrary `level` values creates unbounded Loki streams.
G-24.fix: map `level` to a fixed set (error, warning, info, debug, other).
G-24.reasoning: The stream label is lowercased firmware-supplied `level`. Only the router firmware sets that field. "A LAN device writing arbitrary `level` values" has no shown path, so the router is the only source. Stream cardinality stays bounded by what the firmware emits.

G-25.title: Test quality: real bugs above have no tests, and some test code is noise
G-25.impact: the high and medium bugs above are untested, and the noise hides that.
G-25.fix: add the four missing scenarios, use `kcc_testkit::DEFAULT_PASSWORD`, and remove the cancel-safety comments from tests.
G-25.reasoning: All cited test gaps and noise exist. The `user ` filter in the matrix also hides G-04-style password lines from verification.

W1-01.title: Disabling an account or changing its password from the CLI does not end its live Web sessions
W1-01.rule: overlay http-services (authn/authz) + RUST_GUIDELINES.md §11 Security "Auth attempts and RBAC denials" | none
W1-01.impact: An operator runs `kcc user disable mallory` (or `kcc user passwd`) to lock out a compromised account. Mallory's open browser session keeps every Web permission. An active session refreshes its 30-minute idle deadline on each request, so it lasts until the 12-hour absolute timeout.
W1-01.fix: In `authentication_middleware`, check that the account still exists and is not disabled (a cached `AccountStore` generation or mtime check is enough). Alternatively, have `AccountStore::administer` and `change_password` publish a revocation that `SessionStore` consumes.
W1-01.reasoning: `authentication_middleware` only checks that the session is in the map and that the role name still resolves. It never re-reads the account's disabled flag or password state. The CLI's `Disable` and `Passwd` only write the account store, and `invalidate_user` and `invalidate_other_user_sessions` are only called from Web handlers (`admin_users.rs:390,495,560`, `auth.rs:308`). A SIGHUP reload re-reads keys, roles and routers but no sessions. `SECURITY.md:106-107` says "a password or role change ends the account's other sessions", which is not true for CLI changes. This is not in the BACKLOG.

W1-02.title: Open SSE streams outlive logout, disable, delete and role reduction
W1-02.rule: project rule (e) Web UI hardening; focus "SSE lifetime"
W1-02.impact: An admin disables a user, removes their router scope, or the user logs out. Fleet cards, traffic, router logs and explorer job output keep streaming on the already-open connection for as long as the browser keeps it. KeepAlive keeps it open, and the 12-hour absolute timeout is never applied to it.
W1-02.fix: In `guarded`, re-check the session every N events or every keep-alive tick with `sessions().peek(id)` plus the live role, and end the stream when the session is gone. Also cap a stream at the session's absolute deadline.
W1-02.reasoning: The session is checked once, when the stream opens. `guarded` only polls the source stream, and stream routes are merged after the timeout layer (`lib.rs:490-491`), so nothing ends a fleet, traffic or log stream when the session is invalidated or reaches its absolute deadline. The logout case is weak, because logging out in the same browser navigates away and closes the EventSource. The disable, delete and role-reduction cases (`invalidate_user`, `invalidate_role`) hold fully. Job and wizard streams end on their own, so the open-ended exposure is the fleet, traffic and logs streams.

W1-03.title: Unauthenticated `GET /ui/login` grows the session map without bound
W1-03.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §10 "Validate and sanitize all external input at system boundaries"; focus "session store bounds"
W1-03.impact: A client that sends `GET /ui/login` without cookies in a loop creates one entry of roughly 250 B per request, each kept for 30 minutes. At 1,000 requests per second that is about 1.8 million entries and hundreds of MB. Every authenticated request also takes the same write lock (`get` at `session.rs:297`), and the sweeper's `retain` over millions of entries stalls them.
W1-03.fix: Cap anonymous sessions, for example a separate bounded map or LRU of about 10k entries with a short lifetime of a few minutes. Alternatively, derive the pre-login CSRF token statelessly (an HMAC over a random nonce cookie) and create the server session only at login.
W1-03.correction: Bounded at 600 sessions per minute per source IP by the kit limiter. A real flood needs many addresses. A cap on anonymous sessions is still worthwhile.
W1-03.reasoning: It is true that every cookieless `GET /ui/login` inserts an anonymous session with no cap. However, `kcc serve` sets `.with_extra_route_rate_limit(600)` (`server.rs:147`), and the kit applies it to every route of the extra router (`install_extra_router`, `transport.rs:2345-2375`), keyed by peer IP. The finding's 1,000 requests per second from one client is therefore impossible. One IP can create at most about 18,000 entries per 30-minute idle window, roughly 4.5 MB. The map only grows large with many source addresses, for example IPv6 rotation, which the kit documents as a caveat.

W1-04.title: A failed sign-in shows nothing in the browser (401 is never swapped by htmx)
W1-04.impact: Every wrong password or locked account in a real browser leaves the form unchanged, with no "Invalid username or password" message. `tests/auth.rs:189-224` checks the raw 401 body, so the suite cannot catch this.
W1-04.fix: Answer the failed login with 422, which app.js already swaps and which keeps the uniform text. Alternatively, add 401 to the app.js `beforeSwap` override.
W1-04.reasoning: The login form posts through htmx (`hx-post`, `hx-target="body"`), and a failed login answers 401. The `htmx-config` meta tag does not override `responseHandling`. app.js overrides only 422, 413 with `HX-Retarget`, and 403 with `HX-Retarget`. The responseError toast handles 403 only, and its template is rendered only when the user is signed in. A wrong password or a locked account therefore shows nothing. Sign-in itself works, so the failure feedback is broken rather than the main flow.

W1-05.title: Editing a router seals the new secrets before the profile update, with no rollback
W1-05.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §6 "`core::mem::DropGuard` for One-Off Cleanup and Rollback"
W1-05.impact: An edit changes the URL, login and password together, and `registry.update` then fails (I/O or lock error, or the role lost `ManageRouters` or its scope in between). The stored profile keeps the old URL and login but now decrypts to the new password. The poller and every write then fail to authenticate, and repeated bad logins may trip the router's own lockout (INFERRED). The read-only password breaks the same way.
W1-05.fix: Seal to the new records only after `registry.update` succeeds. Alternatively, snapshot the previous sealed bytes and restore them on any update error.
W1-05.correction: The mismatch shows immediately only for the read-only polling login. For the primary credential it shows after the cached client is evicted, which is still silent and still needs a fix. Snapshotting and restoring the previous sealed bytes is the safe fix. Sealing after the update would briefly point the profile at a record that does not exist yet.
W1-05.reasoning: The ordering is as claimed. `plan.seal` overwrites the fixed `<id>.sealed`, `<id>.token.sealed` or `<id>.read.sealed` in place before `registry.update`, and on an update error nothing restores them. `create` does roll back. `update` can fail after the seal on `PermissionDenied`, `validate()`, `ConfigDefined` (a SIGHUP adding the id), `NotFound` (a concurrent delete), or I/O. The impact timing is overstated, though. The cached primary `RciClient` keeps its in-memory credentials (`client()`, `registry.rs:626-638`), and the cache is only cleared on a successful update. So management writes keep working until the client is evicted (restart or a later profile change). Polling with a read-only login reconnects on every poll (`poll_client`, `:646-651`), so a resealed read password breaks it immediately.

W1-06.title: Connection test ignores the selected sign-in mode and never uses a typed token
W1-06.impact: (a) With Digest, NDW2 or NDW4 selected, the test signs in with Auto, so it can pass while the saved profile fails, or the reverse. (b) On the add form in token mode, a typed token always gives "password required". (c) On the edit form in token mode, the test silently checks the old stored URL and token instead of the typed values.
W1-06.fix: Set `profile.auth` from the parsed form, which needs an accessor on `Parsed`. Make `Typed` expose the primary secret of either kind, and add a `test_connection_with` variant that takes a token.
W1-06.correction: (b) On the add form in token mode, a typed token is never used. The test answers with the id-format error, or "password required" when the id is empty.
W1-06.reasoning: Point (a) is correct. `Parsed::apply` never sets `auth`, `ManagedRouterProfile::new` defaults to `RouterAuth::Auto`, and `detect_with` builds the RCI mode from `profile.auth`. So a test with a typed password always uses Auto, never Ndw2, Ndw4 or DigestProxy. Point (c) is correct: in token mode `typed.password` is filtered out, so the edit form falls back to the stored profile and ignores the typed URL and token. Point (b) is right in substance but wrong in its message. The add form has no `router` field, so when an id is typed the code hits `draft_id != editing` (`:83-87`) and shows the id-format error ("Use 1 to 32 lowercase letters..."). "Password required" appears only when the id is empty.

W1-07.title: The "account kcc signs in with" guard fails open and ignores the read-only login
W1-07.rule: RUST_GUIDELINES.md §2 "DON'T swallow errors" / §11 "Errors propagated with `?`, not swallowed"
W1-07.impact: (a) A transient registry read error during the guard, followed by a successful `action.context()`, lets kcc change the password of its own management login and lock itself out of the router. (b) Changing the password of the read-only polling account in this dialog breaks kcc's polling, with no refusal shown.
W1-07.fix: Make `profile_login` return `Result`, and refuse when the lookup fails or the router is missing. Return both `login` and `read_login`, and refuse either one in the Web check and in the domain `plan_password`.
W1-07.correction: Drop the lockout claim. The remaining issues are that `unwrap_or_default()` and `.ok().flatten()` swallow errors (§2), and that changing the read-only polling account's password is not refused.
W1-07.reasoning: (a) The fail-open path is not reachable in practice. `SET_PASSWORD.open` already calls `context::target`, which runs the same `lookup(fleet, role, router)` and refuses on `Ok(None)` or `Err`. `lookup` reads the in-memory registry (`registry.list()`), which can only fail on a poisoned lock or a `spawn_blocking` join error, and either would also have failed `open`. A router deleted between the two lookups would make `action.context()` fail. What remains of (a) is error-swallowing style. (b) is real: `read_login` is never protected. The consequence is broken polling, recovered by editing the router, not a lockout of management access.

W1-08.title: Each audit-page view and export verifies and loads the whole log
W1-08.rule: overlay http-services "Every listener... DoS bounds"; RUST_GUIDELINES.md §4 "DON'T collect into Vec just to iterate again"
W1-08.impact: With the retention-allowed history (for example a year of MCP and poller-adjacent audit entries), every page click re-hashes and allocates the whole log. The view slows down and eventually hits the 30 s `REQUEST_TIMEOUT` 408. Concurrent viewers multiply the cost.
W1-08.fix: Verify once and cache the result by file length and mtime. Format rows only for the page slice (paginate the `AuditEntry` list first). Stream the export body.
W1-08.correction: This is a real scaling inefficiency on an admin-only page, with no demonstrated timeout at plausible log sizes. Paginating before `row`, and caching the verification result by file length and mtime, are the cheap fixes.
W1-08.reasoning: The code does verify the whole chain on every page and export, maps every matching entry to an `EntryRow` before paginating, and builds the export in one `String`. The page needs `ViewAudit`, and the retention is 365 days by time with no size cap. The cost grows with history, but reaching the 30 s timeout needs a log of hundreds of MB or more, which is not shown. The "collect just to iterate again" rule is only partly relevant, because the code needs `reverse()`.

W1-09.title: Copy-pasted helpers in the admin and auth modules, and the bare 500s don't match the docs
W1-09.rule: BRIEF §4 "copy-paste duplication that drifts"; overlay http-services error responses
W1-09.impact: An htmx admin or auth action that hits a storage error gets an empty 500, which htmx does not swap and app.js does not toast. The user sees nothing, which contradicts `errors.rs`'s "localized error pages". A fix to one `manages` or cookie parser will not reach its copy.
W1-09.fix: Move `manages` and `RoleOption` into `admin_shared`. Delete the 4 `internal`s in favour of `errors::internal` with `fragment_shell`. Keep one cookie parser. Build `role_label` from `built_in_roles()`.
W1-09.reasoning: All the duplicates exist as quoted. `auth.rs`'s doc comment says "generic localized 500 response" but returns a bare `StatusCode::INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR`. An htmx 500 is not swapped (the 4xx/5xx `responseHandling` setting is not overridden), and the toast only handles 403, so the user sees nothing.

W1-10.title: Review-process labels shipped in production JavaScript
W1-10.impact: The comments point at plan items that mean nothing to a maintainer. They also look like open TODOs to grep and to tools.
W1-10.fix: Drop the `todo NN:` prefixes and keep the behavioural sentence.
W1-10.reasoning: Six `// todo NN:` plan labels ship in production JavaScript, and BRIEF §4 names exactly this pattern ("todo 37"). No such labels appear in `src/` or the templates.

W1-11.title: The permission list is hand-maintained in 3 places and silently drops unknown permissions
W1-11.impact: If a permission is added to `Permission` (`kcc-app/src/permissions.rs:17-53`), it cannot be granted in the role form. `permission_list` also omits it, so the 403 refusal fragment can say the role lacks "" (an empty list), and the roles table under-reports grants. Nothing fails at compile time.
W1-11.fix: Derive the label and field name from an exhaustive `match permission { ... }`, iterate over `Permission::ALL`, and parse the form as `Vec<(String, String)>`.
W1-11.correction: Use a unit test asserting that the `PERMISSIONS` column equals `Permission::ALL`, and parse the form generically. An exhaustive match will not give compile-time protection here.
W1-11.reasoning: The 3 hand-kept lists exist and nothing ties them to `Permission::ALL`. But `Permission` is a `#[non_exhaustive]` enum from another crate, as the profile requires for public types (§9 line 2089). So the proposed "exhaustive `match`" in kcc-web cannot fail at compile time, because a `_` arm is mandatory across crates. The cited §3 rule is about `match` arms, not tables. All 10 permissions are covered today, so the cost is only possible future drift.

W1-12.title: Wildcard arms map unknown future variants to a specific behaviour
W1-12.impact: A new `CredentialKind` (say a second token) would be sealed as the password and would clear `token_file`. A new TLS mode (for example a less strict one) would be audited and shown as "verify".
W1-12.fix: For these kcc-owned `#[non_exhaustive]` enums, handle `_` as an explicit error or a neutral value ("unknown"), not as the most privileged known variant.
W1-12.correction: Optionally route `_` to a neutral or error value in `plan.rs` and to an "unknown" audit label. Nothing goes wrong today.
W1-12.reasoning: `CredentialKind` and `RouterTls` are `#[non_exhaustive]` and defined in kcc-app, so every match in kcc-web must have a `_` arm. The `Variant | _` form is the project's way of satisfying `wildcard_enum_match_arm` while still naming the default. The wildcard itself is mandated by the profile. The only open question is which variant absorbs it, and that affects variants that do not exist yet. `RouterTls::Verify | _` in `Draft::from_profile` falls back to the stricter mode, which is the safe direction.

W1-13.title: Localization slips: sign-in error language, "UTC", "(you)"
W1-13.impact: A visitor with `kcc_lang=ru` on a server whose default locale is `en` gets a Russian login page with an English error. The timestamp's "UTC" suffix (visible until app.js runs) and the parentheses around the "you" marker are not translatable.
W1-13.fix: Use `shell.locale()` for the error. Move "UTC" and the parenthesized marker into Fluent messages.
W1-13.reasoning: `prefs::shell` negotiates the page locale from the `kcc_lang` cookie, then `Accept-Language`, then the default. The error text, however, uses `tr(state.default_locale(), ...)`, so a Russian page shows an English error. `"{} UTC"` and the `"({you})"` parentheses are built in Rust, not in Fluent messages.

W1-14.title: Kit routes lose `Cache-Control`, with no deviation recorded
W1-14.rule: overlay http-services "Set OWASP-recommended HTTP response headers on every response" (`Cache-Control: no-store, max-age=0`)
W1-14.impact: `/mcp`, `/healthz`, `/readyz`, `/version` and `/admin/status` responses carry no `Cache-Control`. The rationale lives only in a doc comment. `docs/rust-guidelines/overlays/projects/keenetic-control-center.md` lists no deviation for it.
W1-14.fix: Record it as a project deviation. Better, set `no-store` on the kit routes through the kit's if-not-present mode, if it exposes one, so only the assets differ.
W1-14.correction: Record the deviation in the project overlay, and list an upstream kit option under BACKLOG "Upstream". It cannot be fixed with a setting today.
W1-14.reasoning: `Some("")` makes the kit omit `Cache-Control` (`apply_security_header`), and only the web router adds `no-store` with `if_not_present`. Kit routes therefore send none, and the deviation is not recorded in the project overlay. The suggested kit "if-not-present mode" does not exist, because `apply_security_header` either always inserts or omits entirely. The practical cost is close to zero: POSTs, authenticated GETs, and small documents without validators.

W1-15.title: The connection test shows a server file path to the Web user
W1-15.rule: overlay http-services "DON'T: Leak internal details in error responses" (file paths)
W1-15.impact: A `ManageRouters` Web user, who may be less trusted than the host operator, learns absolute host paths of operator secret files (`kcc.toml` `password_file`) or of the state directory.
W1-15.fix: Show the chmod hint without the path to the Web user, and log the path server-side.
W1-15.correction: The path leak is only reachable for state profiles that point at an operator file outside the managed records, and only to a `ManageRouters` user.
W1-15.reasoning: The finding names `kcc.toml` `password_file` paths, but `kcc.toml` routers are refused before any test runs (`router_check.rs:93-97`, `WEB_ROUTER_CONFIG_DEFINED`). A typed-password test reads no file. `CredentialPermissions` can only come from `stored::secret`, for a state profile whose path is not its managed sealed or legacy record. That means a legacy or hand-edited `routers.json` entry, shown to a user who holds `ManageRouters`.

W1-16.title: A new API key is lost if the page refresh or render fails after creation
W1-16.impact: If the `api_keys.json` re-read fails, the admin gets an empty 500. A valid, working key now exists that nobody can see, and retrying with the same name is refused as a duplicate.
W1-16.fix: Render the plaintext dialog even when the region refresh fails (the refresh is optional), or revoke the key on that error path.
W1-16.reasoning: The key is persisted and installed (`create_api_key`, `reload_keys`) before `region()` re-reads `api_keys.json`. If that read fails, the response is an empty 500, so the plaintext key is lost. The failure is unlikely, because it is a re-read just after a successful write. The admin can recover by revoking the key and creating it again, so low is right.

W1-17.title: Deleting a role counts holders without the users/API-key locks
W1-17.impact: A concurrent `kcc apikey create x --role lab-ops` (or `kcc user add`) in another process, between the count and the write, leaves a key or account bound to a deleted role. That user then gets 500 "account role is not configured" at login, and that key's MCP authorization fails (INFERRED).
W1-17.fix: Validate the role name inside the users and API-key update closures as well, or take the 3 locks in a fixed order.
W1-17.reasoning: The holder count reads `users.json` and `api_keys.json` under the `roles.json` update lock only. `create_api_key` locks only `api_keys.json`, and the CLI's `known_role` check runs before that, outside any roles lock. Inside the Web process, `admin.lock()` serializes the two, so the race is cross-process only (CLI against Web) and the window is narrow. The consequence holds as stated and can be recovered by changing the role.

W2-01.title: Confirmation is opt-in, so management and destructive plans can run with no dialog
W2-01.rule: project rule (e) and the kit contract (`page_kit.rs:13-17`: "management changes explain the fail-safe timer, destructive ones need the router name typed")
W2-01.impact: One click on "Disable" for the access point kcc reaches the router through runs a management change under the fail-safe timer, with no warning dialog. The same happens on any page that forgets the opt-in. The typed-name rule for destructive changes is enforced only where each page remembers to ask for it.
W2-01.fix: In `carry`, always run `action.confirm(planned.risk, …)` once the planned effective risk is Management or above. Make `Resubmit` a required argument of `Submission::new`, or derive it from the request URI. Keep `Ask::First` as an extra early check, not a replacement.
W2-01.reasoning:
- `Course::new()` starts at `Ask::Never`. `carry` calls `action.confirm` only when `course.planned()` is `Some`, and `run_planned`/`plan` never look at the confirmation.
  - `wifi::plan_up(.., false)` takes its risk from `detect_management(..).risk(name)`, which is `Risk::Management` for the access point kcc reaches the router through (or for `Bridge0` when unknown).
  - The settings dialog's Disable button is a plain `hx-post` with no confirm step. Clicking it in a normal browser runs the change under the fail-safe timer with no dialog. That contradicts `stakes.rs:41` (Management means `Guard::Management`) and USER_GUIDE "Risky changes ... ask first".
  - The test at `network_pages/wifi.rs:110` posts `confirm=yes` itself, so it can't see that the dialog is missing.
  - The Wi-Fi schedule edit (`net_wifi_edit.rs:85`, which plans with `plan_schedule` and detects management) has the same gap.
  - Destructive: every current destructive web op does ask: mesh member reboot, reboot and reset (`confirming_planned`), storage (`confirming(Destructive)`), components commit (`action.confirm` at `component_commit.rs:62`). The typed-name half is therefore latent, not exploitable today.
  - The `Ask::First` replacing `Ask::Planned` gap is also latent: no caller sets both.

W2-02.title: Wizard session eviction breaks per-run mutual exclusion; any user with `Migrate` can trigger it
W2-02.impact:
An operator who holds `Migrate` sends 64 GETs to `/ui/migrate/<valid-looking-id>`, which creates 64 sessions. Another user's run is evicted while its launch is in flight:
  - A second request on that run gets a fresh session and turn, so two requests interleave on the record.
  - The `Live` lands on the orphaned session. The page then reads the apply as interrupted (`resume.rs:311`), and finish answers 409 (`finish.rs:212-214`).
  - The verified changes can't be kept, and the router's timer rolls them back.
W2-02.fix: Load and check the record's owner before calling `wizards.session(id)`, then take the turn and re-read. Evict only sessions with `Arc::strong_count(session) == 1` and `live == None`.
W2-02.correction: Evidence is at `wizard/service.rs:73-79` and `wizard/resume.rs:114`; the 409 is at `finish.rs:213-215`. The fix stands as proposed.
W2-02.reasoning:
- The mechanism is real. `Visit::open` calls `wizards.session(id)` before it loads the record or checks the owner, so any `Migrate` holder creates a session per `is_id`-shaped GET and gets a 404.
  - `Wizards::session` evicts the first session (oldest first) whose `live` is `None`. It does not check whether that session's turn is held or whether the session is still referenced.
  - `launch` holds the turn with `live == None` through `Prepared::new`, which reads the router, and calls `set_live` afterwards. The `Live` and the `settle` task then land on the orphaned `Arc<Session>`.
  - On the next request, `resume.rs:114` reads the run as interrupted, `finish` returns 409 because `session.live()` is `None`, and the run can't be kept, so the router timer rolls it back.
  - Concurrent requests on that run get a new turn, so two requests can interleave on the record.
  - Only the citations are wrong: the eviction is at `service.rs:73-79` (the file has 169 lines, not 296-301), and the "interrupted" read is `resume.rs:114` (not 311).

W2-03.title: A wizard commit or rollback that succeeded on the router is not audited if the record save fails
W2-03.rule: project audit contract ("audit of every … failure")
W2-03.impact: If the disk is full or the state directory is unwritable, the router has already committed or rolled back, the user gets a 500, and `web.migrate_commit` / `web.preset_save` is never written. The audit log hides a completed router change.
W2-03.fix: Append the audit entry before `end`, or append it on the error path of `end` too.
W2-03.correction: Only the wizard's finish summary entry is skipped when the record can't be saved; the router operations stay audited. Fix as proposed: append before `end` or on its error path.
W2-03.reasoning:
- The ordering is as described: `end()` returns `Err(500)` when `visit.save()` fails, before `audited.append(.., "done")`.
  - The claim that "the audit log hides a completed router change" is overstated. The router-level steps are audited by the change workflow itself: `router.commit`/`router.save` in `wait_saved`, the CLI rollback/reboot and the disarm through `apply_cli`'s `audit_cli`.
  - What is lost is the web-level summary entry (`web.migrate_commit` / `web.preset_save` with its finish params), not the record of the router change.

W2-04.title: A rollback the router accepted is audited as a failure
W2-04.rule: brief focus ("audit … with the right outcome")
W2-04.impact: On an extender whose reboot goes silent, the page reports the rollback as done (`MIGRATE_ROLLBACK_SAVED`). The audit log says `failed {error: router, fail_safe_armed: false}`. The forensic trail contradicts the UI. `silent_extender_*_rollback_reports_restarting` does not check the audit entry.
W2-04.fix: For `RollbackRestarting`, append the finish outcome (for example `restarting`, or `done` with the finish params) instead of a failed attempt.

  - An audit entry `failed {error: router, fail_safe_armed: false}` (no timer remains after a reboot) is consistent with that. The reboot itself is audited by the workflow's `apply_cli`.

W2-05.title: `Plan::at` drops the management bracket when the effective risk is Destructive
W2-05.impact: A curated plan that combines a management op with a destructive op runs without the fail-safe timer. The field's doc claims the opposite. No current page combines the two (INFERRED from the grep of `Planned::` callers).
W2-05.fix: Carry "contains management" separately in `Planned`, using the max-risk op set plus an OR of management. Set `Plan::at` from `risk == Management || planned.management`.
W2-05.reasoning:
- `Plan::at` sets `management = matches!(risk, Management)`. `apply` ORs back a management flag only for `RawRci` Batch, Cli and Delete changes; `Change::Request` is always `false`. A curated plan whose highest risk is `Destructive` therefore loses the bracket, contrary to the field's doc comment.

W2-06.title: The config page's backup "copy" logic is built on a false premise
W2-06.rule: §11 "no defensive checks in trusted code", plus the brief's dead/duplicated logic
W2-06.impact:
- Extra decryptions on every create and upload.
  - Backup creation is serialized across routers.
  - A 10th upload in one second is refused as `taken` although the store would keep it.
  - `--N` reason mangling, with parsing in `backup_rows.rs:361-365`.
